# CHAPTER 1: THE PEARL ERA

*"The old maps don't work anymore. None of them. We had to learn the stars all over again, one Pearl at a time, and we learned them differently. Not as places we owned. As promises we made to each other to keep*

*meeting in the dark."*

*Captain Maren Solas, Free Fleet, Vagrant Star, on the tenth anniversary of her first solo run*

Picture a ship that should not still be flying.

The hull is a quilt of three other ships that died so this one could live. The galley smells of recycled air and somebody's terrible coffee. There is a captain who is one bad week from losing the vessel, a pilot who grins when she should be afraid, an engineer who talks to the engine like it owes him money, and at least one passenger nobody fully trusts. There is a job two systems away that pays just enough to keep the lights on, and a reason, under the job, that none of them will say out loud.

That ship is yours. That crew is yours. That dark, between the stars, with the warmth of the cabin holding back the cold of a galaxy that does not care whether you make it home, is where *Veilfarers* happens.

This book is going to teach you how to live there.

## WHAT THIS GAME IS

*Veilfarers* is a space opera about a galaxy that nearly died, and the people who hold it together anyway.

It is a game of patched ships and patched lives, of crews who become closer than family, of jobs that go sideways and somehow matter more than the pay. It is adventurous and it has heart. If you have ever loved a story where a misfit crew argues its way across the stars and would still take a bullet for each other, you already understand the feeling we are going for.

You will not be a chosen one. You will not be a god. You will be a survivor with a ship, a debt, and somebody worth crossing the dark for. The galaxy is hard and the work is unglamorous, and your crew does it anyway, because the alternative is unthinkable. That is the whole spirit of the thing. The universe is cold; you are the warmth.

Everything else in this book, the rules, the ancestries, the Houses, the cosmology, exists to serve that feeling. You do not need to memorize any of it to start. You need a character, a crew, and a willingness to walk into the dark together.

## WHAT HAPPENED TO THE GALAXY

Here is everything you need to know about the past, in one breath.

A little over a hundred years ago, the galaxy was a single connected civilization. Every world could speak to every other world instantly. Ships crossed light-years in moments. Distance had been beaten. And then, in a single instant, all of it stopped. The network went silent. Faster-than-light travel turned lethal. Worlds woke up alone, lost contact with everyone they had ever known, and many of them starved. People still call it the **Great Silence**, and it killed more living things than any war in history.

What saved the survivors was an accident dredged from the bottom of an alien ocean: a small, glowing orb produced by a deep-sea creature, an orb that does something impossible. It slows time around itself. Engineered into the heart of a ship's drive, one of these **Quantum Pearls** wraps the crew in a bubble of stopped time and lets the vessel cross the stars in what feels, inside, like ninety seconds. The Pearl burns out in the crossing. Every jump costs one. No Pearls, no travel.

So the galaxy did not rebuild itself into the old seamless civilization. It rebuilt itself into a life-support system, fragile, expensive, improvised, and one bad day from failure. The Empire came later, not as a restoration of what was lost, but as a scaffold built around the new scarcity. This is the **Pearl Era**, a hundred and three years after the funeral. The lights are back on. The scars are everywhere. And the people who fly between the stars are exactly the kind of people your characters are about to be.

## A SHORT HISTORY: FROM THE SILENCE TO THE PEARL ERA

If you remember five turning points, you can hold the whole setting in your head.

**Before the Silence.** For centuries the galaxy was a single, seamless civilization: thousands of worlds bound together by instantaneous communication and faster-than-light travel that made distance almost meaningless. People of the Pearl Era look back on it the way we look at a golden age we can barely believe was real, peaceful, prosperous, casually miraculous, and, it turned out, resting on foundations no one actually understood.

**The Great Silence.** In a single instant, with no warning anyone recorded, the connective tissue of that civilization failed. Instant communication went dead. Faster-than-light travel became lethal; ships that attempted it were simply lost. Every inhabited world woke up cut off from every other, and most were not self-sufficient. The decades that followed were the worst in galactic history: famine, collapse, isolation, and the slow death of worlds that could not feed themselves. No war ever killed on this scale. What actually caused the Silence is still unknown, and remains the deepest mystery of the setting.

**The dying years.** For roughly a generation there was no galaxy, only islands: surviving worlds and stranded fleets scraping by alone, each certain it was the last. Much of what makes the Pearl Era hard, the scarcity, the patched technology, the lost knowledge, dates from these years.

**The Quantum Pearl.** Salvation came from the deep ocean of a single world: a glowing orb grown by a deep-sea creature, an orb that bends time around itself. Engineered into a starship's drive, a **Quantum Pearl** wraps a ship in a bubble of stilled time and carries it safely across the Veil in what feels, inside, like a minute and a half, and burns out in the crossing. Pearls reconnected the islands. They also made travel a consumable luxury, and whoever controlled the Pearls controlled the future.

**The Empire and the Pearl Era.** Out of that reconnection rose a new order: a galactic **Empire**, rebuilt largely by human hands, organized into six **Great Houses** beneath a long-reigning Emperor, and slowly stabilized into the uneasy peace of today. It is now a hundred and three years since the Silence. The lights are back on, the Houses hold, and an entire generation has grown up knowing the stars only as places you reach one Pearl at a time. This is the Pearl Era, and it is where you live.

## THE VEIL AND THE HOPE FREQUENCY

There is one piece of this galaxy you cannot see and cannot do without, and it shapes the dice in your hand, so it is worth a moment here.

When a ship makes a jump, it does not fly *through* normal space faster. It slips beneath it, into the **Veil**, the layer underneath reality that is everywhere at once. Time runs strangely down there, which is why crossing it was lethal after the Silence and is survivable now only inside the stilled bubble a Pearl makes. You will travel through the Veil constantly and never quite understand it. Nobody does.

Here is the strange, load-bearing fact of the Pearl Era: **the Veil notices who is inside it.** A century of measurement has confirmed what every Veil-runner suspected. Crews that fly confident and bonded reach harbor faster and smoother than crews that fly anxious and divided. The effect is small, real, and cumulative, and no one can explain it. It is called the **Hope Frequency**, the substrate's quiet response to the feelings of the people crossing it.

This is the cosmological root of the whole game. When you roll a **Hope die** and a **Fear die** (Chapter 9), you are rolling in the same register the universe itself uses. A crew that cares for one another gathers a real, if subtle, advantage; a crew that turns on itself pays for it. How you treat each other is not only a story choice. The galaxy is keeping score.

The Veil also has weather, **Veil Storms** that tear at a jump's stilled time, **Memory Wakes** that flood a crew with feelings that were never theirs, and stranger things, but those are hazards a crew meets in play. The full cosmology, where the Veil comes from and what the vanished **Precursors** had to do with it, is the deep end, and it waits in "The Galaxy in Depth" at the back of this book. You do not need it tonight.

## HOW THE GALAXY IS GOVERNED

The Pearl Era is neither anarchy nor the old seamless civilization. It is an **Empire**: a loose but real galactic order, rebuilt after the Silence and held together by six powerful dynasties called the **Great Houses**, beneath a long-reigning Emperor whose origins are the subject of endless rumor. You will meet the Houses properly in Chapter 5; here is the shape of the thing.

Humanity rebuilt and runs this order. Humans are not the most advanced people in the galaxy, nor the strongest, but they are the most established and the most numerous in the seats of power, and the head of every one of the six Great Houses is human. That dominance comes with a hard rule, learned the worst way. The early decades of resettlement saw vicious violence between some human enclaves and the other ancestries, and the Empire's founders concluded that a multi-species galaxy could not survive a repeat of it. So the Empire was built on an explicit creed: the nine ancestries are equal under Imperial law, and racial violence or discrimination is among the gravest crimes there is, hunted down and punished hard. The Pearl Era is, by deliberate design, a place where a Kryllian engineer, an Ailuran broker, and a human captain stand as colleagues, not as masters and servants.

**The six Great Houses** each dominate a slice of galactic life. In brief: **Amaranth** keeps knowledge and the long view; **Joric** are the sentinels and protectors; **Kurogane** are the transhumanist makers, forever pushing the border between flesh and machine; **Solari** are the fading Core-Worlds traditionalists and home to the formal Mystic schools; **Valerius** are the merchant princes who control the Pearl trade, and through it nearly everything; and **Volkov** are the war-makers, who hold that strength is the only truth. The Houses cooperate, compete, and feud, and most of galactic politics is the friction between them.

Not everyone bends a knee to a House. The **Free Fleet** is a loose alliance of independent ships and nomadic crews, roughly half human and fiercely self-governing, that takes the work the Houses will not and answers to no one. The **Stellar Commerce Guild** moves the cargo and brokers the deals that keep the Houses fed. The **Explorers' Guild** charts the worlds the Silence cut off. And the **Solara Compact**, a Core-Worlds coalition, dreams of restoring the old seamless civilization, distrusting the new psionics and the Houses alike. Your crew will deal with all of them, and owe favors to several.

## LIFE IN THE PEARL ERA

For most people, the grand politics matter less than the price of a Pearl. Travel between the stars is no longer a right; it is a cost, paid one burned-out Pearl at a time, and that single fact shapes everything. Worlds that sit on Pearl routes thrive; worlds that do not can be one expensive crossing away from help that never comes. House Valerius, which controls the Pearl trade, is richer than the others precisely because it controls the one thing nobody can do without. Wealth in the Pearl Era is less about luxury than about reach: who can afford to cross the dark, and how often.

The galaxy divides roughly into the **Core**, the older, richer, better-connected worlds near the heart of the Empire, and the **Rim**, a frontier of mining moons, salvage fleets, and hard settlements where Imperial law runs thin and a crew's reputation is its only protection. Between

them moves a constant traffic of ships like yours: independent crews who carry the cargo, the medicine, the news, and the people the Houses cannot or will not move themselves. In a galaxy that can no longer talk to itself instantly, those crews are the connective tissue. They are also where the nine ancestries actually mix. A House may be human-led, but a working crew is as likely to be a Kryllian, a Kryx, a Synthetic, and two humans arguing over coffee.

Knowledge itself is uneven. The Silence swallowed whole libraries of pre-collapse science, and much of the technology in daily use is salvaged, patched, or imperfectly understood, including the Pearls, which no one has learned to manufacture. To live in the Pearl Era is to keep a brighter age's machines running by hand, to make do with tools you cannot fully rebuild, and to suspect, quietly, that another Silence could come without warning, just as the first one did. That suspicion is part of why crews hold so tightly to one another. In a galaxy this fragile, the people beside you are the one thing you can be sure of.

## WHO YOU ARE

Your character is a working person in a broken galaxy. A pilot who reads paths in the chaos. An engineer who can coax life out of dead tech. A scoundrel who trades in secrets. A medic, a soldier, a scholar, a diplomat, an explorer. Whatever they are, they have lost things, gained things, and got a reason to take the first job that comes through the door.

You are also not alone out there. Humanity shares the Pearl Era with other peoples: luminous **Celestiari** who feel the emotions of a room like weather, insectile **Kryllian** engineers who build to last a thousand years, **Ethereals** who stand half a step out of phase with reality, **Ailurans** who cannot help but uncover every secret in reach, and several more besides. Your crew can be drawn from any of them. The full cast lives in Chapter 3.

One more choice shapes who you are. A rare few people, roughly one in forty thousand, are **Awakened**: they can feel the Hope Frequency directly and spend their own Hope to do things that should be impossible. Everyone else is **Sleeping**, deaf to the Frequency and running on their own hard-won skill. Sleeping characters are not lesser; they are the medic, the captain, the friend who reminds the Awakened that they used to be a person. Most crews are a mix of both. You will make this choice in Chapter 2.

## HOW IT PLAYS

The entire engine of *Veilfarers* fits in a paragraph.

When your character tries something and the outcome is in doubt, you roll two twelve-sided dice of different colors: one **Hope** die, one **Fear** die. Add them together, add a small bonus from one of your six Traits, and compare the total to a target number the Keeper sets. Meet it or beat it and you succeed. Miss it and you fail. So far this is an ordinary dice roll.

Here is the part that makes it *Veilfarers*: look at which of the two dice rolled higher. If **Hope** is higher, things break your way, you gain a little luck, a clean result, a token of Hope to spend later. If **Fear** is higher, you get what you wanted but the universe takes something back, an alarm sounds, an ally is hurt, the wrong person overhears. This is true even when you fail: a failure carried by Hope leaves you a thread to pull, a failure carried by Fear makes the situation worse. Roll the same number on both dice and you score a critical success. That is it. Every roll is a small story, never just a yes or a no.

You will learn the full procedure in Chapter 9. But you already understand the heart of it. Hope and Fear, every time, hand in hand.

## THE KIND OF NIGHTS YOU WILL HAVE

A few flavors of the stories this game is built to tell.

The crew runs medicine through a Veil storm because children three jumps away will die if the ship arrives late. A routine cargo run turns out to be carrying a person, and that person is being hunted. An engineer spends six years trying to fix a piece of pre-Silence tech that cannot be fixed, and keeps trying anyway. A captain takes a job that, by no coincidence at all, drifts within reach of the sister who vanished eleven years ago on a world the Houses swear does not exist.

These are not grim stories. They are hopeful ones, set in a hard place. The pilot dances through the storm with white knuckles and a grin. The crew is tired and underpaid and would not trade any of it. That is the music we are playing. The rest of the book just hands you the instruments.

## WHERE TO GO NEXT

You can read this book front to back, or start playing immediately. Both work.

- **To play your very first session tonight,** turn to **Appendix A: A Spark in the Dark**: ready-made characters and a complete starter adventure, no other reading required.

- **To build your own character, Chapter 2** walks you through the Awakened and Sleeping paths, then the nine ancestries (Chapter 3), the communities (Chapter 4), the six Houses (Chapter 5), and everything that turns an idea into a character sheet (Chapter 8).

- **To learn the rules in full,** Chapters 9 through 12 cover rolling, combat, recovery, and advancement.

- **To understand the galaxy you fly through,** equipment and communications (Chapter 13), wealth (Chapter 15), reputation (Chapter 16), and starships (Chapter 17) make the world concrete.

- **To go deep on the cosmology,** the Veil, the Hope Frequency, and the Precursors are explored in full in "The Galaxy in Depth" at the back.

A note on optional rules. Throughout the book you will see a gear marker. That is the **Gears framework**: everything marked with it is optional. The base game is everything *not* marked. A table that wants something lean can ignore every Gear and still have a complete, working system; a table that wants depth can switch them on.

The Pearl Era is waiting. There is a ship in a port somewhere with your name on the manifest, a crew that may not yet know one another, and a first job being argued over in a bar two parsecs away, where someone is about to have a very bad week. You are going to be the people who help. Or not. Depending on what the manifest pays.

Turn the page.

# CHAPTER 2: TWO PATHS

*"To be Awakened is to be reached for. To be Sleeping is to be reached toward. Neither comes first. Neither*

*comes second."*

*Master Vocator Hilde Tyrell, Joric Hall*

***At a glance. Your first choice is what kind of being your character is. The Awakened (about 1 in 40,000) perceive and bend the Veil; they run on Hope and Domain Powers (Chapters 6 and 18). The Sleeping are deaf to the Veil and run on themselves: Effort for everyday play and a scarce Resolve pool for signature*** *Moves (Chapter 7). Both use the same nine Classes, the same Traits, and the same Duality Roll. Neither is stronger. Pick the one that fits the character you want to play.*

This is the foundation the rest of character creation builds on, so make it deliberately. You can read Chapters 4 through 7 first and come back, but decide before you commit. (The cosmology behind the split, why some wake and most do not, lives in "The Galaxy in Depth"; you do not need it to choose.)

## THE TWO KINDS OF BEING

Most beings interact with the Veil only indirectly: they live in normal space and cross the Veil in Pearl-driven ships, never touching the substrate directly. This is the **Sleeping** state. A small fraction, roughly one in forty thousand, spread evenly across every ancestry, can perceive the substrate and, with training, act on it. This is the **Awakened** state.

Both are equally valid, equally supported, and equally effective. A Sleeping character is not a "non-Awakened" character; they are a character whose interface with the cosmos is the ordinary one, and who therefore brings a different and equally deep toolkit. The right question is never *which is better*. It is *which fits the character I want to play*.

## WHAT EACH PATH PLAYS LIKE

**Awakened.** You live with a constant low awareness of the substrate, a hum, a pulse, dreams of things that never happened to you. You can feel the emotional weather of a room (not read minds, but read the Veil's response to them), and you can spend Hope to do things ordinary physics forbids. The perception is a gift and, in crowds or wounded places, a burden. Your successes are partly joint actions with the universe; your costs are real (Hope, Stress, and the risk the substrate pushes back).

**Sleeping.** You have no substrate-access; the Veil is strange physics, not a presence. What you have instead is yourself: training, discipline, and nerve. Your competencies are not magical, they are *real*, and they do not depend on the day's emotional weather. When a Sleeping character does the impossible, it is theirs alone. This is the dignity of the path, and the post-Silence galaxy, every ship and House and library, was built mostly by Sleeping hands.

How you *feel* about your path is part of your character. Awakened may embrace, resist, or still be making peace with what they are; Sleeping may carry comparison, romanticized expectation, or a complicated relationship with an Awakened relative. A clear stance here earns richer scenes than treating the path as a mere category.

## MECHANICAL DIFFERENCES

Both paths use the same nine Classes, the same Traits, the same Duality Roll (Chapter 9), and both invoke Experiences for a flat bonus. They diverge in their engines.

**Awakened characters use:**

- **Domain Powers** (Chapters 6 and 18), drawn from the Domain Pair their Class grants.

- **Hope**, the working currency: gained on Hope-favored rolls, spent on Powers and Experience invocations.

- **Stress**, which fills with Power costs and pushes, and clears on rest.

- **Loadout**, the equipping system that rewards advance preparation.

**Sleeping characters use:**

- **Effort**, their everyday currency (the parallel to Hope): gained through play, spent on their Class's Effort Feature and reactions.

- **Resolve**, a small, scarce pool of d4 (base 2, rising by 1 at levels 3, 5, 7 and 9) spent on signature **Moves** (Chapter 7).

- **Honed Edge**, a passive that raises their damage every level, and **free Experience invocation** plus one extra Experience.

- **Recovery**, a rest-anchored practice that clears Stress. It never generates Effort; Effort comes from the Track in Chapter 7 and only from exceptions that name themselves explicitly.

Neither toolkit subsumes the other. The Awakened do things that violate normal physics; the Sleeping do things that exceed normal capacity. The abilities differ in kind, not in magnitude, and a Tier 3 character of either path has comparable decision-density in any scene.

## CHOOSING YOUR PATH

**Choose Awakened if:** you want abilities that feel cosmically significant; you enjoy resource management and preparation; you like successes that are partly the universe's doing; your concept centers on a relationship with the Veil.

**Choose Sleeping if:** you want abilities grounded in earned, human capability; you prefer competence won through training; you want successes that are yours alone; your concept centers on a craft or profession; you like being the steady hand in a crew of more dramatic crewmates.

Both paths carry any kind of story; the choice shapes the *flavor* of your actions, not their importance. **If you cannot decide, lean Sleeping**, not because it is safer (both are), but because it lets a new player focus on who their character is without also learning the Domain Powers and Loadout systems in session one. Experienced players should simply pick what resonates.

## MIXED CREWS

A typical crew mixes both, and that is the assumed default: the Awakened reach across, the Sleeping hold the line, and the most memorable scenes come from the gap between them (the Awakened does something impossible; the Sleeping has to decide what to do *next*, including who must not have seen it). All-Awakened and all-Sleeping crews both work, the latter is excellent for

grounded, espionage-flavored play, and no particular ratio is required. Let the crew be what the players want.

> **Gear, the Concealed Awakened Identity** *(Recommended Optional).* Some Awakened hide what they are, for family, House politics, or privacy. A character may take the **Concealed** tag: while Concealed, every Domain Power activation costs +1 Stress (the strain of suppressing visible substrate traces), and NPCs assume the character is Sleeping until evidence forces otherwise. Concealment can be dropped in play, often dramatically.

## A FEW COMMON QUESTIONS

- **Can a character switch paths?** Yes, through a deliberate **Awakening**: a Sleeping character discovering they could hear the Veil all along. It is a transformational arc, one of the biggest a campaign can carry, never a casual swap or an optimization lever; the guidance, including how path-specific advancement is handled, lives at the end of Chapter 7. The reverse, an Awakened going deaf to the Veil, is so rare the galaxy has no settled name for it, and the table should not assume the mechanics simply mirror.

- **Can a character be partly both?** No. The calibration is binary at the individual level. Mixed *heritage* is a backstory, not a mechanical state.

- **Can any ancestry be Awakened?** Yes, all nine, at comparable rates. Cultural attitudes vary widely (some venerate it, some are neutral, some distrust it); that detail lives in Chapters 4 and 5.

- **Do Houses exclude a path?** No. Some skew (Solari has the most Awakened per capita; Volkov the fewest on record, likely through concealment), but membership turns on family and politics, not Awakening.

## WHAT COMES NEXT

You have made the decision, or chosen to make it after reading on. Either is fine.

- **Chapter 3** introduces the nine ancestries (independent of path).

- **Chapter 5** covers the Houses, the Free Fleet, and the Explorers' Guild.

- **Chapter 6** is the Awakened Classes; **Chapter 7** is the Sleeping Classes. Read your path in full and skim the other for awareness of your crewmates.

- **Chapter 8** finishes the build for everyone: Traits, Experiences, Connections.

Make the choice deliberately. The character you build will live inside it.

# CHAPTER 3: ANCESTRIES

*"There are nine of us at this table. Nine ancestries, nine biologies, nine ways of seeing. We do not agree on what is real. We agree only that the cargo has to reach Hydros by tenday's end. That is enough."*

*Senior Liaison Velara Thessen, Inter-Species Office of the Free Fleet, opening remarks at a routine sector*

*council meeting*

This chapter introduces the nine playable **ancestries** of the post-Silence galaxy: **Ailurans, Bloomstriders, Celestiari, Ethereals, Humans, Kryllians, Kryx, Rift Spinners**, and **Synthetics**. Your character's ancestry sets their biology, their cognitive architecture, their cultural starting point, and their place in the post-Silence ecology. It does not set their character, that part is yours.

The nine ancestries are presented in alphabetical order. Equal weight is given to each. The Pearl Era's working population includes representatives of all nine, and the campaign assumes a mixed-ancestry crew is the default. A player who chooses any of the nine will find their character at home.

A note on inclusivity: the system is designed so that any ancestry can take any path (Awakened or Sleeping), any class, any role. The biological differences between ancestries are real and produce real flavor, but they do not constrain the choices a player can make at the character sheet. A Bloomstrider scout, a Synthetic mystic, an Ethereal soldier, a Kryllian diplomat, all are mechanically supported, narratively interesting, and welcome at the table.

Each ancestry profile below covers the essentials: identity, physical description, culture, place in the galaxy, **Ancestry Gifts** (the mechanical features that distinguish the ancestry at the table), and **Ancestry Complications**. The Ailuran section also includes the **Sub-Strain** mechanic, the only ancestry-internal split with mechanical weight at character creation.

**Master Ancestry Complication procedure.** At most once per character per session, after a **player-rolled Fear-dominant noncritical Roll** that materially used one of that character's Ancestry Gifts, the Keeper may spend 1 Fear and roll 1d6 on that ancestry's table. Never choose the row. Matching dice never trigger a complication, and no row selects the player's Action. Apply only numbers, resources, Conditions, durations, movement, or item effects explicitly printed in the row. If a row does not print a complete mechanical effect, its complete effect is to **mark 1 Stress** and use the row only as narration; it cannot also create an NPC, hazard, lost item, disabled device, position change, or hidden penalty.

Read all nine before deciding. Your ancestry will color every interaction your character has, with crew, with Houses, with the Veil, with strangers in spaceports, for the duration of the campaign.

## AILURAN

*"I have already been inside your ship. I have already read your cargo manifest. I have already memorized the access codes on your captain's terminal. You did not see me because I did not wish to be seen. Now, shall we negotiate, or shall I tell you what you had for breakfast?"*

*Nyx of the Locked Vault, Arbiter of the Apex Accords*

**Identity.** The Ailurans are the galaxy's newest mystery. Revealed only in the wake of the Veil Rip, the catastrophic tearing of the Stellar Veil that continues to reshape known space, they are a feline species of solitary predators, infiltrators, and information brokers whose existence was unknown to galactic civilization until months ago. They were here all along: residents of the settled galaxy, living in the margins, watching from the

shadows, and cataloging secrets in silence. The Veil Rip simply destroyed the cloaking infrastructure that kept their enclaves hidden. Now exposed, they have stepped into the light with an unnerving calm, as though they had been expecting this moment all along.

**Physical Description.** Ailurans are lean, digitigrade humanoids standing between 1.6 and 1.9 meters tall, descended from feline ancestors. Their bodies are covered in short, dense fur ranging from deep charcoal to pale silver-gray, sometimes marked with darker rosettes or tabby-like striping along the shoulders and spine. Their faces are distinctly feline, high cheekbones tapering to a narrow muzzle, wide-set eyes with vertical-slit pupils, large independently rotating ears. Four-fingered hands with retractable claws; a prehensile tail that conveys involuntary emotional signals. Their most striking feature is their eyes: Ailurans see the world in perfect grayscale, they are completely colorblind, but they perceive thermal radiation and bio-electric fields as overlapping luminous auras. To an Ailuran, the galaxy is a cathedral of gray light and living fire.

**Homeworld.** Ailurans acknowledge no homeworld, and they prefer it that way. They live in hidden enclaves rather than on any one planet, quiet warrens tucked into the margins of other people's stations, asteroid clusters, and border worlds, kept invisible until the Veil Rip stripped away their cloaking. Where they came from, whether they evolved on some lost world or have simply always lived in the cracks of galactic civilization, they will not say, and a careful listener learns that an Ailuran asked directly about origins becomes very still and changes the subject. The honest answer may be that they do not know. The likelier answer is that, like everything else, they are keeping it.

**Culture.** Ailuran society, if it can be called society, rejects every form of permanent hierarchy. There are no kings, no councils, no governments. They operate on the **Apex Accords**, a system of strict, temporary contracts negotiated between individuals. If terms are met, the contract is sacred. If terms are broken, the offender is marked, not with violence, but with silence. An Ailuran who breaks an Accord is simply never spoken to again by anyone who knows. In a species that trades exclusively in information, this is a death sentence. Disputes are settled by **Arbiters** respected individuals who have earned reputations for fairness through decades of honest dealing. Ailuran names consist of a Root (Dax, Nyx, Kel, Voss) and a Focus, an earned title based on current obsession (Nyx of the Locked Vault, Dax of the Burning Signal). The Focus changes when the obsession does. Underneath the Accords runs a single shared value the Ailurans call the economy of truth: information is the only real currency, a debt of knowledge is as binding as any contract, and a fact freely given is either a gift of enormous weight or a trap. They keep no temples and few celebrations; what they have instead is the Exchange, a neutral meeting under truce where secrets are traded face to face, and the slow accumulation of a personal reputation that can take a lifetime to build and a single broken word to lose.

**Place in the Galaxy.** Ailurans are present in every major Houses' workforce and across the Free Fleet, typically as independent contractors. House Volkov has cultivated long working relationships with Ailuran operatives, treating them as the most reliable solo agents available. House Valerius is one of the largest customers of Ailuran intelligence networks, paying premium rates for information that the Pearl trade cannot acquire by other means. The Free Fleet has a small but distinguished tradition of Ailuran captains, who run their crews with tight informational discipline and tend to retire wealthy.

**Society and Daily Life.** Day to day, Ailuran life runs on the quiet management of information and obligation. An Ailuran keeps meticulous private records, pays debts of knowledge precisely, and treats a careless word the

way others treat a spilled drink: a small, fixable embarrassment that still should not have happened. They work alone by preference and meet in neutral exchanges, a back room, a quiet dock, an agreed frequency, where secrets change hands under the protection of the Accords. Hospitality among them is real but formal: a guest is owed safety and honesty for the length of a stated visit, and nothing beyond it. To outsiders this can look cold. To an Ailuran it is simply clean.

**Relations with Other Ancestries.** Ailurans find Humans fascinating and a little pitiable, tireless producers of secrets who are catastrophically bad at keeping them. They share a wary, respectful arms race with Kryllian security engineers: one builds the vault, the other opens it, and both take it as a compliment. They feel genuine kinship with Synthetics, whose private, unreadable inner states an Ailuran finds restful, and several enclaves now host Synthetic residents. They avoid Celestiari, whose glow blinds their aura-sight, and they baffle the Kryx, whose pack instincts have no slot for a creature with no pack at all.

**Distinctive Traits and Customs.** Ailurans groom obsessively, sit through long silences without discomfort, and treat direct eye contact as a small intimacy reserved for trusted partners. Their names announce their current obsession, so a Focus that has not changed in years tells you a great deal about a person. An Awakened Ailuran is treated by other Ailurans as simply carrying one more interesting capability; the path impresses them far less than a well-kept secret does.

### ANCESTRY GIFTS

**Achromatic Aura-Sight.** Your eyes perceive thermal radiation and bio-electric fields rather than visible light. You see perfectly in total darkness out to Far range, reading the world as overlapping auras of heat and life. You can detect living creatures behind thin barriers within Close range by their thermal signature. However, you are completely colorblind, any check that relies exclusively on color identification is made at Disadvantage unless you use assistive technology. Creatures with no thermal output (certain Synthetics, Bloomstriders in dormancy) appear as cold silhouettes, visible but unreadable.

**Perfect Equilibrium.** Your digitigrade legs, prehensile tail, and predatory reflexes grant you supernatural balance and climbing ability. You are immune to fall damage from medium heights (roughly two stories or less). You gain Advantage on all Agility rolls to balance, climb, or move silently across unstable or narrow surfaces. You can scale vertical surfaces with even minimal handholds without rolling, provided you are not in combat or under immediate time pressure.

**Irrepressible Curiosity.** Once per session, when hidden information exists that you could plausibly discover, the Keeper may point out the lead. You choose whether to pursue it; this Gift never selects your Action or charges a cost for refusing. If you pursue it and uncover the hidden truth, gain **1 path resource**: 1 Hope if Awakened or 1 Effort if Sleeping, subject to the normal cap.

**Sub-Strain (Choose One at Character Creation).** The Ailuran genome expresses in two divergent phenotypes, each shaping not only physiology but approach to every problem encountered. Choose one Sub-Strain at character creation; you gain that Sub-Strain's feature in addition to your three core Ancestry Gifts above.

***Shroud-Strain, The Still Hunters***

*Sleeker, lightly built, with chromatophore fur that shifts in real time. They are patient to the point of unsettling stillness, capable of waiting for hours without moving a muscle.*

***Static Cloak.*** Your chromatophore fur provides active camouflage. While completely motionless, with no movement, speech, or active equipment use, you are effectively invisible to visual and thermal detection. A creature actively searching for you makes an Instinct Roll, DC 15. The effect ends immediately if you move, speak, attack, or take any Action; reassuming stillness requires spending your full Spotlight doing nothing. This is biological camouflage, not technology, and cannot be jammed by electronic countermeasures.

***Surge-Strain, The Kinetic Predators***

*Heavier, more powerfully muscled, frames built for explosive acceleration. Their leg musculature is visibly denser, packed with fast-twitch fibers.*

***Kinetic Battery.*** Your metabolism can store and release kinetic energy in controlled bursts. Once per scene, mark 1 Stress to activate a Metabolic Burst: you move instantly to any point within Far range that you can see, ignoring difficult terrain and obstacles shorter than your height. This movement does not provoke reactions. Upon arriving, you gain Advantage on your next Agility or Finesse roll made before the end of your next Spotlight. Observers see a blur of fur and feel a displacement of air.

**Playing an Ailuran.** You are the crew's specialist in finding what others have hidden, the one who already read the manifest, already mapped the exits, already knows which guard is lying. Your value is rarely raw combat; it is the moment the locked door becomes an open door and the secret nobody else thought to look for changes the whole job. Lean on Irrepressible Curiosity as your engine: let it pull you somewhere you should not be, and trust the Keeper to make the trouble worth it. Watch the two classic pitfalls, hoarding information from your own crew until it is too late to matter, and treating people as puzzles rather than partners. The richest Ailuran arcs are about an operator who deals only in contracts learning, slowly and reluctantly, to give something away for free.

### ANCESTRY COMPLICATIONS

**Ailuran Complications.** At most once per Ailuran per session, after that character resolves a Fear-dominant noncritical Roll that materially used an Ailuran Gift, the Keeper may spend 1 Fear and roll 1d6 on this table. Do not choose a result. Matching dice never trigger it, and the complication never selects the player's Action.

| D6 | COMPLICATION |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Compulsive Fixation.** Become Dazed; clear it through the normal condition rule after the next Action. |
| **2** | **Thermal Misread.** The next Instinct Roll you make through aura-sight before the end of your next Spotlight has Disadvantage. |
| **3** | **Exposed Position.** Lose Hidden, and the next attack against you before the start of your next Spotlight has Advantage. Your position does not change. |
| **4** | **Broken Silence.** Lose Hidden. If an established alarm is present, it activates; otherwise mark 1 Stress. |
| **5** | **Information Debt.** Record a named information debt to a known NPC or faction. It is a campaign hook with no immediate modifier, cost, or compelled Action. |
| **6** | **The Itch That Won't Stop.** Mark 1 Stress and take Disadvantage on the next Roll unrelated to the discovered lead before the end of the scene. The player still chooses every Action. |

## BLOOMSTRIDER

*"We are gardeners in the empty void. We tend to life where others see only death. Empires fall, so we plant seeds. We are not conquerors. We are companions to the places we live."*

*Verdant Conclave proverb, taught to all young Bloomstriders before their first off-world voyage*

**Identity.** Bloomstriders are children of living planets, their bodies a genuine fusion of animal and plant life.

Glowing sap flows through their veins, their hair grows like moss or ferns, and living patterns on their skin shift with the seasons. They believe life is a promise, not a possession, and act as gardeners and companions to the places they inhabit. They see the Great Silence as an opportunity for new growth, a chance to bring life back to the stars.

**Physical Description.** Bloomstriders possess a strange, natural beauty. Their skin feels like tree bark and changes color with their moods and the seasons, brown, green, or gold, while glowing sap pulses through visible veins beneath. Their hair is living moss, ferns, or vines that moves and reacts to surroundings; some have flowers or leaves growing from their skin, others thorns or ridges along their arms. Their deep green and brown eyes have pupils that open and close like blooming flowers.

**Homeworld.** Bloomstriders trace themselves to the living worlds: warm, water-rich planets whose whole biospheres behave like a single slow organism, where forests share root-networks for thousands of kilometers and the weather answers the season rather than the other way around. Their ancestral world, which Groves still call simply the First Garden, is a place of cathedral-canopy forests and luminous wetlands, more grown than built. Few Bloomstriders alive have seen it; most were born in transplanted Groves aboard ships and on reclaimed worlds. But every Grove keeps a seed-line said to descend from the First Garden, and to plant one on a dead world is, for a Bloomstrider, the closest thing to going home.

**Culture.** Bloomstrider society resembles a grove of trees. They live in groups called **Groves** large families spread across many planets, connected by shared seeds and beliefs. Each Grove has a special purpose: some focus on healing, others on defense, still others on exploration to spread new life. A traveling Bloomstrider always carries seeds from home. Two main factions have emerged across the Groves: the **Verdant Conclave**, gardeners who unite many Groves under the symbol of the Spiral Leaf, working slowly and gently; and the **Thornbind Covenant**, guardians who train their bodies as living weapons of thorns, poisons, and strangling vines, acting as the galaxy's immune system against threats that would otherwise consume the gardens. Within a Grove, decisions are reached by long consensus rather than command, and an individual's standing grows with what they have nurtured rather than what they have won. They mark the turning of seasons even on lightless ships, keep elaborate grief-rites built around planting, and treat the deliberate killing of a living system, a poisoned well, a burned forest, a strip-mined moon, as the one truly unforgivable crime. To a Bloomstrider, time spent is not lost if something grew in it.

**Place in the Galaxy.** Bloomstriders are present across the Free Fleet and increasingly in House service, particularly with House Amaranth (whose long-range planning aligns with Bloomstrider time-scales) and House Joric (whose protective doctrine matches the Thornbind ethos). House Kurogane has a complicated history with Bloomstriders, having historically attempted to commercialize Bloomstrider biology. The wounds of that history have not fully healed.

**Society and Daily Life.** A Grove is less a government than a household stretched across worlds, run by long discussion and a shared sense of season. Bloomstriders measure time in growth and decay rather than hours; they tend to reach decisions slowly and then hold to them stubbornly. They keep gardens wherever they settle, on

ships, in stations, in the cracks of dead worlds, and a Bloomstrider with nothing living to tend grows visibly unwell. They are physical, tactile people: they greet by touch, mourn by planting, and find the sterile corridors of most stations quietly depressing.

**Relations with Other Ancestries.** Bloomstriders get on easily with Celestiari, both patient, both drawn to care-work, and with Humans, whose improvisational energy they find endearing if exhausting. They carry a guarded history with House Kurogane over old attempts to commercialize their biology, and that wariness colors their dealings with Kryllians and Synthetics, whose instinct to optimize living systems can feel, to a Bloomstrider, like being treated as a resource. With the Kryx they share a surprising warmth: both prize loyalty and the protection of one's own.

**Distinctive Traits and Customs.** Bloomstriders mark important events by planting, and many carry a personal seed-line traceable back to their home Grove. They are slow to anger and slower still to forgive an injury done to a living place. Awakening, when it comes to a Bloomstrider, tends to arrive late and root deep; their communities regard an Awakened member as a particularly patient kind of gardener.

### ANCESTRY GIFTS

**Plant-like Body.** You can derive energy from light and your organs filter toxins efficiently. Gain Advantage on Instinct Rolls to survive hostile environments. This Gift grants no Core Resistance, immunity, atmosphere, pressure seal, or automatic protection from printed damage; equipment is still required when a hazard says so.

**Nurturing Touch.** After several minutes of focused contact with another creature, roll 1d4 once. At the start of each of that target's next that many Spotlights, it clears **1 HP**. Reapplying Nurturing Touch before the effect ends keeps only the higher remaining duration; its healing never stacks. Faint root-like patterns appear on the healed skin and fade shortly afterward.

**Playing a Bloomstrider.** You are the crew's tie to natural cycles, biological wisdom, and the long view, the medic who keeps everyone alive and the conscience that asks what a plan will cost the living things in its path. Your timescale is longer than the others': your patience can frustrate them, and your survival and healing skills will repeatedly save them. Play the Conclave-Covenant tension openly; a Bloomstrider torn between gardener and guardian always has something to wrestle with. The pitfall to avoid is becoming the table's scold, your slowness and your reverence for life are strengths, not lectures. The best Bloomstrider beats come when patience finally breaks, or when the gardener has to pick up the guardian's weapons.

### ANCESTRY COMPLICATIONS

| D6 | COMPLICATION |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Sap-Bleed** Your luminous sap leaks visibly. You are easier to track or detect until you can recover. |
| **2** | **Rootshock** A sudden wave of empathic feedback overwhelms you. Mark 1 Stress. |
| **3** | **Symbiotic Overgrowth** Vines, spores, or fronds react uncontrollably, entangling gear or slowing movement. |
| **4** | **Echo of Decay.** Mark 1 Stress. You sense only corruption or infestation already established within Close range; if none exists, the sensation is a false echo with no other effect. |
| **5** | **Hungry Symbiosis** You must consume scarce resources (biomass, nutrients) or take 1 Stress. |
| **6** | **Pollen Bloom** You release spores that alter the social atmosphere, helpful to some, alarming to others. |

## CELESTIARI

*"People expect me to glow with wisdom. Truth is, my skin does that when I skip lunch. I can feel the mood of a room, which is handy at a customs desk and tiring everywhere else. I check cargo manifests for a living. That is the whole mystery."*

*Sera Lumen, customs inspector, Solari Prime orbital authority*

**Identity.** Celestiari are a long-settled people of the Core Worlds whose skin carries a faint natural bioluminescence and whose nervous systems read the emotions of those around them. Generations of myth have dressed them up, and a stranger meeting one often half-expects a saint. The living article is more ordinary and more interesting: a citizen, a neighbor, a dockhand, a clerk, a teacher, or a member of the clergy, someone who glows a little when they feel strongly and who tends toward patience and the long view. The Great Silence struck their communities as hard as anyone's, and what came through was a scattered, resilient people keeping its old traditions alive on reduced means.

**Physical Description.** Celestiari are tall and fine-boned, with skin that holds a soft inner light, brightest at the throat, the palms, and the line of the spine, that strengthens with strong feeling and dims with fatigue, hunger, or illness. The glow is real but modest, about the strength of a candle, enough to read by in a dark cabin. Their eyes are pale and luminous, from silver to cold gold, and many keep their hair cropped or bound because it picks up a faint static charge in dry air. They register the moods of nearby people as a kind of warmth or pressure, an empathic sense that is useful, tiring, and sometimes unwelcome. Their lifespans run a little longer than a human's, but they are plainly mortal: they age, they sicken, they die.

**Homeworld.** The Celestiari heartland lies in the Core Worlds, on long-settled, sunlit planets civilized for so long that their cities are layered like sediment, old foundations under newer ones, shrines worn smooth by generations of hands. The best-known is a temperate world of white-stone terraces and long twilights, where the slow sunsets

suit a people who glow faintly and prefer soft light. It is an ordinary place, with its slums, droughts, bad governments, and traffic, like anywhere. What it offers, and newer worlds are still too young to have grown, is age and continuity: a long, continuous thread of ritual and record that the Great Silence frayed badly yet left standing, and which scattered Celestiari communities now work to keep tied together across the dark.

**Society and Daily Life.** Celestiari communities tend to be close, ritual-minded, and quietly proud. Daily life turns on shared meals, recitation, and a strong norm of emotional honesty, lying is hard among people who can feel the tension in a room, so the culture leans on directness softened by elaborate courtesies that let hard things be said kindly. They are over-represented in work that rewards composure under strain: counseling, mediation, hospice care, teaching, arbitration, and the Mystic disciplines of House Solari. The old religious framework survives, and most working Celestiari treat it the way most people treat an inherited faith: a source of holidays, grief rites, and lively arguments. Two broad currents run through them: the **Guardians of the Light**, traditionalists who frame Celestiari sensitivity as a duty of care owed to others; and the **Seekers of the Spark**, who treat the same sensitivity as a teaching gift and tend to leave home, take students, and marry out.

**Place in the Galaxy and Relations.** Celestiari concentrate in House Solari and Solari-aligned communities, where their temperament suits the formal Mystic tradition; the Spire of Verita on Solari Prime is heavily Celestiari-staffed, though "Solari Mystic" and "Celestiari" are overlapping rather than identical categories. They also appear across the Free Fleet, the Explorers' Guild, and House Amaranth as analysts and counselors. Other ancestries tend to find them easy to trust and hard to lie to. Humans warm to them quickly; Kryx respect their steadiness but find their stillness strange; Ailurans avoid them, because a Celestiari's glow and aura read in Ailuran thermal-sight as a painful flare, and the Celestiari in turn find the Ailuran's deliberately blank surface unsettling, "like talking to an empty chair." The legend of the radiant immortal is a weight the average Celestiari carries, and most spend a fair part of their lives gently correcting strangers' expectations.

**Distinctive Traits and Customs.** Celestiari dim their own glow as a courtesy in close quarters, the way others lower their voices, and they read a person's mood aloud only when invited, treating anything more as a serious rudeness. They keep dawn and dusk observances even far from any star, as much from habit and belonging as from belief. They produce Mystics at the ordinary rate, the same as anyone, despite the stubborn rumor that every Celestiari is secretly Awakened.

### ANCESTRY GIFTS

**Stellar Meditation.** An old meditative discipline lets you steady yourself in quiet light. Once per long rest, you may meditate for 10 minutes under starlight (or any light source) to clear 1 Stress and gain 2 path resources: 2 Hope if you are Awakened, or 2 Effort if you are Sleeping.

**Celestial Grace.** The light your skin sheds can be drawn, briefly, into your hands. Your unarmed attacks deal d6 void damage instead of normal damage. Once

per session, when you deal damage that causes HP loss with this ability, you may heal the same amount of damage to any allies within Very Close range.

**Playing a Celestiari.** You are often the crew's steady center, the one who can feel the room and say the true thing kindly. That sensitivity is a gift and a burden: you carry other people's moods whether you want to or not, and the interesting Celestiari stories live in the gap between the calm you project and the strain underneath. Play them as a working person with a tiring sense and a lot of strangers' expectations to manage, and let the serene-saint image fall away. Let the composure crack sometimes. A Celestiari who finally loses patience, or whose kindness turns into fierce, unglamorous protectiveness, is far more memorable than one who only glows.

### ANCESTRY COMPLICATIONS

| D6 | COMPLICATION |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Blinding Flare** Your glow surges uncontrollably, dazzling allies or exposing your position. |
| **2** | **Resonant Disruption** Your aura interferes with nearby technology. |
| **3** | **Emotional Backlash** Empathic resonance overwhelms you; mark 1 Stress. |
| **4** | **Fractured Halo** Your light flickers, sowing unease. |
| **5** | **Attractive Beacon** Enemies or desperate refugees are drawn to you. |
| **6** | **Radiant Fatigue** Your brilliance wanes; Disadvantage on your next roll. |

## ETHEREAL

*"Everyone wants the prophecy. What I actually have is half a second of warning before things go wrong, the same as a good driver, except mine comes with a headache. Out past the Veil that half-second is worth real money, so that is where I run cargo. That is the whole of it."*

*Tarn Vesse, independent Veil navigator, Free Fleet registry*

**Identity.** Ethereals are a small, scattered people whose bodies sit slightly out of phase with ordinary matter and whose perception runs a little ahead of the present: they catch the most likely next moment the way most people catch a scent on the wind. Folklore reaches for grand words, oracle, ghost, prophet, while the reality is a person with an unusual nervous system and a genuinely strange set of senses. Most Ethereals are working travelers: navigators, researchers, and quiet fixtures of out-of-the-way stations. The Great Silence scattered their already-thin population further still, and they have made their way ever since as individuals more than as a nation.

**Physical Description.** Ethereals look almost solid, their edges seeming to stay in motion, as if always mid-settle. Their bodies are faintly translucent at the edges and tend to blur when they move quickly, leaving a brief

afterimage. Their coloring shifts slowly across a narrow range, eyes drifting from violet to grey, skin catching light like frosted glass, and their apparent age stays hard to place. The phasing is a real physiological trait: under stress or concentration they can let parts of themselves go briefly insubstantial, which is unnerving to watch and useful in tight spaces. Their forward perception is short and unreliable, a constant low hum of what is about to happen, and a lifetime of living with it tends to leave them deliberate, a little detached, and careful about what they say.

**Origins.** Ethereals turn up thinly across many populations, more often born into other communities than gathered into their own; they claim many homes and a single homeworld eludes them. The Great Silence scattered them further than any other people, since a population already spread across stations and ships simply dispersed wider, holding together through its own loose threads. Some Ethereals hold that they were always rare and always dispersed; others suspect the Silence itself made more of them, jolting something latent in scattered nervous systems into waking. No one can prove either story. What an Ethereal calls home is almost always a particular ship, station, or study circle rather than a planet: the people who got used to them, and whom they got used to in turn.

**Society and Daily Life.** Ethereal life plays out in small, loosely connected communities: a few families on a station, a study circle attached to a House research post, a handful of navigators who keep in touch across a sector. Because their perception makes small talk exhausting, they often sense where a conversation is going before it arrives, Ethereal social life prizes economy: few words, long silences, and a firm taboo against using foresight to steer the people close to you. Two outlooks divide them, more as temperaments than factions: the **Weavers of Fate**, who hold that the future is largely fixed and the decent thing is to help it arrive cleanly; and the **Shapers of Tomorrow**, who hold that it can be nudged, and that nudging it carefully is a duty. Most Ethereals drift between the two over a lifetime.

**Place in the Galaxy and Relations.** Ethereals are rare enough that a single one aboard a ship is already at the high end of typical density. They cluster in scholarly settings (House Amaranth research stations, the Spire of Verita) and in the Free Fleet as solo navigators, where half a second of warning in Veil work is worth a great deal. Houses tend to value them on the research side and keep them at arm's length on the operational side, because an Ethereal's warnings are often inconvenient and come hedged with more doubt than the listener would like. Other ancestries find them hard to read: Kryllians are frustrated by their roundabout way of explaining things; Ailurans treat them warily, since an Ethereal can sometimes notice a hidden Ailuran that nothing else can; and crews that travel with one long enough come to treat the warnings as what they are: a useful, if fallible, early-warning sense attached to a private and often tired person.

**Distinctive Traits and Customs.** Ethereals dislike being startled, since a missed warning is genuinely disorienting for them, and they consider it deeply rude to ask one to predict a personal matter for amusement. They tend to speak in conditionals and probabilities, which strangers mistake for evasiveness. An Awakened Ethereal unsettles even other Ethereals: their native foresight and a Domain's power overlap in ways that leave everyone, themselves included, a little wary.

### ANCESTRY GIFTS

**Phase Shift.** Ethereals can step outside the normal flow of reality. You may mark 1 Stress to become incorporeal. You remain incorporeal as long as you continue to mark 1 Stress at the start of each of your Spotlights. While incorporeal, you can pass through solid objects that are **thinner than your body width and not protected by energy** (energy fields, wards, force barriers, or any active substrate-shielding block this ability). You are immune to physical attacks while incorporeal but cannot affect the physical world. The body-width constraint means you can pass through standard walls and ordinary closed doors, but not through massive bulkheads, deep-rock barriers, or vault walls thicker than yourself.

**Temporal Perception.** Your existence spans multiple timelines, giving you glimpses of possible futures. You automatically sense temporal anomalies and distortions within Close range. Once per session, you may ask the Keeper about the most likely immediate consequence of a proposed action.

**Playing an Ethereal.** You are the crew's early-warning sense, the one who flinches a half-second before the ambush and is often at a loss to explain why. Your read on cause and effect is genuinely different, and the friction between what you half-see coming and what your crewmates are willing to hear is your richest material. Choose your warnings carefully: cry wolf and they stop listening; stay silent and you carry the guilt alone. Play the foresight as short, fallible, and exhausting, the kind that proves wrong often enough to keep you humble; humble suits an Ethereal far better than smug. The strongest Ethereal arcs are about a tired, private person deciding how much of an unwelcome future to share, and with whom.

### ANCESTRY COMPLICATIONS

| D6 | COMPLICATION |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Time Stutter.** You become Dazed; describe the skipped instant. |
| **2** | **Echoed Actions.** Your next Action has Disadvantage as competing versions interfere. |
| **3** | **Premonition Paralysis** A vision of failure freezes you; Disadvantage on your next roll. |
| **4** | **Temporal Strain** The effort fractures your composure; mark 1 Stress. |
| **5** | **Continuity Drift** An NPC reacts as though you've already acted. |
| **6** | **Future Shadow** You glimpse a looming threat; the Keeper foreshadows new danger. |

## HUMAN

*"We are the survivors. The scattered. The ones who refuse to break. When the galaxy fell silent, we learned to shout. When the stars went out, we became our own*

*light. We are not the strongest, nor the most gifted. We are simply too stubborn to die."*

Captain Maren Solas, Free Fleet, Vagrant Star

**Identity.** Humans are the great survivors of the galaxy, and in the Pearl Era they have become something more: its rulers. Once the masters of a galaxy-spanning civilization, they were shattered by the Great Silence and scattered to the winds, and then, slowly and stubbornly, they put the pieces back together. Today humans run the Empire. They are not the most advanced ancestry, nor the strongest, nor the most gifted, Kryllians build better, Kryx fight harder, others see farther, but they are the most established and most powerful society in known space, and the political and administrative machinery of the post-Silence galaxy runs largely through human hands. The heads of all six Great Houses are human. Their strength was never a single talent; it was endurance, adaptability, and an unmatched gift for organizing other people, including, now, eight other ancestries who live and work alongside them as equals.

**Physical Description.** Humanity is a kaleidoscope of physical forms. The "human" look is really a thousand looks. Skin from void-dark to pale-frozen-moon. Hair in any imaginable color. From the gene-sculpted elite of the Core Worlds to the hard-bitten void-miners of the Rim, their appearance is as varied as the stars. Where other ancestries carry natural armor, a glow, or an extra pair of arms, humans carry adaptability: an unspecialized, generalist biology that bends to any environment through ingenuity and tools. Their lifespans, once stretched into centuries with advanced technology, are now as unpredictable as a Veil storm.

**Homeworld.** Humanity had a homeworld once, the green cradle every human culture still half-remembers in its oldest songs, and lost it in the chaos of the Silence; whether it was destroyed, cut off behind dead jump-lanes, or simply forgotten under generations of exile, no one now can say for certain, and rival accounts are a minor industry. What replaced it is a diaspora: humans are from everywhere and nowhere, born on ships, in stations, on toxic rocks and gene-sculpted Core estates. A human asked where they are from will name a vessel, a deck, a moon, or a fleet, not a species homeworld. The loss is old enough to be a wound only on holidays, and the stubbornness it bred is the most human thing about them.

**Culture.** Human culture is a shattered mirror, each fragment reflecting a different facet of former glory, held together by stubborn resilience and a hard-learned commitment to order. They are masters of forming communities in the most desolate places, building homes on toxic worlds and in the husks of dead starships. Two major human-led currents run through Imperial politics: the **Solara Compact**, a coalition of Core Worlds bent on restoring the old ways and deeply suspicious of post-Silence psionics; and the **Free Fleet**, a loose alliance of independent systems and nomadic fleets that has accepted the new reality and resists any fresh tyranny. The early decades of human resettlement were scarred by ugly violence between some human enclaves and the other ancestries, and the Empire's founding generation concluded that a stable multi-species order could not survive a repeat of it. The modern Empire is therefore built on an explicit creed of equality: the nine ancestries hold equal standing under Imperial law, and racial discrimination or violence against another ancestry is

among the gravest crimes on the books, investigated hard and punished harder. Most humans of the Pearl Era grew up inside that order and genuinely welcome other ancestries as colleagues, neighbors, and crew; the old bigotries survive only at the margins, where the Empire stamps on them without mercy. What ties the fragments together is a talent for improvised institutions: humans throw up councils, guilds, unions, congregations, and crews wherever a few of them gather, argue endlessly about who is in charge, and somehow keep the lights on. They are storytellers above all, carrying their lost worlds forward in songs and grudges and recipes, and they absorb the customs of whoever they live beside until a Rim-born human and a Core-born human can feel like two different peoples wearing the same face.

**Place in the Galaxy.** Humans sit at the commanding heights of the post-Silence galaxy. They hold the administration of the Imperial throne, the leadership of all six Great Houses, and the bulk of the institutions that keep the Empire together; they dominate the population of House Joric and House Volkov and have a heavy presence in Valerius, Kurogane, Solari, and Amaranth. The Free Fleet is roughly half human; the Explorers' Guild is heavily human and often bridges Guild expertise to other-ancestry crews. The galaxy's basic infrastructure, its trading networks, ship classes, lingua franca, and the augmentation industry, was largely human-developed and remains largely human-maintained. But in the modern Empire, power is meant to carry responsibility: humans run the order, and they are bound by law and custom to run it for everyone. A human official who abuses another ancestry does not merely break a law, they embarrass the whole project, and the Houses come down on them to prove the project still means something.

**Society and Daily Life.** There is no single human way of living, which is the point. A Core-Worlds human raised under Solara Compact restoration politics and a Rim-born void-miner share little but a stubborn refusal to quit. Humans build community fast and anywhere, improvising institutions, slang, and holidays within a generation of arriving somewhere new. They are the galaxy's natural generalists and brokers: comfortable in mixed company, quick to pick up another ancestry's customs well enough to do business, and prone to a confidence that others read as either inspiring or reckless.

**Relations with Other Ancestries.** Because human hands built so much of the shared infrastructure, the lingua franca, the common ship classes, the augmentation industry, almost every other ancestry deals with humans constantly, and opinions are correspondingly mixed. Celestiari and Bloomstriders warm to them; Kryllians respect their ingenuity while wincing at their sloppiness; Synthetics regard them with a complicated mix of resentment and kinship, since humans both made them and, often, freed them. Ailurans treat humans as a renewable harvest of secrets. The Kryx, who value loyalty over cleverness, trust a proven human absolutely and an unproven one not at all.

**Distinctive Traits and Customs.** Human customs vary wildly by world, but the shared habits are improvisation, storytelling, and an almost reflexive drive to organize, give three humans a week and they will have formed a committee. They adopt other ancestries' practices freely, sometimes clumsily, and they meet Awakening with the same range of attitudes as everything else: reverence in the Core, suspicion in the Compact, opportunity in the Fleet.

### ANCESTRY GIFTS

**Adaptive Spirit.** Humanity's greatest asset is its refusal to stay down. Once per game session, when you fail an action roll, you may spend **2 path resources** (2 Hope if Awakened; 2 Effort if Sleeping) to gain Advantage on your next roll of the same type. The mechanic represents the human pattern of turning a failure into the lesson that drives the next attempt.

**Cultural Bridge.** Humans are found everywhere and have learned to read the motivations and customs of many other species. During a rest, you can mark 1 Stress to represent the mental effort of sorting through cultural knowledge. You may then ask the Keeper one question

about a specific group's core motivations or most important customs. The Keeper answers truthfully.

**Made for the Graft.** Augmentation is overwhelmingly human work, built by human engineers around human anatomy, and human physiology accepts grafted hardware with a readiness no other ancestry quite matches. You gain **+2 Augment Capacity** (Chapter 13). Where another ancestry leans on an innate gift, a human as often leans on a better arm.

**Inheritance of the Builders (Choose One at Character Creation).** Human civilization built most of what the galaxy buys, flies, and grafts, and a human character starts play already holding a piece of that inheritance. Choose one:

- **The Graft.** One free augmentation of Common (TT1) or Military (TT2). If Common (TT1), it does not consume an Augment Slot; if Military (TT2), it occupies 1 slot as normal. This augmentation has no drawbacks, and its expression is entirely yours to define: genetic modification, mutation, or chrome.
- **The Tool.** One item of equipment of Experimental (TT3) access and 9 Cr (WT3) value, chosen from any equipment catalog in play. It is yours, paid for, and nobody asks how.

**Playing a Human.** You are the crew's adaptable generalist and its most natural bridge to the rest of human-built civilization, the one who can talk to anyone, improvise a fix, and refuse to stay down. Your strength is breadth rather than any single signature trick; you cover the gaps, hold the team together, and turn yesterday's failure into today's plan. Lean into resilience, ingenuity, and stubbornness. The pitfall is becoming the bland 'normal one' in a crew of wonders, so give your human a sharp, specific culture: a home deck, a grudge, a faith, a trade, and let that texture show. The best human stories are about what a person does when adapting is not enough and they simply have to endure.

### ANCESTRY COMPLICATIONS

| D6 | COMPLICATION |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Overreach** You succeed, but attract more danger than expected. |
| **2** | **Burnout** You push beyond safe limits; mark 1 Stress. |
| **3** | **Fractured Unity** Your choices spark division among allies or NPCs. |
| **4** | **Collateral Damage** Your improvisation causes unintended harm or loss of resources. |
| **5** | **Haunted Past** Memories of Earth or exile distract you, costing tempo. |
| **6** | **Resource Drain** Supplies run dry faster than planned; the Keeper removes or reduces a resource. |

**Silver Linings.** Humans are not spared trouble. If anything they make more of it. But human trouble rarely stays clean. When a Human Complication triggers, resolve the cost first: the mistake still hurts, the door still closes, the resource is still lost, the danger still arrives. Then the fallout reveals a small way forward, a clue, a route, an exposed weakness, a warning, a surviving tool, a sudden distraction, an opportunity nobody saw before. A Silver Lining never cancels the Complication; it gives the crew something useful to do with the damage. The Keeper picks the opening from the fiction, and it should always be small, immediate, and actionable: a new choice, not a solution.

*Cost first, opening second.* A Silver Lining is not luck that prevents consequences. It is the shape left behind after consequences land. Do not use it to erase harm, ignore loss, avoid Stress, cancel failure, or hand out extra path resources unless another rule says so. Use it to reveal motion: a way through, a new angle, a dangerous shortcut, a person who reacts, a system that glitches, a truth exposed by the mess. Humans do not have fewer problems. They have problems that leave doors.

## KRYLLIAN

*"The universe is a machine. A complex, beautiful, and often malfunctioning machine. We are the engineers, the mechanics, the ones who understand how it works. When it breaks, we fix it. We are the unbreakable forge."*

*Kryllian engineering proverb, attributed to the foundational Star-Forger Thokk-Var-Ironhold*

**Identity.** Kryllians are the builders and makers of the galaxy, a species for whom engineering is a way of life. They see the universe as a series of systems, some elegant, some flawed, and their purpose is to understand, maintain, and improve these systems. The Great Silence was, to them, the ultimate system failure, a puzzle to be solved.

**Physical Description.** Kryllians are insectoid humanoids, proof of evolution in harsh environments. Born on high-gravity worlds, they are willowy but extraordinarily robust, with dense chitinous exoskeletons providing natural armor. Their most striking feature is

their **four arms**: two larger upper arms for combat and heavy lifting, two smaller lower arms positioned at the rib-line for fine manipulation. A Kryllian mechanic can simultaneously weld a plate, tighten a bolt, consult a schematic, and hold a light. Their compound eyes grant a wide field of vision and the ability to perceive details invisible to other species. They are long-lived, with natural lifespans exceeding three centuries.

**Homeworld.** Kryllians evolved on high-gravity worlds: dense, mineral-rich planets where the air is thick, the horizon close, and a fall can kill, which is why their bodies are willowy yet astonishingly strong and their building habits obsessively sound. Their ancestral world is a place of deep canyon-cities and vast subterranean foundries, engineered down to the airflow, where the highest honor is to have built something that still stands long after you are gone. Kryllians abroad carry that world's habits with them, the immaculate workshop, the doubled load-bearing, the deep distrust of anything jury-rigged, and they tend to judge a station or ship instantly and silently by how well it is made.

**Culture.** Kryllian society is built on logic, efficiency, and deep respect for engineering principles. To them, the Great Silence was not a mystical event but a catastrophic system failure waiting to happen. Their communities are models of order and cooperation where every individual has a role and every action is calculated for maximum benefit. They have little time for art or philosophy; their dedication to craft is itself a form of worship. Two factions divide the species: the **Machine Cult**, a quasi-religious sect that believes technology is the only true god and views all other forms of life as inferior; and the **Star- Forgers**, a more moderate faction believing technology should serve all living things, working as diplomats and traders to build a stable galaxy from the old's ashes. Authority among Kryllians is earned through demonstrated competence rather than seniority or charm: the one who understands the system best leads the work on it, and is expected to step aside when someone better appears. They keep meticulous shared records of every build and failure, treat teaching an apprentice as a sacred obligation, and find waste, of material, of motion, of a life's potential, faintly obscene. Their warmth is real but practical, expressed in solved problems rather than soft words.

**Place in the Galaxy.** Kryllians are concentrated in House Kurogane (where their engineering precision is highly valued) and substantially present in House Joric (where their craftsmen, including the Steelforge clan, supply much of the House's specialty equipment). The Free Fleet relies heavily on Kryllian engineers; many of the most-respected ship's-soul mechanics in the Fleet are Kryllian. House Amaranth maintains long-standing scholarly exchange programs with the Star-Forger faction.

**Society and Daily Life.** Kryllian life is organized, scheduled, and quietly warm beneath its precision. Work sits at the center of it, a well-run shop or ship is, to a Kryllian, a kind of home, and craft is treated with the seriousness others reserve for faith. They speak plainly, dislike wasted motion, and show affection through maintenance: a Kryllian who keeps your gear in perfect order is telling you something. The four-armed physiology shapes everything from their tools to their manners; offering only your two lower hands signals that you come unarmed and ready to work.

**Relations with Other Ancestries.** Kryllians and Synthetics get on famously, two kinds of mind that agree the universe is a system to be understood. They keep up

long scholarly exchanges with House Amaranth and supply much of House Joric's specialty work. They find human improvisation maddening and indispensable in equal measure, respect the Ailurans who keep breaking their security (a compliment, mostly), and lose patience quickly with Ethereal and Rift Spinner non-linearity. With Bloomstriders they tread carefully, aware that the urge to optimize a living thing can give deep offense.

**Distinctive Traits and Customs.** Kryllians keep their workspaces immaculate, regard a broken promise as a kind of structural failure, and consider it real respect to repair something for you unasked. Their lower hands handle fine work and courtesy; their upper hands handle force and labor, and confusing the two in company is a small social blunder. An Awakened Kryllian treats their Domain like any other system, to be mastered through disciplined practice.

### ANCESTRY GIFTS

**Master Craftsman.** The Kryllian mind is uniquely suited for building and repairing. When making any roll related to crafting or repairing a piece of technology, you may choose to mark 1 Stress to gain Advantage on the roll. This represents a flash of insight or a moment of intense focus.
