> **Rule Take-Away:** Failure with Fear resolves its one predeclared or printed consequence now and also generates Fear. Later Fear spending uses only printed Keeper Moves or abilities; it cannot retroactively add a second consequence to this Roll.

> **GEAR 1, NARRATING THE** **COMPLICATION** *(OPTIONAL ATMOSPHERIC RULE)*

If this optional atmospheric rule is adopted before play, the affected player narrates how the already declared or printed consequence looks. Narration cannot change its target, cost, damage, Condition, duration, clock movement, resource effect, or end condition. If no consequence was eligible before the Roll, this option creates none.

## DIFFICULTY CLASSES

The Keeper assigns one of six Difficulty Classes. Use only these values. Fictional advantages and disadvantages normally change positioning, grant Advantage or Disadvantage, alter the consequence, or remove the need for a roll; they do not create intermediate DCs.


| DC | DIFFICULTY | WHEN TO USE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **5** | Routine | A trained character succeeds unless pressure or interference matters. |
| **10** | Easy | A straightforward task under meaningful pressure. |
| **15** | Challenging | The standard difficulty for a consequential task. |
| **20** | Difficult | Requires strong aptitude, preparation, or favorable positioning. |
| **25** | Extreme | A feat expected only from exceptional specialists or with major assistance. |
| **30** | Nearly Impossible | A legendary attempt at the edge of plausible capability. |

Choose the rung that best represents the fiction. Do not round an imagined hidden number; decide whether the task is Routine, Easy, Challenging, Difficult, Extreme, or Nearly Impossible. If circumstances change enough to matter, move by one rung or apply Advantage or Disadvantage. A task with no meaningful uncertainty or consequence does not require a roll.

## HOPE

Hope is the player's currency. It represents the character's inner reserve, the flicker of conviction, the moment of clarity, the small private store of *yes, I can do this* that experienced characters draw on when the situation demands more than ordinary effort.

Each player tracks their character's Hope on the character sheet. The standard cap is **6 Hope**. A character cannot hold more than 6 at any time; additional Hope earned beyond the cap is lost. Awakened characters have access to Hope as a working resource. Sleeping characters do not gain Hope from rolls (Hope-favored Successes give them no token), they have other resources covered in Chapter 7 that fill the same narrative role.

**Session Start.** At the start of each session, every Awakened character begins with **2 Hope**, regardless of how much Hope they held at the end of the previous session. Hope does not normally carry between sessions. If a session begins *in medias res*, continuing the same scene with no fictional time between sessions, the Keeper may allow characters to retain their current Hope instead. The cap of 6 still applies.

Hope is gained from:

- **Success with Hope**: 1 Hope.

- **Critical Success**: 1 Hope (and 1 Stress cleared). This is the Awakened payout; the Sleeping are paid in Effort and Resolve instead, per *What a Critical Success Pays* above.

- **Certain abilities**: some Domain Powers, Experiences, and Class features generate Hope under specific conditions. These are detailed in their respective entries.

- **Printed grants**: a Class, Ancestry, Connection, Power, adventure, or other rule may grant the amount of Hope stated by its explicit trigger. Roleplay quality alone never creates an unbounded Hope award.

Hope is spent on:

- **Invoking an Experience**: Spend 1 Hope before rolling. Add the Experience's flat bonus to the total. Note that this adds the bonus *itself*, the modifier number written on the Experience entry. It does not grant Advantage. Experiences are flat numerical additions, not dice manipulation. (See Chapter 8 for Experiences in detail.)

- **Helping a teammate**: Spend 1 Hope to grant another character Advantage on a roll, provided your character can plausibly help with the action and is present in the scene.

- **Spending on Domain Powers**: Most Domain Powers cost 1, 2, or 3 Hope to invoke. The full catalog is in Chapter 19; the structure of how Powers consume Hope is in Chapter 18.

- **Other printed uses**: Specific Class, Ancestry, Connection, Power, equipment, or adventure features may call for the stated Hope spend. A Keeper-created house option must be declared before play and is not Core canon.

Hope cannot be spent on rolls that have already been made. The decision to spend Hope happens *before* the dice are rolled, except for Hope spends explicitly tied to outcomes (such as some Domain Powers triggered by a Failure with Hope).

A useful mental model: Hope is the character's *agency budget*. A character with 6 Hope has many options open. A character with 0 Hope has only what their dice and their wits can manage. The arc of a session is, in part, the arc of how Hope flows in and out of the players' hands.

## FEAR

Fear is the Keeper's currency. It represents the universe's resistance, the small, accumulating ways the world pushes back against the crew. It is the Veil Frequency in its other register: not the lift of companionship, but the drag of weight, complication, and consequence.

The Keeper tracks Fear in a visible pool, physical tokens, a number on a notepad, a clock-style counter, whatever the table prefers. Visibility is important. The players should know roughly how much Fear the Keeper has, because the dramatic weight of a Keeper spending Fear lands harder when the players have been watching the pool grow.

Fear is generated as follows.

**At the start of each session**, the Keeper rolls **1d4+2** for the starting Fear pool. This pool resets each session, *Fear does not carry over between sessions*. The reset is intentional. Each session begins with the universe roughly at neutral; the game does not punish a crew for having had a hard previous session by starting them already deep in the hole. The Keeper's pressure is renewed but not compounded.

**During the session**, Fear is generated by:

- **Success with Fear** rolls: 1 Fear.

- **Failure with Fear** rolls: 1 Fear.

- **Printed environmental triggers**: an adopted environment rule may generate its stated Fear only when its exact trigger occurs. Merely entering a hostile or Veil-disturbed scene never generates Fear by implication.

- **Explicit rule triggers**: an environment, antagonist, adventure, clock, or feature may generate the stated amount of Fear when its printed trigger occurs. Risk alone never grants Fear; risk determines whether a roll is needed and what consequences are plausible.

Fear is spent on:

- **Spotlight enemies:** Spend 1 Fear to let one eligible NPC that has not yet acted in the current Spotlight cycle take its Spotlight now. This changes order but never grants a second Spotlight in that cycle. A defensive Reaction still requires its own printed trigger.

- **Declare a complication:** Spend 1 Fear after a noncritical Roll to activate one threat, clock trigger, witness, alarm, or equipment risk established before that Roll. Apply its printed or predeclared effect. This move cannot invent damage, item failure, an enemy, or a retroactive fact.

- **Interrupt a player's Action:** After the player declares an Action but before dice are rolled or costs paid, spend 2 Fear to activate one previously established threat. Resolve that threat, then the player may continue, change, or cancel the Action. No cost is lost for changing or canceling it.

- **Trigger an antagonist's signature ability**: Many adversaries have signature abilities that cost Fear. These are detailed in the bestiary (Keeper's Companion).

Fear has a hard maximum of **12**. The pool can never exceed 12; any Fear generated while the pool is full is lost. Hoarding Fear is poor pacing, and unspent Fear is discarded when the pool resets at the next session.

> **GEAR 2, VISIBLE FEAR** *(RECOMMENDED OPTIONAL)*

Many tables benefit from physical tokens for Fear, small stones, dice, glass beads, anything tactile, that the Keeper places in front of themselves as they accumulate. The visual presence of the pool changes the table's emotional register. Players watch the pile grow. Players brace when the Keeper picks one up. This rule is technically optional but is recommended for nearly every table; it costs nothing and meaningfully increases the dramatic weight of the resource.

## STRESS

Stress is the third major resource and the only one tracked symmetrically between every character. It represents the cost of pushing, physical exhaustion, emotional wear, the mounting toll of operating beyond your safe range.

Each character has a **Stress track** with a default capacity of **6**. As the character takes Stress, the player marks boxes on the track. When all boxes are marked, the character is **Overwhelmed**: they cannot mark or spend more Stress, cannot pay Stress costs, and have **Disadvantage on all Rolls** until they clear at least one Stress slot. Overwhelmed does not authorize additional consequences and does not make the character unconscious.

Stress is gained from:

- **Domain Power costs**: Many Domain Powers require the user to take Stress as part of their cost. The Power's entry will specify how much.

- **Specific Class features**: Some Classes have signature abilities that cost Stress.

- **Damage taken in combat**: Some forms of damage are converted directly into Stress rather than HP loss (see Chapter 10).

- **Declared consequences:** A risky Roll may include exactly 1 Stress as a stated consequence fixed before the dice come to rest. A printed feature may impose its stated amount. An interpersonal scene marks Stress without a Roll only with the affected player's consent; the Keeper cannot add unannounced Stress retroactively.

- **Ailuran Irrepressible Curiosity**: An Ailuran character whose Curiosity has been invoked by the Keeper can spend 1 Stress to resist the urge (or yield to it on their own terms, the choice is the player's, and the compulsion is never automatic). See Chapter 3 for the full mechanic.

Stress is cleared by:

- **Long Rest**: Choose **Decompress** as one of the two different Long Rest moves to clear the Stress track, including Long Bruise.

- **Short Rest**: Clears `1d4 + Tier` Stress, if you choose Clear Stress as one of your two moves.

- **Critical Success**: Clears 1 Stress.

- **Specific abilities**: Some Domain Powers, Class features, and Vocations can clear Stress under particular conditions.

Stress is, in a sense, the character's *near-term sustainability budget*. A character can do extraordinary things by spending Stress, but they cannot do extraordinary things forever. The track fills. Rest is required. The game's pacing assumes characters will accumulate Stress over the course of an adventure and clear it during downtime. A campaign without rest beats, a campaign that runs the crew from one crisis to the next without breathing room, will see Stress tracks fill, characters become unable to use their best abilities, and the system's intended rhythm break down. Plan for rest.

## REST AND RECOVERY

Rest restores characters through deliberate choices rather than automatically resetting every track.

### SHORT REST

A Short Rest is a brief pause of roughly one hour in a place where the crew can stop, breathe, and perform basic maintenance. Each character chooses **two different Short Rest moves**:

- **Tend Wounds:** Clear `1d4 + Tier` marked HP.
- **Clear Stress:** Clear `1d4 + Tier` marked Stress.
- **Repair Armor:** With suitable tools or materials, restore `1d4 + Tier` spent Armor Slots, up to the armor's maximum.
- **Prepare:** Gain 1 Hope if Awakened, or 1 Resolve if Sleeping (up to your pool). Rest never generates Effort; the Effort Track is its only source (Chapter 7).

A character cannot choose the same move twice during one Short Rest unless a feature explicitly allows it. Special armor, shields, repair rigs, and class features may restore additional Armor Slots.

### LONG REST

A Long Rest is several hours of safe, uninterrupted recovery. Each character chooses **two different Long Rest moves**:

- **Recover:** Clear all marked HP.
- **Decompress:** Clear all marked Stress, including Long Bruise.
- **Repair All Armor:** Restore all spent Armor Slots.
- **Prepare:** Restore Hope to its normal starting value if Awakened, or restore Resolve to its pool maximum if Sleeping. Rest never generates Effort (Chapter 7).

A character cannot choose the same move twice during one Long Rest unless a feature explicitly allows it. Features that refresh on a Long Rest do so after the chosen moves are resolved.

### DOWNTIME

Downtime lasts days or weeks between active arcs. All HP, Stress, Armor Slots, and renewable character resources return to maximum. Characters may also undertake advancement, projects, training, repairs, relationship work, and other Downtime activities.

## ADVANTAGE AND DISADVANTAGE

When the situation favors or hinders an action, the player rolls with **Advantage** or **Disadvantage**.

A roll with Advantage adds an extra **d6** (the **Hope boon die**) to the total. A roll with Disadvantage adds an extra d6 (the **Fear bane die**) and *subtracts* it from the total. Only one Advantage die or one Disadvantage die may apply to any given roll, they do not stack, regardless of how many sources contributed. If both Advantage and Disadvantage apply to the same roll, they cancel out and the roll proceeds without either.

Sources of Advantage include:

- **Help action**: Another character spends 1 path resource (Hope if Awakened, Effort if Sleeping), or takes 1 Stress if a feature or the Keeper permits it, to assist.

- **Favorable conditions**: The Keeper grants Advantage when the fiction warrants, high ground, a relevant tool, surprise, a well-prepared plan that has been laid in advance.

- **Specific abilities**: Some Class features, Experiences, and Domain Powers grant Advantage on specific roll types.

Sources of Disadvantage include:

- **Adverse conditions**: Wounded, exhausted, in a hostile environment, working with broken equipment.

- **Compounding penalties**: Multiple problems pressing on the same action simultaneously.

- **Specific abilities used against the character**: Some adversaries impose Disadvantage on their targets.

The boon/bane die does not count toward the Hope-vs-Fear comparison. Only the two main d12s determine which side of the duality favored the roll. The d6 is a pure modifier on the total.

## ACTION TYPES

Most rolls in *Veilfarers* are **Standard rolls**: one player rolls, the result is compared to a DC, the outcome is narrated. Most of this chapter so far has assumed Standard rolls. Three additional action types appear regularly enough to warrant explicit description.

**Contested rolls** happen when two characters are actively opposing each other and there is no clean DC to set. Both characters roll a Duality Roll for their respective actions; the higher total wins. If totals are equal, the character whose Hope-vs-Fear comparison was more favorable wins; if those are also equal, the situation continues unresolved and is rerolled or handled narratively. Contested rolls are common in opposed actions like sneaking past a guard, arm-wrestling, or attempting to outmaneuver a pursuer.

**Group rolls** happen when multiple characters attempt the same action together. Before any dice are rolled, fix one standard DC and one threshold from the list below according to the declared task; neither changes after a result is visible:

- **Anyone**: at least one character must succeed.

- **Half**: at least half the group must succeed.

- **Most**: a clear majority must succeed.

- **All**: everyone must succeed.

Each character rolls their own Duality Roll; the success threshold determines whether the group action succeeds. Path resources and Fear are tracked individually for each player Roll, so a group action can produce multiple gains. A group sneak that produces three Successes with Fear gives the Keeper 3 Fear, subject to the hard maximum of 12; the group still gets past the guard.

**Extended actions** are actions that take time or accumulate progress. The Keeper sets up a **progress clock** typically a circle divided into 4, 6, or 8 segments, and each roll the players make against the action fills segments based on the outcome. A standard structure:

- Critical Success: fill 3 segments.

- Success with Hope: fill 2 segments.

- Success with Fear: fill 2 segments, but the Keeper takes 1 Fear, subject to the hard maximum of 12.

- Failure with Hope: fill 1 segment.

- Failure with Fear: fill 0 segments, the Keeper takes 1 Fear, subject to the hard maximum of 12, and a complication arrives.

When the clock fills, the action completes. Extended actions are useful for scenes that should take time, repairing a damaged drive, investigating a complex mystery, persuading a reluctant dignitary across multiple conversations.

> **GEAR 2, TENSION CLOCKS** *(RECOMMENDED OPTIONAL)*

Many Keepers run *opposing* clocks alongside player progress clocks. As the player clock fills toward success, a Keeper-controlled tension clock fills toward consequence, the building alarm, the approaching enemy, the deteriorating situation. Whichever clock fills first determines the outcome. This rule sharpens extended actions by giving them a deadline; it works particularly well in heist-style or chase-style scenes. The Keeper's Companion expands on parallel clocks and their pacing in depth.

## SPOTLIGHT AND PACING

*Veilfarers* does not have rigid initiative outside of structured combat. Most of the time, the **spotlight** moves around the table organically: the Keeper describes a scene, players say what their characters do, the Keeper resolves and describes the consequences, and the cycle continues. Players naturally take turns; characters who have something to do tend to act, and characters who are quiet tend to stay quiet. The Keeper's job is to ensure that no player goes too long without the spotlight resting on them.

A useful pacing tool is the **spotlight check**: at any moment the Keeper should be able to name, off the top of their head, which player has had the spotlight least recently in this session. If the answer is "I don't know," the Keeper should pause, look around the table, and direct attention toward whoever has been quiet. This is not about forcing reluctant players to act; it is about ensuring that players who *want* to act but have been crowded out by louder voices get their moment. In shared scenes, a drone run, a ritual, a bridge crewed by three, move the spotlight by asking who takes control, who interprets, who risks, and who pays. Fictional characters can be quiet for narrative reasons; players generally should not be quiet for table-dynamics reasons.

In combat (Chapter 10), the Spotlight is more structured. Every eligible participant receives one Spotlight per round. NPC Spotlights do not cost Fear; spending 1 Fear only moves one eligible NPC that has not acted yet earlier in the current cycle, and never grants a second Spotlight.

The Hope and Fear economy interacts with spotlight in subtle ways. A player whose character has just had a long spotlight may find that the Keeper is sitting on Fear and looking for a moment to spend it; this is the system telling the table that pressure is mounting and a complication is approaching. A Keeper whose Fear pool is nearly empty cannot push hard, and the players can lean into that breathing room to take risks they might otherwise avoid. The flow of the resources, made visible to the table, becomes part of the pacing language.

## COMMON QUESTIONS AND EDGE CASES

A few questions arise often enough at new tables to warrant explicit answers.

**Can a player spend Hope after seeing the dice?** No. Hope is committed before the roll. The exception is Hope spent on outcomes the player did not choose to spend on, Domain Powers explicitly triggered by a Failure with Hope, for example, or post-roll abilities tied to specific outcomes. The general rule is: pre-roll commitment for advantage; post-roll spends only when the rules text explicitly allows it.

**Can the Keeper raise the DC after the dice are rolled?** No. The DC must be set before the dice come to rest, even if it is not announced to the players. A Keeper who finds themselves wanting to adjust the DC after seeing the result is a Keeper whose intuition about the difficulty was wrong; the correct response is to honor the original number and remember the calibration error for next time.

**What if a player wants to retry a failed action?** The fiction has to support the retry. A failed lockpick attempt cannot simply be re-rolled, the lock has not changed, the character's skill has not changed, and the previous failure is part of the story now. A retry is appropriate when something has *changed*, the character has new information, new equipment, or new help from a teammate. Otherwise, the failure stands and the story moves to whatever happens next.

**What happens at zero path resource?** Nothing mechanical, by itself. A character with zero Hope (Awakened) or zero Effort (Sleeping) simply has none to spend until they earn more. They can still roll Duality Rolls normally, generate path resources on Hope-dominant outcomes, and act on the fiction. The character is operationally fine; they just have fewer options for forcing outcomes.

**What happens at full path resource?** An Awakened character at the 6 Hope cap simply does not gain additional Hope; a Sleeping character at their Effort cap still marks the Effort Track, but a completed track grants nothing until there is room. Rolls that would have produced resource above the cap produce nothing. Many players play at or near the cap intentionally, leaning on Hope as a constant resource. This is fine. The cap exists to prevent unbounded accumulation, not to punish careful play.

**How does the table handle disagreements over what a roll meant?** The fiction-first principle answers most of these. If the Keeper's interpretation of a result feels wrong to the players, the table talks about it. A Keeper who has narrated a Success with Fear in a way that feels unfair can be asked to renegotiate the complication. A player whose Critical Success seems undersold can ask for the bonus to land harder. The dice produce the broad shape of the outcome; the table fills in the specifics together.

**Does the Keeper roll Duality Dice?** Outside of combat, almost never. For non-combat uncertainty, the Keeper sets DCs and adjudicates outcomes; the players roll the dice that resolve it. When a player rolls to deceive a guard, it is the *player* who rolls against a DC the Keeper has set, not the guard rolling Insight against the player's roll. **Combat attack rolls are the standing exception**: the Keeper rolls Duality Dice for every NPC's attack against a target's Evasion, exactly as a player rolls an attack against an NPC's Evasion (Chapter 10, and see *Keeper Critical Damage,* above). This keeps the dice in the players' hands for the game's non-combat uncertainty while giving combat, where both sides are actively opposing each other, its own symmetrical procedure. Some further specific subsystems (mass combat, ship-to-ship, certain extended actions) call for additional Keeper rolls; these are detailed in their respective chapters.

> **GEAR 1, SAYING YES TO STYLE** *(OPTIONAL ATMOSPHERIC RULE)*

When a player invokes a specific fact already established in play and explains how it materially improves the approach, grant Advantage. Style or performance quality alone grants no modifier, and this optional rule never changes a DC after it is fixed.

## PUTTING IT TOGETHER: A WORKED EXAMPLE

The following is a short scene from an imagined session, with all rolls shown.

Captain Maren Solas of the Free Fleet vessel *Vagrant Star* has docked at a station on the rim and learned, from a contact in a back-alley bar, that her engineer Yelena's missing brother is being held by a House Volkov enforcer in a private suite four levels up. Maren has decided to confront the enforcer directly. Her crew, Yelena (engineer, Sleeping); Doctor Tibalt (medic, Awakened Mystic); and Riven (pilot, Awakened, Free Fleet-trained), accompanies her.

The crew rides the lift to level four. The corridor is empty. The suite door is at the end.

The Keeper describes the door, heavy, House Volkov insignia, and asks Maren what she does. Maren chooses to knock, calmly, presenting herself as a courier with a delivery. This is a Presence-based action with deception; the Keeper sets DC 15.

Maren rolls **2d12 - 1 (Presence)**. Hope die shows 6. Fear die shows 10. Total before modifiers: 16. Minus 1 Presence: 15. The Fear die was higher.

**Success with Fear**, total 15 vs DC 15. The door opens, but the Volkov enforcer at the threshold takes one look at Maren, recognizes she is not actually a courier, and decides he is interested in why she is pretending to be one. The Keeper takes 1 Fear, subject to the hard maximum of 12.

The enforcer asks Maren to come in and explain herself. The crew enters. The room is luxurious, ill-lit, and holds two more Volkov enforcers Maren had not anticipated. Yelena's brother is sitting on a chair against the back wall, alive but not unbound.

Maren considers her options. She is outnumbered and the situation has shifted. Riven, who is good in a fight but worse in a conversation, declares he wants to scan the room for tactical opportunities, exits, cover, line-of-sight problems, before anyone makes a decisive move. This is a Knowledge-based observation roll. The Keeper sets DC 10.

Riven rolls **2d12 + 1 (Knowledge)**. Hope die shows 9. Fear die shows 4. Total: 14. Hope was higher.

**Success with Hope**, total 14 vs DC 10. Riven gains 1 Hope. The Keeper describes what Riven sees: a service door behind a tapestry on the left wall, a window that opens onto an exterior gantry, and a tell on the head enforcer's body language that suggests he is more nervous than he is showing.

Maren now has actionable information. She pivots: rather than continuing the courier ruse, she addresses the head enforcer directly, naming him by what she can guess of his rank, and offers to negotiate for the brother's release. This is a Presence Roll to persuade, and the Keeper, given the difficulty of the situation, sets DC 20.

Maren (Awakened) spends 1 Hope to invoke her Experience: *Free Fleet Lifer*, +2.

Maren rolls **2d12 - 1 (Presence) + 2 (Experience)**. Hope die shows 9. Fear die shows 9.

**Critical Success**. The doubles override the comparison; the result is automatic and exceptional. Maren is Awakened, so she gains 1 Hope and clears 1 Stress.

The Keeper describes the result: the head enforcer's posture shifts. He has been hoping someone would offer him a face-saving way out of this contract, which has gone badly and which his House superiors are not going to be pleased about. He lowers his weapon, gestures for the others to do the same, and tells Maren he will release the brother in exchange for her solemn word that she will not report the encounter to House Valerius. Maren agrees. The brother is freed. The crew leaves.

This is approximately five minutes of session time. It involved three rolls, one Success with Fear, one Success with Hope, one Critical Success, and saw 1 Fear into the Keeper's pool, 2 Hope and 1 Stress cleared into the players' hands, and one tense scene resolved without violence. The five-outcome Duality Roll structure gave the scene its texture: the door opened with a complication; the observation gave a clean win; the negotiation broke through cleanly when the universe simply *agreed* with what Maren was trying to do.

A thousand such scenes build into a campaign.

## WHAT COMES NEXT

This chapter has introduced the Duality Roll, the resources that flow with it, and the action types that extend it. **Chapter 10** covers personal combat in detail: turn structure, damage, conditions, and death moves. Ship-to-ship engagement is its own scale and has its own chapter, **Chapter 17**. **Chapter 11** covers multiclassing and the addition of a second Calling. **Chapter 12** covers advancement, how characters grow over the arc of a campaign. Rest and recovery are defined in this chapter.

For Keepers, the **Keeper's Companion** covers the philosophy and pacing of running *Veilfarers* tables. The technical procedures are in this chapter; the art of running them is there.

For now: you have the resolution mechanic. You have Hope, Fear, Stress, and the DC ladder. You have enough to play. The next thing the system asks you to learn is what happens when the talking stops, when the dice come out for a different reason, and the room becomes something the crew has to survive.

Combat is next.

# CHAPTER 10: THE WEIGHT OF STEEL

*"There is a moment, after the first shot, before anyone has thought to fire the second, when you can still feel the room. You can still hear breath. You can still smell the air the way it smelled before. After the second shot, you can hear nothing for a while, and the air smells of metal, and the people who are going to die have started*

*dying. Spend that moment well. It is the only one you get."*

Sergeant-Instructor Hira Volkov, Joric Defensive Academy, opening lecture, On the Discipline of the First

***Beat***

## WHAT THIS CHAPTER IS FOR

**At a glance.** Combat in *Veilfarers* uses the **Duality Roll** from Chapter 9 plus four mechanical layers: **HP** (your life), **Stress** (your composure), **Armor Slots** (a pool that absorbs hits before the body; characters, drones, and vehicles all use the same armor terminology), and **Damage Thresholds** (Major/Severe, these decide how each hit lands). Each round, characters take **one Action** during their **Spotlight**. Attacks roll against **Evasion**; on a hit, roll weapon damage, apply Proficiency scaling, then compare the result to the target's Damage Thresholds. The fiction governs everything; the numbers describe outcomes.

Chapter 9 taught you to roll the Duality Dice. This chapter is what happens when the rolls have weapons in them.

It is not a new game. Combat uses the same Duality Dice, the same Hope and Effort, the same Spotlight and fiction-first principles; only the **stakes** change, because this is where the body breaks and the crew can lose someone. Where this chapter and Chapter 9 ever seem to disagree, Chapter 9 is the foundation, and the first question in any fight is still *what does my character do?* The dice come after.

## WHEN COMBAT BEGINS

Combat begins when the fiction tips into violence, and violence becomes the most interesting question in the room. A few patterns:

- **The Ambush.** One side is unprepared. The Keeper narrates the trigger: a door opens, a shot is fired, a body falls. The unprepared side reacts. (See *The First Beat,* below.)

- **The Standoff.** Both sides are aware. Weapons are drawn or implied. The room is tense. The first action, the first roll, is the question of who breaks the tension and how.

- **The Slide.** A scene that did not start as combat tips into it. A negotiation breaks down; a search uncovers a hostile presence; a calm moment is interrupted by an alarm. The Keeper marks the transition by calling for the first combat-relevant roll.

**What a round is.** A **round** is one full pass of the Spotlight: it ends the moment every eligible participant, players and the Keeper's NPCs alike, has taken one Spotlight. Effects that trigger "at the end of each round" - Bleeding, On Fire, a Veil-Disturbed roll - resolve at that moment, before the next pass begins. The Spotlight is the unit of action; the round is the unit of time built from it.

In all three patterns, the structural change is the same: **the Spotlight tightens.** Outside of combat, the Spotlight passes loosely from player to player as the scene unfolds. Inside combat, it passes deliberately, around the table and to the Keeper's NPCs in turn, with each holder taking one significant action before passing it on.

### THE FIRST BEAT

The first action of any combat scene is, by tradition, the most narratively weighted. It sets the tone, establishes positions, and often determines how the rest of the scene will pace. The Keeper should treat the first beat with care:

- **In an Ambush:** the aggressor takes the first Spotlight. The defending players choose which of their characters receives the first PC Spotlight in response.

- **In a Standoff:** the participant whose declared Action breaks the tension takes the first Spotlight. If declarations are genuinely simultaneous, the players choose one PC to act first, then the Keeper takes the next eligible Spotlight. Do not roll initiative.

- **In a Slide:** the player whose scene was interrupted takes the first Spotlight. The Keeper is patient with them; the slide is disorienting, and the first action can be a reaction rather than a strike.

The first beat is not the most important roll; the third or fourth often is. But it is the one the table remembers, and it deserves a moment of attention.

## THE ATTACK ROLL

When you act against an opponent who is trying to avoid being hit, you make an **Attack Roll**. This is a specific shape of Core Trait Roll.

### PROCEDURE

- **Choose the Trait.** Usually obvious from the action: melee strikes use Strength or Finesse; ranged weapons use Finesse or Instinct; certain class abilities specify their own Trait. The Keeper has final say in ambiguous cases.

- **Roll the Duality Dice.** Two d12, as always, with the Hope/Fear distinction.

- **Add modifiers.** Your Trait modifier, any relevant Experience invocation (spend 1 Hope or Effort), any situational bonuses or penalties (Advantage, cover, suppressive fire, equipment, scene effects).

- **Compare to the target's Evasion.** Evasion is the target's passive defense Difficulty Class. Equal to or above is a hit; below is a miss.

> **QUICK PROCEDURE - THE ATTACK ROLL**
>
> | STEP | WHAT HAPPENS |
> | --- | --- |
> | 1. Declare | Weapon, target, range band, and what it looks like in the fiction. |
> | 2. Attack roll | Duality Roll + Trait vs the target's **Evasion**. Matched dice hit automatically and critically, whatever the total. |
> | 3. Damage | On a hit, roll weapon damage and apply **Proficiency** scaling. |
> | 4. Penetration | The damage type may lower the target's thresholds for this hit (Energy −2, Void −4). Reflective cancels Energy; Wards cancel Void/Neural. |
> | 5. Thresholds | Compare the total to **Major / Severe** for severity; **Overkill** adds 1 HP per 10 over Severe. |
> | 6. Armor | The defender may mark an **Armor Slot** to drop the severity one tier. |
> | 7. Mark HP | The target marks the resulting HP. |
> | 8. The dice speak | On a player attack, resolve Path progress or Fear as normal. On a Keeper-controlled attack, nonmatching dominance grants no resource; only a printed action rider may use it. |

### HIT, MISS, CRITICAL

- **Miss (below Evasion):** The attack does not connect. On a player attack, resolve Path progress or Fear and only an established Failure-with-Fear complication. On a Keeper-controlled attack, nonmatching dominance grants no resource or free complication; a printed action rider may still apply.

- **Hit (equal to or above Evasion):** The attack connects. Roll damage; see below.

- **Critical Hit (matched Duality Dice, both** **showing the same number):** A signature moment, and it does not care about the total. Matched dice are a Critical Success everywhere in this game (Chapter 9), and combat is not an exception: a Critical Hit **connects regardless of the target's Evasion**. A pair of ones against a heavily armored foe still lands. Roll **double the weapon's damage** **dice** (keep modifiers single) and clear 1 Stress. An **Awakened** character also gains **+1 Hope**. A **Sleeping** character instead resolves the critical as Chapter 7 defines it: mark both Effort Track segments, clear the completed Track to gain 1 Effort, then gain one further point in either Effort or Resolve; if Effort is at maximum, take Resolve. See *Critical Damage,* below, for the full treatment.

### SPENDING HOPE OR EFFORT ON THE ATTACK

Before rolling, you may declare that one of your **Experiences** applies to this attack. An **Awakened** character spends **1 Hope** to invoke it. A **Sleeping** character spends **nothing**: the Sleeping invoke their Experiences free, once per roll, as Chapter 7 sets out. Add the Experience's flat modifier to the roll. *I held the line at Titan Station* might apply to a defensive shot in a corridor; *Hunter on the Edge of the Wastes* might apply to a long-range rifle shot. The Keeper has final say on relevance.

You may also spend Hope to grant another character **Advantage** on their next attack (see Chapter 9). This is a powerful crew-level option that is often undervalued: a Diplomat with 4 Hope can convert two of them into Advantage for two ally shots, which is sometimes more impactful than the Diplomat spending them on a class feature.

### UNARMED STRIKES

**Unarmed strikes.** An unarmed strike is a Melee attack (Strength) dealing **d4** physical damage. Proficiency applies normally. Ancestry gifts and class features that modify unarmed damage build on this baseline.

## DAMAGE, PROFICIENCY, AND ARMOR

If the attack hits, you roll damage. The procedure:

### THE DAMAGE ROLL

- **Roll the weapon's damage dice.** Each weapon lists a die expression, *1d6*, *2d8*, *1d10+2,* and so on. Roll that expression.

- **Apply Proficiency to one listed die.** A weapon's damage expression is its base damage. Choose one die in that expression as the Proficiency Die; for standard weapons, this is the first listed die. Roll that die once per Proficiency rank, and roll every other listed die once. Add the listed flat modifier once. Thus, a `2d8+2` weapon at Proficiency 3 deals `4d8+2`: three copies of one d8, plus the second base d8, plus 2. A `3d6` weapon at Proficiency 2 deals `4d6`. For mixed-die expressions, the weapon entry must identify the Proficiency Die.

- **Add the weapon's damage modifier.** Listed alongside the dice (the *+2* in *1d10+2*).

- **Do not add Trait modifiers to damage.** Trait modifiers go on the *attack roll,* not the *damage roll.* This is intentional and keeps the math fast.

### DAMAGE THRESHOLDS & ARMOR

Once damage is rolled, the target compares the total against their two **Damage Thresholds**, **Major** and **Severe**, determined by their level and their armor. Where the total falls sets how many HP the hit marks:

- **Minor (below the Major Threshold):** the hit marks **1 HP**. Any attack that connects and is not soaked away costs at least this much.

- **Major (at or above the Major Threshold, below** **the Severe Threshold):** the hit marks **2 HP**.

- **Severe (at or above the Severe Threshold):** the hit marks **3 HP**.

- **Overkill:** for every full **10 points** by which the damage total exceeds the Severe Threshold, the hit marks **1 additional HP** (Severe plus 10 marks 4 HP, plus 20 marks 5, and so on). Under the optional **Deadly** variant for grittier campaigns, mark 1 additional HP for every **5 points** over Severe instead.

- **Natural Thresholds (no armor).** If you are wearing no armor, your **base Damage Thresholds are Major 2 / Severe 4**, unless an Ancestry Gift says otherwise. Any level bonuses or effects that raise your thresholds still apply on top of the base. Skin, cloth, and everyday clothing do not count as armor: they neither raise your thresholds nor grant Armor Slots.

This means the *amount* of damage rolled translates to *severity* of harm rather than direct HP-by-HP conversion. A glancing 6-point shot hurts the same way as an 11-point shot if both fall below the Major Threshold. A 22-point shot that crosses into Severe territory hurts the same as a 28-point shot that does, until a total climbs a full 10 past the threshold and Overkill begins to bite. This is deliberate: it makes weapons feel weighty (you know if you got hit *badly*) without the math turning combat into a calculator. A hit marks **no** HP only when your armor soaks it entirely (an Armor Slot dropping a Minor hit to nothing), not because a low roll is ignored: any attack that connects costs at least 1 HP unless something actively absorbs it.

### WHAT YOUR DEFENSES DO

It is worth being explicit about what each defensive layer actually does, because they work in sequence and every one of them matters:

> **QUICK PROCEDURE - THE DEFENSE STACK**
>
> | LAYER | WHAT IT DECIDES | IN PLAY |
> | --- | --- | --- |
> | **Evasion** | Whether you are hit at all | An attack that fails to meet your Evasion does nothing. |
> | **Damage Thresholds (Major / Severe)** | How hard a hit lands once it connects | Better armor and higher level raise your thresholds - most hits against a well-armored target land as a single HP. |
> | **Armor Slots** | Active soak on top of the thresholds | Mark one to drop a hit a full severity tier, including a Minor hit to no HP at all. |
> | **HP** | The body itself | Marked only after the thresholds and any marked Armor Slots have done their work. |

The intent is simple: armor should absorb the brunt of most attacks. A character in good armor shrugs off the majority of hits as a single HP, spends slots to blunt the dangerous ones (or to wave off a glancing hit entirely), and only bleeds real HP when something heavy, sustained, or *penetrating* gets through. Penetration is the job of the damage type, covered later in this chapter.

### ARMOR SLOTS

Armor reduces specific incoming hits via **Armor Slots.** Each armor piece provides a maximum number of slots. Spent slots are restored by choosing **Repair Armor** during a Short Rest or **Repair All Armor** during a Long Rest. Specific gear and abilities may restore additional slots. When you would take HP damage from an attack, you may spend one Armor Slot to **reduce the damage tier**

**by one step** (Overkill becomes Severe, Severe becomes Major, Major becomes Minor, Minor becomes no HP). Armor Slots are a precious tactical resource, there are scenes where you want to save them for the inevitable third or fourth hit rather than block the first.

A few effects interact with this soak directly. *Crushing* weapons ignore one Armor Slot per hit as the plating buckles. The penetrating damage types (Energy and Void) do **not** ignore Armor Slots; instead they lower your thresholds for the hit, see **Damage Types**, later in this chapter. Nothing in standard Veilfarers ignores your thresholds outright: armor always does *something.*

> **WORKED EXAMPLE - SPENDING AN ARMOR SLOT**
>
> A shot rolls 24 against Saber's thresholds of Major 9 / Severe 17 - Severe, 3 HP incoming. She marks an Armor Slot: the hit drops one tier, to Major, and she marks 2 HP instead of 3. The slot did not subtract 24 down to some lower number; it moved the *hit itself* one rung down the Minor -> Major -> Severe ladder.
>
> **Rule Take-Away:** An Armor Slot reduces the severity *tier* of a hit, not the damage total rolled. A Crushing weapon's ignored slot works the other way - it removes the defender's ability to spend a slot on that hit at all; it does not add anything to the incoming damage.

### DIRECT DAMAGE

Some effects deal **direct HP damage**: the target marks the listed HP without rolling damage against Thresholds and without spending Armor Slots, unless the effect states otherwise. Direct damage is the shared language of structural trauma, of certain Powers, and of technology that ignores plate entirely; when a rule says *mark N HP directly*, this is what it means. If an effect says you take 2 HP, mark 2 HP.

### CRITICAL DAMAGE

This is the **player-character** procedure. When a player character scores a Critical Success on an attack roll (matched Duality Dice, whatever the total), they deal **Critical Damage:** roll **double the weapon's damage dice** and add modifiers once. A weapon that deals 2d8+2 with Proficiency 2 (i.e., 4d8+2 at standard scale) becomes **8d8+2** on a Critical Damage roll. A weapon that deals 4d10+4 with Proficiency 2 (effectively 8d10+4) becomes **16d10+4** on a Critical.

Critical Damage does **not** automatically push the target into Severe or Overkill territory, the rolled total still compares against thresholds. But the doubled dice make it more likely. A Soldier on a Critical Damage roll against a lightly armored opponent is often a one-shot kill, and that is by design: the Soldier earned the moment.

Critical Damage applies to ship weapons and to Domain Powers that resolve via attack rolls. It does *not* apply to abilities that deal *automatic* damage (no attack roll involved) or to environmental hazards that resolve on Reaction Rolls rather than attacks.

**Keeper-controlled adversaries do not roll Critical Damage.** When a Keeper-controlled attacker scores a Critical Success, use *Keeper Critical Damage* instead (Chapter 9, under *Reading the Outcome*): every damage die in the attack's normal pool is treated as having rolled its maximum value, with no dice rolled at all. The two procedures produce a comparable spike in severity without asking the Keeper to roll double dice pools for every adversary at the table.

## HP, DYING, AND DEATH

Every character has **Hit Points.** When you take damage, you mark HP slots off your sheet. When all HP are marked, you are **Dying.**

### THE DYING STATE

A character who has marked all their HP is Dying, not dead. Dying is a state, not an event. While Dying:

- **You cannot take actions.** You are unconscious, gravely wounded, or otherwise out of the fight.

- **You are not yet beyond saving.** Allies may attempt to stabilize you (Medical Technician class features apply; the basic Stabilize action requires an adjacent ally and a Knowledge or Finesse roll DC 15).

- **At the beginning of each of your Spotlights while Dying, roll 1d12.** On an 8 or higher, mark 1 Dying Progress. On a 7 or lower, mark no progress and remain Dying. When you mark your second Dying Progress, you enter *Final.*

### THE FINAL STATE

A character who has reached Final has minutes, sometimes seconds, left. While Final:

- **Stabilization requires a higher DC.** Use a Knowledge or Finesse Roll against DC 20, or a Medical Technician's specialized Stabilize feature.

- **Some classes can revive you.** The Sleeping Medical Technician's *Last Rite* Mastery feature, certain Mystic procedures, and rare Synthesis Powers can pull a Final character back. Most cannot.

- **At the beginning of each of your Spotlights while Final, roll 1d12.** On an 8 or higher, mark 1 Final Progress. When you mark your second Final Progress, the character dies. Stabilization clears all Dying and Final Progress but does not restore HP.

### THE DEATH MOVE: BLAZE OF GLORY

A Dying or Final character may choose to spend their last moment on a **Death Move**, a final act called a **Blaze of Glory**. It is always optional and always the player's choice. Declaring it on your Spotlight replaces your Dying or Final Progress roll: you act one last time, at the height of your power, and then your character dies.

When you make a Death Move, choose one:

- **Overload a Power.** Resolve one Power you can normally use at **double its normal effect**, doubling its dice, duration, targets, or area as the Power defines.

- **Reach beyond your grasp.** Resolve one Power up to **two Levels higher** than you can normally cast, drawing on a Power your character could not otherwise reach.

- **A perfect final act.** Take one action and treat it as an automatic **Critical Success**, with no roll.

- **A killing blow.** Deal damage equal to the **maximum result of your damage dice, resolved as a Critical Success**: maximum dice plus the critical bonus.

A Death Move is a true sacrifice. Once it resolves, the character **dies irrevocably**. They cannot be stabilized, revived, or resurrected by any feature, Power, ancestry trait, or circumstance, and the Long Aftermath does not apply. The death is chosen, final, and complete.

Ship-scale weapon damage uses the same Dying, Final, and voluntary Death Move procedure; see Chapter 17.

### DEATH

When a character dies in Veilfarers, they die. The Keeper and the table acknowledge the death. The player takes a short break if they want one. A new character can be introduced in the next session, or the existing player can run an existing NPC for a session, or the table can simply continue with the remaining crew.

Death is **rare** in standard Veilfarers, the threshold system, Armor Slots, Stress mechanics, and the Dying-not-Dead structure all combine to make on-screen PC death an unusual outcome. But death is **possible**, and the system supports it intentionally. A campaign in which no PC has ever been in danger of dying is a campaign whose stakes have never quite been real. The Keeper should not seek deaths; the Keeper should also not prevent them when the fiction calls for them.

### THE LONG AFTERMATH

A character who is brought back from Dying or Final does not return at full HP. The default is *return at 1 HP, with one Stress slot newly marked as Long Bruise,* representing the body's memory of having almost ended. Long Bruise persists across short rests; only a Long Rest clears it. Some Mastery features and ancestry traits (Bloomstrider Healing Sap, certain Synthetic features) modify this; consult the relevant entries.

Healing is reflavored by what you are. Organics use First Aid, stims, and rest; a Synthetic is repaired, not treated, and gains nothing from organic medicine. A Synthetic mends mid-fight by injecting Reconstructive Nanites, its equivalent of a stim, or out of combat through self-repair and an engineer's tools. See Chapter 13 for both.

## RANGE BANDS AND POSITIONING

Veilfarers uses **abstract range bands**, not a grid. Positions in combat are described by which band the character occupies relative to other combatants and to features of the scene.

### THE FIVE BANDS

- **Melee:** Within arm's reach. Hand-to-hand range, knife range, point-blank pistol range. Most melee weapons require Melee. Many ranged weapons take penalties or are unusable at Melee.

- **Very Close:** Within five meters or so, across a room, down a short corridor. Most ranged combat happens here. This is the band that defines "in the fight" for most Veilfarers encounters.

- **Close:** Five to twenty meters. A long room, a city street, a clearing in the brush. Most rifles operate well at Close. Pistols take a penalty.

- **Far:** Twenty to a hundred meters. The far end of a warehouse, a city block, the length of a docking bay. Specialized weapons; sniper territory.

- **Very Far:** Beyond Far. Visible but functionally out of normal combat reach. Requires explicit equipment (long-range scopes, vehicle-mounted weaponry, sniper rifles) to engage.

### MOVEMENT BETWEEN BANDS

Moving one range band is **a free part of your action**, in most cases, you can take an action and move one band as the same Spotlight beat. Moving two bands costs your action; moving three bands is, for most characters, only possible across multiple turns. Class features and Domain Powers may modify this (the Ailuran *Metabolic Burst* moves *two* bands free as part of an action, for instance).

Movement remains normal unless a location, Environment Feature, or equipment entry declared before movement states otherwise. **Difficult Terrain** makes movement of one band consume the character's Action and prevents movement of two bands in the same Spotlight without an explicit feature. Zero-G, vertical movement, and other special traversal use their printed environment or equipment procedure; description alone creates no hidden Roll or penalty.

### COVER

Characters in cover gain defensive bonuses:

- **Light Cover** (waist-high obstacles, partial concealment): +1 Evasion against ranged attacks.

- **Heavy Cover** (full-body obstacles, doorways, vehicle hulls): +3 Evasion against ranged attacks. Some ranged attacks may be blocked entirely if line of sight is broken.

- **Total Cover** (full concealment, no line of sight): cannot be targeted by direct attacks. Indirect attacks (grenades, area effects) may still affect.

A character announcing they are taking cover (a free effect, on their Spotlight) gains the appropriate bonus until they move or take an aggressive action that breaks cover.

### LINE OF SIGHT

A character cannot be targeted by a direct attack if they cannot be seen by the attacker. Hidden characters (see *The Hidden Condition,* below), characters behind Total Cover, and characters in heavy fog, smoke, or Veil- induced visual disturbance are not valid targets for direct attacks.

This is sometimes ambiguous; the Keeper has final say.

## CONDITIONS

When a character takes a condition, through an attack, an effect, an environmental hazard, or a Domain Power, the condition modifies their capabilities until cleared. The canonical conditions are listed below; a handful of abilities reference bespoke named conditions (Bloomstrider Sap-Bleed, Synthetic Recursive Doubt) defined in their respective entries.

Weapon features that apply conditions (*Stunning, Entangling, Knockdown, Ignite,* and the rest of the Chapter 13 glossary) state their own trigger, Resistance Roll, and DC. A feature's Resistance line names the roll used to resist it: the listed Trait as a Reaction Roll against the feature's DC. The condition itself always works as written here.

### THE STANDARD CONDITIONS

- **Bleeding.** Mark 1 Stress at the end of each round until stopped (First Aid, or any healing effect). Targets that do not bleed, including most Synthetics, are immune.
- **Blinded.** Disadvantage on attacks and Instinct rolls. Cleared by removing the visual obstruction or a successful Long Rest.
- **Confused.** On your Spotlight, you act against the nearest creature, ally or enemy, or as the inflicting effect specifies. Cleared at the end of the stated duration, or when an ally spends an action to snap you out of it (Presence or Knowledge, DC 10).
- **Cornered.** Cannot move out of Melee with the attacking character. Disadvantage on Agility and Finesse rolls until the cornering ends. Cleared by moving the cornering character out of Melee, knocking them down, or escaping by a successful Strength or Finesse contest (DC 10).
- **Dazed.** Disadvantage on the character's next single action. Cleared after the action resolves.
- **Fleeing.** On your Spotlight, you must move away from the source by the most direct safe route and cannot take aggressive actions against it. Cleared at the end of the stated duration, or when you can no longer see or hear the source.
- **Frightened.** Disadvantage on rolls made against the source of the fear, and you cannot willingly move closer to it. Cleared at the end of the stated duration, when the source is gone, or by an effect that steadies the mind.
- **Hidden.** Cannot be directly targeted by ranged attacks; Advantage on the character's next attack from cover. Broken when the character takes an aggressive action, moves out of cover, or fails an Agility Roll to maintain concealment in changing circumstances.
- **Incapacitated.** Cannot take actions, reactions, or movement; you are unconscious or helpless, but not Dying. Cleared at the end of the stated duration, or when an ally spends an action to rouse you (Knowledge or Instinct, DC 10). Damage dealt to an Incapacitated target hits automatically.
- **Infected.** A wound or contamination is working against you. The inflicting effect states the symptom (commonly 1 Stress per round, or HP that cannot be healed by normal means). Persists through rests until treated: a Knowledge roll with medical training (DC 15), a specialized antidote, or Tier 2+ medical care.
- **On Fire.** Take 1d4 Energy damage with the Fire tag at the end of each round until extinguished by your Action, an ally's Action, immersion, or a source-specific method. Damage applies to Thresholds normally.
- **Poisoned.** Mark 1 Stress at the end of each round until treated (First Aid DC 10, an antidote, or a Long Rest) or until the stated duration ends. Some poisons state a different effect; the source's text prevails. Synthetics and targets immune to toxins ignore this condition.
- **Prone.** Disadvantage on attacks; ranged attackers gain Advantage against you. Cleared by spending a part of an action to stand (free if moving one band).
- **Restrained.** Cannot move. Disadvantage on Agility and Strength rolls. Cleared by an ally taking an action to free you, or by a successful Strength roll (DC 15) on your Spotlight.
- **Silenced.** Cannot speak, cast verbal-component Domain Powers, or coordinate verbally. Cleared by the silencing effect's stated duration or by removing the source.
- **Stunned.** Cannot take any action. Cleared after the next round, or when an ally takes an Action to rouse you with a Knowledge or Instinct Roll, DC 10.
- **Vulnerable.** Attacks against you have Advantage until the condition ends. Cleared at the end of the stated duration; if the source states none, it ends at the end of your next Spotlight.
- **Weakened.** Disadvantage on Strength rolls, and your damage rolls lose your flat modifiers (dice are unaffected). Cleared by the method the source states, or by a Long Rest.

### STACKING AND CLEARING

Conditions are durations, not pools, a character is either Stunned or not, regardless of how many sources tried to stun them. A new application does not extend the duration; it refreshes it (the higher of the two durations applies).

A character with multiple conditions applies all of them: a Blinded, Prone character has Disadvantage on attacks (twice, but Disadvantage does not stack mechanically; it just is) and grants Advantage to attackers. The character can still act; they will simply do so badly.

Some Domain Powers and class features apply *Inflicted* versions of conditions that are harder to clear or carry additional effects. These are described per ability.

> **GEAR, CONDITIONS VS STATES.** *Conditions* are what the fight does to you; they clear fast and are listed above. *States* are what the campaign does to you, and each is defined where its system lives: **Dying** and **Final** (this chapter, under HP), **Overwhelmed** (Chapter 9), **Burned Out** (Chapter 7, Sleeping path), and **Long Bruise** (this chapter, under returning from Dying). A Bounty Hunter's *marked quarry* is a class mechanic, not a condition.

## HEALING IN COMBAT

Combat healing is fast, partial, and dramatic. There are three main healing avenues during a combat scene:

### FIRST AID

Any character may, as an action, perform First Aid on an **organic** ally within Melee range. Synthetics gain nothing from it; see *Field Repair,* below. This requires:

- **A Knowledge or Finesse roll, DC 10.**

- **Access to a basic medkit.** Most characters carry one as part of their starting kit.

On Success: the ally clears 1 HP (one slot) and clears the *Bleeding* condition if present.

On Success with Hope: as Success, plus the ally also clears 1 Stress.

On Failure: no effect. On Failure with Fear: the patient becomes Dazed until the end of their next Spotlight and the medkit use is consumed. Bleeding does not worsen beyond its printed condition.

### FIELD REPAIR

A Synthetic is repaired, not treated. Any character may, as an action, perform **Field Repair** on a Synthetic ally within Melee range. This requires a **Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 10**, and an engineer's toolkit or a dose of Reconstructive Nanites (Chapter 13) in place of a medkit. On Success the ally clears 1 HP. On Success with Hope it also clears 1 Stress. On Failure there is no effect. On Failure with Fear the Synthetic becomes Dazed until the end of its next Spotlight and the toolkit use or nanite dose is consumed.

### CLASS HEALING FEATURES

Several classes have signature healing abilities. The Engineer's Medical Technician subclass is the obvious specialist; certain Diplomat and Vanguard subclasses also have healing-adjacent features. See the relevant class entries.

### ANCESTRY-GRANTED HEALING

The Bloomstrider Healing Sap feature is a heal-over-time effect (1 HP per Spotlight for 1d4 of the affected character's Spotlights). Some other ancestry features grant minor regeneration or specific resistance. These are not actions; they apply automatically when triggered.

### WHAT HEALING DOES NOT DO IN COMBAT

- **Healing does not clear the Dying or Final** **state.** A Dying character must be *Stabilized* (DC 15 or higher, depending on state) before normal healing applies. A character cannot be healed back to full HP mid-combat by routine means; the design assumes some persistent injury until the scene ends.

- **Healing does not clear Long Bruise.** That's a Long Rest mechanic only.

- **Healing does not undo Stress in most cases.** Stress is a separate track (Chapter 9); only specific effects clear it.

## SPECIAL COMBAT ACTIONS

Beyond standard attacks, combat permits a range of named special actions. Most are available to any character; some require specific class features or proficiency.

### AIM

You may spend an action to *aim* at a specific target. Your next attack against that target, taken before your next Spotlight, gains **Advantage.** Aiming is a strong choice when the target is critical (a Keeper-named enemy, a fleeing NPC, a fragile system on a vehicle); it is a poor choice when you might be interrupted before the follow-up.

### DISARM

You attack with the explicit goal of stripping a target's weapon from its grip rather than wounding it, so the **attack Roll takes a -4 penalty**. On a Hit you deal no damage; the target chooses Strength or Finesse and makes a Reaction Roll against your attack total. On failure the weapon falls at Melee range, or one band away on a Critical Success; on success the target keeps it. Retrieving it is part of an Action. A weapon fixed to the body or an object the attacker cannot physically move is an invalid target, and the Keeper must state that before the Roll.

### PUSH

You attack with the explicit goal of moving the target one range band away. Resolve as a normal attack; on a Hit, no damage, but the target moves one band. On Critical, two bands and the target is Prone. Push is a strong tactical option in environments with hazards (cliffs, open spaces, doors that close).

### GRAPPLE

You initiate a clinch with an adjacent target. Resolve via an opposed Strength roll. On Success, the target is *Restrained* and so are you (you are both grappling). The grapple is maintained until one of you breaks free (Strength contest on your Spotlight) or one of you falls Unconscious.

### SUPPRESS

You unload a sustained burst from a ranged weapon at an area, aiming to make it unsafe rather than hit a specific target. Before the Roll, set **DC 10 for open ground, DC 15 for broken or Light Cover, or DC 20 for fortified or Heavy Cover**. Make one Finesse or Instinct Roll. On success, every enemy in the targeted area not in Total Cover has Disadvantage on its next Action before your next Spotlight; no damage is dealt. Suppression consumes ammunition rapidly, so the weapon's *Ammo* tag applies if present.

Do not confuse this action with the ***Suppressive*** weapon tag (Chapter 13), which any character can use *without* giving up their attack. The action costs your whole Spotlight and hobbles every action in the area; the tag rides along with a normal attack for 1 Stress and hobbles attacks only. A character carrying a Suppressive weapon may do either, and the choice is a real one.

### CALLED SHOT

Choose one visible called effect before attacking: make one held item drop at Melee range, make one fictionally exposed device go offline until an Action and Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 10, restores it, or make the target Dazed. The attack has Disadvantage and deals no damage on a Hit; on a Critical Success it also deals its normal damage. An impossible target must be rejected before the Roll.

### DEFEND

You spend your action focused on *not being hit.* Gain +2 Evasion until your next Spotlight. A weak action by itself; a strong action when combined with cover, or when used to wait for an ally's intervention.

## STRESS IN COMBAT

Combat is, by its nature, stressful. Beyond the HP track, characters accumulate **Stress** during combat, from near-misses, from witnessing wounds, from the specific cognitive load of violence.

The standard Stress triggers in combat:

- **Marking a Severe wound.** Mark 1 Stress.

- **Watching an ally fall to Dying.** Mark 1 Stress.

- **Burning out (Sleeping path).** Spending HP for Effort, as Burnout, marks 1 Stress automatically.

- **Specific class abilities.** Some class features mark Stress as part of their cost or consequence; follow the feature's current text.

- **Declared mental stakes.** On Failure with Fear, a character may mark 1 Stress as the complication only when shock, terror, exposure, or cognitive overload was named as a plausible stake before the Roll. This is the result's single complication, not an additional penalty.

A character whose Stress slots are all marked is **Overwhelmed.** Overwhelmed characters take Disadvantage on all rolls until they clear at least one slot. Clearing Stress in combat is rare, some class features (the Soldier's *Rally,* the Vanguard's *Unbroken Focus*) permit it; otherwise, Stress is cleared by Short and Long Rests outside of combat.

The interplay of HP, Stress, and resource pools (Hope or Effort) is the core texture of how combat *feels* in Veilfarers. A character with full HP and full Stress is *not okay,* even though they are taking no immediate injury. A character with low HP and zero Stress is *grimly competent.* The system is designed to surface both states in interesting ways.

## CRITICAL HITS

Matching Duality Dice always resolve as a Critical Success, including 1+1. Apply the master payout and the appropriate player or Keeper critical-damage procedure. A nonmatching roll below its DC with Fear dominant is Failure with Fear, the worst normal result. Do not attach a separate negative-critical table, automatic friendly fire, equipment breakage, or catastrophic blowback to matched dice.

## MULTI-TARGET AND AREA EFFECTS

Some attacks affect more than one target. These come in two main shapes:

### BURST FIRE AND MULTI-ATTACK

A weapon with the *Burst* tag, or a class ability that grants multi-target attacks, resolves as a *single attack roll* against each target in range. Damage is rolled separately per target. Hope/Fear distinctions are tracked per-attack. A Burst weapon firing at three targets makes three attack rolls; each can independently Hit, Miss, or Critical.

### AREA EFFECTS

A Power, weapon, or environmental hazard with an *Area* tag affects all characters in a defined region. The effect sets a **DC** before anyone rolls, and each character in the area makes the relevant **Reaction Roll** (2d12 plus the listed Trait against that DC, never adjusted after the fact):

- **Agility Reaction Roll:** for blasts, explosions, sudden falls.

- **Strength Reaction Roll:** for area poisons, environmental damage, and sustained physical effects. Use another Trait only when the Feature itself names that Trait as an option before the Roll.

- **Instinct Reaction Roll:** for area mental effects, fear, and social cascades (Presence may stand in where composure rather than perception is what holds).

A character who *succeeds* takes half damage (or no effect, depending on the source). A character who *fails* takes the full effect. A character who Critically Succeeds takes no damage and clears 1 Stress.

Area attacks ignore most cover unless the cover is explicitly *Total Cover* with respect to the source. A grenade thrown into a room ignores Light and Heavy Cover within that room; a thick blast door blocks it entirely.

## VEHICLE AND STARSHIP COMBAT

The combat described in this chapter is **personal- scale** combat, characters with weapons, in rooms or open ground, exchanging fire at human ranges. Veilfarers also has rich rules for **starship combat** (the Spotlight system applies; the scales are different) and **vehicle combat** (lighter rules, often resolved as one or two attack rolls at vehicle-appropriate damage).

Starship combat is covered in detail in Chapter 17. The headline differences:

- **Scales.** Range bands at the starship scale are *kilometers,* not meters. Hull integrity replaces HP. Crew positions matter; the Finesse (Pilot/Navigate) Rolls, the Engineer rolls repair rolls, the Gunner rolls weapon rolls.

- **Round timing.** A starship combat round takes longer in fiction than a personal-scale round, a full Spotlight pass may represent thirty seconds to two minutes of weapon exchange.

- **Death.** Starship "death" is the destruction of the vessel; PC death within a destroyed vessel is then resolved at personal scale (some PCs make it to escape pods, some do not).

- **Specific class roles.** The Pilot is, obviously, the star of starship combat. Soldiers and Vanguards have less to do unless they are crewing weapons; this is intentional. Different scenes belong to different characters.

For now, the rules in this chapter apply to all personal-scale violence: corridor fighting on a station, an ambush in a Frontier Colony's market, a dueling-room standoff between Houses, a boarding action's deck-by-deck advance. Whenever the question is *who shoots whom at human scale*, the answer is here.

## COMMON EDGE CASES

A few combat situations come up often enough that they deserve direct treatment.

### SURPRISE

A character who is genuinely surprised by an attack, they did not know combat was beginning, the attacker was Hidden, the attack is the first event of the scene, grants the attacker **Advantage on that first attack**; Evasion itself never changes. After the first action, surprise has resolved; the rest of the scene is normal combat.

Surprise is not a tactical condition the players can routinely set up; it is a narrative phenomenon that the Keeper rules on. The Hidden condition above is the closest tactical analogue.

### OUTNUMBERED

A character outnumbered three-to-one or worse in Melee takes Disadvantage on all attacks (the body cannot maintain three simultaneous fronts). The single-character Defend action is a good response; allies arriving to break the surround is the better response.

### WOUNDED BUT FUNCTIONAL

A character at 1 HP, the last slot, is still functional. They can act, attack, move, take Spotlight beats. They are not Dying until the *next* HP-causing hit. This is significant: a 1-HP character can still be the difference between victory and loss in a final exchange, and many of Veilfarers's most cinematic moments happen at 1 HP.

A character at 1 HP, however, is *visibly hurt.* The Keeper should describe this, labored breath, blood on the wall, a hand pressed to a wound, and NPCs may react accordingly. Some enemies will press the wounded character; some will hesitate; some will spare them entirely. The fiction continues to operate.

### FRIENDLY FIRE

In a chaotic combat scene, allies can be hit. The Keeper resolves friendly fire as a standard attack roll with the attacking character's Trait, against the ally's Evasion, *if* the situation plausibly demands it. The trigger is usually a Failure with Fear on a ranged attack in a crowded area. Friendly fire is a dramatic consequence, not a tax: it belongs to the worst moments of a chaotic scene and should never become a routine punishment for shooting near allies.

Friendly fire is uncomfortable and dramatic, and should be used sparingly. The system does not require it; the Keeper invokes it as a story choice.

### SURRENDER

> **Surrender is always on the table, and the game does not punish it.**

Combat does not have to end in death or unconsciousness. NPCs may surrender; the players may

surrender (some of the most interesting campaigns we have seen feature one or more surrendered moments). Surrender is a fiction-first move: the surrendering side puts down arms and accepts whatever comes next. The Keeper handles the consequences.

Players considering surrender should know: Veilfarers does not punish surrender. The character lives. What happens after is the next session's question.

## DAMAGE TYPES

Every hit has a **damage type**, and the type sets a single value that matters at the table: its **Penetration.** Penetration does not add to the damage roll. Instead it *lowers the defender's Damage Thresholds for that hit only,* making the same roll more likely to climb from Minor into Major or Severe. This is how Veilfarers models armor-piercing weapons without turning them into instant death: armor still cushions, it simply cushions *less* against the right tool.

### THE CANONICAL DAMAGE TYPES

- **Physical (Kinetic). Penetration 0.** Mundane force: fists, blades, clubs, slugs, shrapnel, falls, and crushing impacts. Your thresholds apply unchanged. This is the baseline, and it is what most *melee* and *primitive* weapons deal.

- **Energy. Penetration -2.** Coherent or superheated discharge: plasma bolts, las-fire, arc, ion, and particle beams. Treat the target's Major and Severe Thresholds as **2 lower** against the hit. Energy is the standard of the Pearl Era: **nearly every manufactured ranged** **weapon in this book deals Energy damage,** and it is the assumed default for a modern sidearm or rifle unless its entry says otherwise.

- ***Void.*** Penetration -4. Force drawn through the Veil, slipping between the layers of ordinary matter. Treat the target's thresholds as 4 lower against the hit. This is heavy penetration, and it is deliberately rare. Any weapon that deals Void damage is always Experimental (Chapter 13): unstable, hand-built or Precursor-salvaged, never mass-produced, and never simply bought off a rack. Domain Powers that deal Void damage are abilities, not weapons, and channel this penetration freely. That is the quiet advantage of the Awakened.

### SUBTYPES AND TAGS

- **Neural** is a Void subtype (Penetration -4) that also frays the mind: a successful Neural hit marks **1 Stress** in addition to its HP. Dealt by Neural-Domain Powers and a handful of Experimental Veil-tech weapons.

- **Bleed** is a weapon tag, not a separate type. A Bleed weapon applies the *Bleeding* condition on any Hit regardless of tier; its damage uses whatever base type the weapon lists (usually Physical). The Ailuran *Slash Claw* and certain ceremonial blades carry it.

- **Crushing** is a weapon tag (heavy mauls, gravity slams, vehicle strikes): the hit ignores one Armor Slot. Its base type is Physical unless stated.

### COUNTERING PENETRATION: WARDS AND ARMOR TAGS

Penetration is not unanswerable. Specific protections cancel it:

- A **Ward** (against Void or Neural) reduces that type's Penetration to **0** against you: resolve the hit as if your full thresholds applied. Wards are bought through Advancement (Chapter 12) or granted by class and Ancestry features. Under the old rules Void ignored armor outright; it no longer does, so a Ward now sharpens a defense you already have rather than being the only thing between you and a Void blade.

- The **Reflective** armor tag cancels **Energy** Penetration (treat Energy as Penetration 0 against you). The **Composite** tag blunts **Crushing** the same way. See Chapter 13 for the armors that carry these tags.

When you take damage, the Keeper names the type and its penetration ("7 points, Energy"). **Subtract** 2 for Energy, or 4 for Void and Neural, from *both* your Major and Severe Thresholds for that hit only. Resolve severity against the reduced numbers, then spend Armor Slots as normal. Physical subtracts nothing, and a Ward or Reflective tag returns the subtraction to zero against the type it counters.

| DAMAGE TYPE | PENETRATION | TYPICAL SOURCE | CANCELLED BY |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Physical (Kinetic)** | 0 | melee, slugs, fists, falls, shrapnel | (full thresholds already) |
| **Energy** | -2 | plasma, las, arc, ion, particle (most weapons) | Reflective armor |
| **Void** | -4 | Experimental Veil-tech weapons; Veil Powers | Wards |
| **Neural (Void subtype)** | -4, +1 Stress | Neural Powers; Experimental tech | Wards |

## COMBAT IN UNUSUAL ENVIRONMENTS

Veilfarers's setting is overwhelmingly *space*, which means the standard rules of "two characters on a flat floor with reasonable air" frequently do not apply. The procedure for unusual environments is the same as standard combat, with the modifications listed below.

### ZERO-GRAVITY COMBAT

Combat in zero-G, boarding actions on vessels with damaged grav-plating, EVA encounters, asteroid mining accidents, has the following texture:

- **Movement requires a Reaction or push-off.** A character in zero-G cannot simply walk a band. They must brace, push off a surface (or another character), and travel in a straight line until they hit something. Moving one band costs an action unless the character has *Vacuum Training* (an Experience or feature granted by Free Fleet community, by Pilot class, or by extensive scene-time in zero-G).

- **Recoil matters.** Firing a ranged weapon in zero-G with no brace point creates equal-and-opposite movement. The character is pushed one range band away from the target unless braced.

- **No Cover, mostly.** Most zero-G environments are open. Cover is rare and valuable; debris fields and broken hull sections can provide it, but the default is "exposed."

- **Falling is different.** A Prone character has lost orientation. They cannot clear Prone through ordinary standing movement; they must spend an Action and make an Agility Roll, DC 10, to reorient.

- **Bleeding and breathing.** Bleeding and suffocation use their printed timing. Reaching 0 HP in zero-G or vacuum enters Dying and then Final normally; the environment never skips either state or the voluntary Death Move.

### VACUUM

Combat in actual vacuum, no atmosphere, adds the constraints of zero-G plus:

- **Suit integrity matters.** An intact pressurized suit prevents vacuum exposure. After an attack resolves Failure with Fear and causes the wearer HP loss, that player either spends 1 available Armor Slot or the suit becomes **Breached**. A Breached or unsealed character marks 1 direct HP and 1 Stress at the end of each round. Spend an Action and succeed on Knowledge (Tech), DC 10, with a patch kit to restore the seal. At 0 HP use normal Dying and Final. No separate Seal Integrity track exists.

- **Sound does not carry.** Communication is via radio only. A character whose helmet radio is destroyed is, effectively, silenced.

- **No ambient combustion.** Weapon damage is unchanged in vacuum. On Fire applies only when the source explicitly carries oxidizer or the target is inside a pressurized atmosphere; otherwise a Fire-tagged hit deals its listed Energy damage without applying On Fire.

- **The Free Fleet's specialty.** A character with Vacuum Training ignores the movement Disadvantage from zero-G or vacuum. A character without it has Disadvantage on Agility or Strength Rolls made to move, brace, or reorient there.

### HOSTILE ATMOSPHERES

Name the atmosphere's one active hazard before the scene. An unsealed character who enters or begins a Spotlight exposed makes a Strength Reaction Roll: DC 10 for irritating, DC 15 for toxic, DC 20 for lethal. On failure take 1d6 Energy damage with the appropriate Chemical or Corrosive tag and mark 1 Stress; on success take half damage and no Stress. A sealed suit prevents exposure while intact.
