## WEAPON FEATURES GLOSSARY

The following entries are authoritative for personal-scale weapons. When a feature calls for a Feature DC, use TT1 10, TT2 15, TT3 20, or TT4 25.

Read every entry below as answering three questions and no more: **what triggers it**, **who rolls against what DC**, and **what it then applies**. Where the third answer is a named condition, the condition is defined in Chapter 10 and works there as written; the entry names it, it does not redefine it.

> **WORKED EXAMPLE - A WEAPON FEATURE IN PLAY**
>
> Saber closes on a pirate with a **Shock Baton**: Strength, *d6+1 phys.*, Feature *Stunning*. She is at Proficiency 2, so the d6 is her Proficiency Die and her damage is **2d6+1**. She hits, rolls 4 and 3, and adds 1 for **8** - under the pirate's Major threshold, so a Minor hit: **1 HP**.
>
> *Now* the Feature fires, as its own separate step. *Stunning* triggers on a damaged target, and the pirate did lose HP. The Shock Baton is Common, **TT1**, so its **Feature DC is 10** - the item's number, not Saber's attack total, and not the pirate's Evasion. The pirate makes a **Strength Reaction Roll** against DC 10, rolls 8, and fails. It is now **Stunned**, and what that costs it is Chapter 10's business, not the weapon's: a Stunned creature cannot take any action at all, and stays that way until the condition clears as Chapter 10 describes.
>
> One 8-point swing therefore produced one point of HP and took an enemy entirely out of a round. That is what Features buy, and it is why a d6 weapon is not a weak weapon.
>
> **Rule Take-Away:** A Feature resolves *after* damage, on its own roll, against the **item's** Feature DC - never against your attack total. The Feature entry tells you the trigger, the roll, and the DC; Chapter 10 tells you what the resulting condition actually does.

- **Accurate.** Gain +1 on attack rolls made at Far or Very Far range.

- **Adaptive.** Once per scene, change this weapon’s damage type to Physical, Energy, Void, or Neural until changed again.

- **Arcing Shot.** Ignore cover when there is a clear vertical or indirect trajectory to the target.

- **Area.** The effect applies to every creature in its listed area, including allies, rather than to a single target.

- **Armor Piercing.** Reduce the target’s maximum Armor Slots by the listed rating until its next Long Rest. Multiple applications stack.

- **Automatic.** After a successful attack, mark 1 Stress to apply the same attack result to a second valid target within range and Very Close of the primary target. Roll damage separately.

- **Brittle.** A target that loses HP is left Brittle: the next instance of Physical damage it takes deals **+1d6** damage, then Brittle ends. This is not the *Vulnerable* condition and does not grant Advantage.

- **Burst Fire.** Whenever a damage die rolls its maximum value, roll one additional die of the same size and add it. Additional dice do not explode again.

- **Cleave.** After a successful Melee hit, immediately make one additional attack against a different target within this weapon’s reach.

- **Concealable.** While concealed on the body, this weapon does not count toward Burden. A routine search finds it only on a successful Instinct Roll, DC 15.

- **Continuous.** The target marks 1 Stress at the start of its next Spotlight.

- **Cutting.** Armor Slots cannot be spent to reduce this instance of damage.

- **Deployable Cover.** Deploy a one-way energy wall approximately 5 m × 3 m. It grants **Total Cover** (Chapter 10) from one side and has 10 HP and 6 Armor Slots. It lasts for the scene or until destroyed.

- **Devastating.** When damage equals or exceeds the target’s Severe Threshold, the hit marks 1 additional HP.

- **Disintegrating.** When any damage die rolls its maximum value, the **target's player** chooses one fictionally exposed carried item to go offline or reduces maximum Armor Slots by 1 until Repair All Armor; for an NPC, the Keeper chooses. Restore an offline item with suitable tools during a Short or Long Rest and a successful Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 15. A target reduced to 0 HP becomes Dying normally. If it later dies before stabilization, no recoverable body remains. This never skips Final or the voluntary Death Move.

- **Disorienting.** The affected creature is **Dazed** (Chapter 10).

- **Dispersal Wave.** The effect fills a Close-range cone. Each creature in the cone makes a Presence Reaction Roll, DC 15; on failure it suffers the weapon’s listed effect. Resistance: Presence vs DC 15.

- **Energy.** This is an Energy weapon. Energy damage treats the target’s Major and Severe Thresholds as 2 lower. The damage line remains the authoritative damage type.

- **Energy Surge.** Deal +1d6 Energy damage and the target marks 1 Stress.

- **Entangling.** After a hit causes HP or Stress loss, the target makes a Strength Reaction Roll against the weapon's Feature DC. On failure it becomes **Restrained** under the normal Core condition. Resistance: Strength vs Feature DC.

- **Entrapping.** On a hit, the target chooses Strength or Knowledge (Tech) and makes a Reaction Roll against the weapon's Feature DC. On failure it becomes **Incapacitated**. The condition clears as Chapter 10 defines it. Resistance: Strength or Knowledge (Tech) vs Feature DC.

- **Existence.** This is a descriptive Precursor tag, not an independent effect. The item entry must define its exact trigger, target, effect, duration, and end condition before use; without that complete entry, Existence has no mechanical effect.

- **Explosive.** This is a delivery procedure, not a damage line: the item’s own listed damage is what lands. Every creature within Very Close of the impact point makes an Agility Reaction Roll against the item’s Feature DC. On a failure it takes the item’s **listed damage in full**; on a success, half. Total Cover blocks the blast. Resistance: Agility vs Feature DC.

- **Guided.** You may attack a target you are aware of within range without direct line of sight. Guided attacks ignore cover except a completely sealed barrier or other Total Cover that leaves no viable path.

- **Ignite.** A target that loses HP is **On Fire**. The condition itself works exactly as Chapter 10 defines it.

- **Lightweight.** This weapon does not count toward Burden. A one-handed Lightweight weapon may be used comfortably in the off hand, but does not grant an extra attack.

- **Massive.** The wielder suffers -1 Evasion. On a hit, roll one additional normal damage die and discard the lowest normal damage die before totaling damage.

- **Messy.** This weapon leaves unmistakable residue, damage, or biological evidence. Concealing that a confrontation occurred is normally impossible without extensive cleanup.

- **Mind Link.** This Psionic weapon may target a creature the wielder is aware of within range even without line of sight.

- **Mind-Lock.** When this weapon causes a target to mark Stress, that target makes a Presence Reaction Roll against the weapon’s Feature DC. On a failure, it may only Move on its next Spotlight. Resistance: Presence vs Feature DC.

- **Overheating.** After each attack, roll d6. On 1-2, either mark 1 Stress to force cooling or spend an Action cooling before the weapon can attack again.

- **Paired.** When wielding two weapons that both have Paired, add the listed Paired bonus from one of them to the damage of an attack made with either weapon. Only one Paired bonus applies per attack.

- **Phasing.** The weapon deals Void damage, ignores cover on ranged attacks, and ignores one Armor Slot on a hit. Its Void damage also applies the normal -4 Threshold Penetration. A Void Ward cancels the Penetration but not the ignored Armor Slot unless it explicitly cancels the whole feature.

- **Poison.** When the attack causes HP loss, the target marks 1 Stress. A Poison (Special) item replaces this effect with its own text.

- **Powerful.** This weapon’s listed damage die is one size larger than the standard die for its chassis. The damage line already includes this increase.

- **Probability Shift.** After rolling the attack, you may reroll both Duality Dice. You must use the new result.

- **Psionic.** This weapon makes no attack roll against Evasion. Instead the target makes a **Presence Reaction Roll** against the item’s Feature DC; on a failure it takes the weapon’s damage in full, and on a success it takes none. Wards and effects that block Veil contact block the attack outright. Resistance: Presence vs Feature DC.

- **Quick.** After attacking, mark 1 Stress to immediately make a second attack against the same target.

- **Reach.** This Melee weapon may attack a target at the listed distance, normally Very Close, without entering Melee range.

- **Reality Shift.** After a hit but before damage is rolled, the wielder chooses Physical, Energy, Void, or Neural for that hit. This changes only the canonical type; tags, dice, Penetration, Conditions, and every other property remain as printed.

- **Reliable.** Gain +1 on all attack rolls made with this weapon.

- **Reload.** After each shot, spend an Action reloading before the weapon can attack again.

- **Salvo Fire.** After a successful attack, mark 1 Stress to apply the same attack result to a second target within Close of the primary target. Roll damage separately.

- **Shield Piercing.** Only half of the target’s available Armor Slots, rounded down, may be spent against this hit.

- **Shredding.** When the attack causes HP loss, reduce the target’s maximum Armor Slots by 1 until the armor is repaired during Downtime.

- **Silent.** Using this weapon creates no report or muzzle flash and does not automatically break stealth or alert creatures beyond the immediate victim.

- **Singularity.** Choose a point at Far range. Creatures within Close of it make a Strength Reaction Roll against the item’s Feature DC; on a failure they are pulled toward the point and **Restrained** (Chapter 10). Resistance: Strength vs Feature DC.

- **Smart Scope.** Gain +2 on attack rolls at Far or Very Far range.

- **Stable.** This weapon ignores Overheating and other sustained-use malfunctions unless a rule explicitly overrides Stable.

- **Stagger.** A target damaged by this weapon has Disadvantage on its next action.

- **Stunning.** A damaged target makes a Strength Reaction Roll against the item’s Feature DC. On a failure it is **Stunned** (Chapter 10). Resistance: Strength vs Feature DC.

- **Stunning on crit.** On a Critical Hit, the target is **Stunned** (Chapter 10).

- **Suppressive.** Mark 1 Stress. Every creature within Close of the target has Disadvantage on attacks until the end of its next Spotlight. This rides along with a normal attack; it is not the **Suppress** action (Chapter 10), which costs your whole Spotlight but hobbles every action in the area rather than attacks alone.

- **System Shock.** Against Synthetics and machines, deal normal damage. Against organic targets, deal only 1d4 Stress. If any damage die rolls its maximum and the attack causes HP or Stress loss, the target's player chooses one fictionally exposed electronic device; it goes offline until an Action and a Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 10, restores it. The Keeper chooses for an NPC. This damage-die trigger never alters the Duality result.

- **Taser Charge.** The target makes a Strength Reaction Roll against the item’s Feature DC. On a failure it is **Stunned** (Chapter 10). Resistance: Strength vs Feature DC.

- **Unraveling.** When any damage die rolls its maximum value, a player target chooses one Class or Ancestry Feature to suppress until the end of the scene; the Keeper chooses for an NPC. The target keeps control of all decisions and cannot lose its Path resource engine.

- **Vibration.** Armor Slots cannot be spent to reduce this instance of damage.

- **Waveform.** The attack affects every creature in a Close-range cone. Roll once and compare the result with each target's Evasion.

## ARMOR: THE RULES

Armor in Veilfarers is rated by three properties:

- **Damage Thresholds (Major / Severe).** The two damage points at which a hit climbs to a higher tier of HP loss (Chapter 10). The two numbers in an armor's stat line are its base Major and Severe thresholds; add your level to both.

- **Armor Slots.** The armor's pool of soak. Spend one to reduce a hit by one severity tier (including dropping a Minor hit to no HP). Restore through the Repair Armor Short Rest move or Repair All Armor Long Rest move unless a rule explicitly states otherwise.

- **Features.** Special properties, defined in the *Armor Features Glossary* below. Armor never adds a flat bonus to Evasion: a few Features adjust Evasion directly (*Flexible* +1, *Heavy* -1, *Very Heavy* and *Massive* -2), and that is the only way armor changes how hard you are to strike.

(Earlier drafts listed a separate *Armor Score* that added to Evasion; that stat is removed. Armor never modifies Evasion except through the Features noted above. The unified term for an armor's pool of soak is **Armor Slots**, shown in the tables below.)

A character wears one armor type at a time. Switching takes ten minutes (longer for Powered/Pressurized).

**Armor and your class.** Each class's Technology Access (Chapters 6 and 7) lists the armor categories it is trained to wear. You may physically put on heavier armor than your class trains for, but wearing armor above your class's access imposes **Disadvantage on everything involving movement**, Agility rolls, maneuvers, evading, climbing, and piloting while wearing it, as the unfamiliar weight and servos fight you instead of working with you. This is mechanical, not just flavor: a Mystic can strap into Heavy plate, but will move like they are underwater in it until they train the access for it.

**Weapons and gear outside your access.** A weapon family outside your Class Technology Access imposes **Disadvantage on attacks made with it**, regardless of Tier. Other inaccessible augments or equipment cannot be installed or operated until the access is trained. Training comes from Class progression or from a completed story project with a teacher and adequate time; the Class entry remains the default.

- **Infiltrator Suit.** Specialized stealth. Enhanced *Cloaking* and sound-dampening.

## ARMOR FEATURES GLOSSARY

The following entries are authoritative for personal-scale armor. Starship features with the same ordinary-language name are separate rules.

- **Assault.** Gain +1 on attack rolls made with weapons that have Automatic.

- **Cloaking.** Mark 1 Stress to become invisible until the end of your next Spotlight, or until you attack or are hit.

- **Environmental.** While sealed and powered, the armor protects against vacuum, toxic atmospheres, and extreme temperatures. Breathable-air duration is listed by the item; if none is listed, use 24 hours.

- **Flexible.** Gain +1 Evasion while wearing this armor.

- **Fortified.** When you mark an Armor Slot, reduce the hit by two severity tiers instead of one.

- **Heavy.** Suffer -1 Evasion while wearing this armor.

- **Jury-rigged.** This armor may be repaired without a workshop. After Failure with Fear on a Roll where the armor materially protected or assisted you, one powered armor feature goes offline; if none is powered, reduce maximum Armor Slots by 1. Spend an Action and make a Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 10, with common scrap to restore the feature or Slot. Matching dice remain a Critical Success and never cause a malfunction.

- **Life Support.** A self-contained atmosphere and thermal system protects the wearer in vacuum or hostile air for the item's printed duration; if none is printed, the duration is 2 hours on a full charge.

- **Massive.** Suffer -2 Evasion. Whenever you mark an Armor Slot, roll d6; on 5-6 reduce the hit by one additional severity tier.

- **Powered.** Integrated servos negate the Evasion penalty from Heavy or Very Heavy. If power is lost, the wearer suffers -3 on Agility Rolls until exiting or restoring power.

- **Composite.** Crushing is blunted against you: a Crushing hit no longer ignores one of your Armor Slots, and you may spend slots against it as normal.
- **Reflective.** Energy Penetration is cancelled against you (treat Energy as Penetration 0): resolve the hit against your full Major and Severe Thresholds.
- **Resilient.** Before marking your final available Armor Slot, roll d6. On 6, ignore the hit and do not mark the slot.

- **Self-Repair.** During any Short or Long Rest, automatically restore one marked Armor Slot in addition to other repairs.

- **Tactical.** Gain +1 on Instinct Rolls for perception.

- **Very Heavy.** Suffer -2 Evasion and -1 on all Agility Rolls. Powered servos are required to move normally and do not remove these penalties.

## AUGMENTATION SYSTEMS

The Great Silence broke not just our communication networks but our assumptions about human limits. Augmentation technology, the fusion of flesh and machine, became both salvation and curse. It offers the power to transcend, but always at a cost.

### AUGMENT CAPACITY

Your body and nervous system can host only so much hardware before they begin to rebel. How much you can carry is your **Augment Capacity.**

- **Your capacity.** Choose three of these four traits, **Strength, Agility, Finesse, or Presence.** Your Augment Capacity equals the sum of those three trait values (minimum 0). These are the traits that measure the frame, the reflexes, and the force of will a graft has to integrate with; raw intellect does not help your body carry steel.

- **Human and Synthetic frames.** Humans and Synthetics gain **+2 Augment Capacity.** Human physiology adapts to grafted hardware with unusual ease, and a Synthetic chassis is built from the start to be extended.

- **Each augment costs 1.** Every augmentation you install spends **1 point** of your capacity. While your installed augments total no more than your capacity, they sit comfortably and carry only their own listed costs (credits, and any Stress cost when active).

- **Going past your limit.** You may install augments beyond your capacity, but the body pays for what it cannot comfortably hold: for **each point installed past** **your Augment Capacity, your maximum Stress** **drops by 1** for as long as you remain over capacity. This is not a permanent scar. The moment your capacity catches up, raising one of your three chosen traits as you level up frees a slot, or you remove an augment, the freed point restores 1 to your maximum Stress. A chrome-heavy enforcer with more steel than frame is formidable and fragile in the same breath, and any Pearl Era surgeon will tell you the quiet wards are full of people who insisted on one more implant.

This is the *installation* limit, how many augments you can bear at once. Once an augment is in, the Degradation and Stress rules below govern how it behaves under load.

### OPTIONAL RULE: SCARCE CHROME

Some tables want a grittier galaxy, one where augmentation is rare enough that a single implant turns heads. For those campaigns, **halve each character's Augment Capacity, rounding up.** Everything else works exactly as written: each augment still costs 1, and going past the lower limit still trades maximum Stress point for point while you remain over it. The effect is to make chrome a deliberate, expensive commitment rather than a default loadout, and to push most characters toward one or two meaningful implants instead of a full rack. Set this at the start of a campaign, not partway through an arc.

### THE PRICE OF POWER: DEGRADATION

Augmentations are a permanent part of your body. When a character's Stress would exceed maximum, they can choose to push their augmentations beyond safety limits.

- **Mechanic.** The character forces an augmentation to stay online by paying excess Stress in another currency: **HP** or **Hope**.

- **The Cost.** Each point of HP or Hope spent covers 1 point of excess Stress. The act of overclocking inflicts 1 **Degradation Level** on the augmentation.

- **Degradation.** This term uses Rust & Steel's optional four-state Condition Track only when that module was adopted before play. Without it, Overclocking takes the chosen augmentation offline when the effect ends; restore it during a Long Rest with suitable tools and a Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 15. No undefined Degradation Level or discretionary flaw exists in Core play.

### STRESS COST (WHEN ACTIVE)

Some augmentations have a per-scene activation cost in Stress. The Stress is marked when the augmentation's benefit is invoked.

## NEURAL AUGMENTATIONS

Upgrading the mind, boldest and most dangerous attempts to expand cognitive capabilities.

- **Memory Chip.** Perfect recall. Drawback: "data-ghosts", inability to forget the face of every person you have killed.

- **Pain Suppressor.** Common implant for frontline soldiers. Once per scene after one hit causes the wearer to mark 2 or more HP, clear 1 Stress. It never reduces HP or hides the wearer's HP, Conditions, or injury severity from the player.

- **Combat Precognition.** Glimpses of potential futures. Invaluable in firefights. Devastating in social situations.

- **Combat Reflexes.** Reaction speed beyond human limits.

## THE GALACTIC COMMUNICATIONS NETWORK

*"You can hear the whole galaxy. You just can't afford to talk back."*

*Dispatch-Warden Imre Sol, Temple of Information, Boros-9*

The Q-Net is gone. What replaced it is slower, costlier, segmented into tiers, and gated by a single House. This section tells you, first, what your crew can and cannot do with it at the table, and then, for the curious, how it actually works and why it is shaped the way it is.

### AT THE TABLE: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

Read this much and you can run comms in any session.

- **Talking nearby is easy.** Within a building, a city, a ship, or out to the nearest orbital relay, communication is instant, cheap, and reliable. This is most of daily life.

- **Talking across a star system is slow but** **normal.** Messages ride conventional signal (radio, laser, tightbeam) through satellites and repeaters. Seconds across a planet, minutes across a system. Reliable. Cheap. This is where most data moves.

- **Talking across the Veil goes through a** **Temple.** Interstellar messages reach another star only through a **Temple of Information**, a quantum-crystal node. A Temple link is *instantaneous* but *low-bandwidth, queued, and expensive*, fit for short, high-priority messages, not bulk data. There are only about two hundred Temples; not every system has one.

- **You cannot "phone home" instantly and** **privately.** Reaching across the Veil means handing your message to a Temple (House Kurogane sees the traffic and sets the speed) or sending it by courier (slow). Plan around this. The crew operates mostly on what they carry and what they learn on arrival.

- **A ship can carry its own Veil link, barely.** A shipboard **Quantum Comm** can send only terse on/off bursts, the read comes back noisy, and a long transmission can be *detected and located*. Use it for emergencies: *"Compromised. Send extraction."* Never for conversation.

- **Out of coverage is a real condition.** In Veil transit, in disturbed regions, or in unsurveyed space, the crew cannot reach the Temple network at all. Their last word from home may be days or weeks old.

### COMMUNICATIONS EQUIPMENT


| NAME | TECH TIER | RANGE | COST |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Personal Comm** | Common (TT1) | Line-of-sight to local relay | 1 Cr (WT1) |
| **Encrypted Comm** | Military (TT2) | Same range; resistant to interception | 4 Cr (WT2) |
| **Long-Range Comm** | Military (TT2) | Inter-system, via standard relay | 4 Cr (WT2) |
| **Quantum Comm** | Experimental (TT3) | Inter-system, instantaneous; binary, terse, detectable | 9 Cr (WT3) |

### SENDING A MESSAGE ACROSS THE VEIL: THE CHANNELS

When the crew needs word to cross a stellar gap, they choose a channel. Each trades speed, bandwidth, secrecy, and cost differently.

- **Temple link (quantum crystal).** Instantaneous. Low bandwidth. Queued and prioritized by the operating House. Best for short, urgent, structured messages. Subject to the Kurogane monopoly and to Temple status (a Temple can be backed up, in binary mode, or offline).

- **Pearl Courier (physical).** A ship carries data-cores or sealed dispatches along Veil routes. Days to weeks. High bandwidth, anything fits. The most reliable and most secure option, and the slowest and most expensive. Run by House Valerius, the Explorers' Guild, and the Free Fleet.

- **Celestiari Resonance Instrument (emotional).** Two grown, paired instruments carry *feeling* across light-years in close to real time, well or unwell, calm or alarmed, plus simple structured concepts (*yes, no, come, flee*). No data, no detail. Rare, expensive, Celestiari-operated. Used when an institution needs urgent emotional confirmation of a distant event.

- **House intelligence networks (proprietary).** Each House runs its own blend of couriers, encrypted broadcasts, and dead drops. Outsiders reach these only by infiltration, recruitment, or favor.

### ENCRYPTION TIERS

Most traffic on any channel is encrypted. The DC is the difficulty to intercept and read it.


| ENCRYPTION | INTERCEPT DC | TYPICAL USE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Open (none)** | 5 | Public broadcast; anyone can listen |
| **Standard commercial** | 10 | Routine business |
| **Military-grade** | 15 | House internal, frontier security |
| **House-grade** | 20 | Actionable House intelligence |
| **Ailuran cipher-protocol** | 25 | Ailuran brokers; reputed to need an Ailuran bio-signature |
| **Physical courier** | Cannot be intercepted remotely | Acquire the courier or nothing |

### THREE IMPLICATIONS FOR EVERY CAMPAIGN

- **Information has distance.** Leave a known port and you leave behind the ability to call for help in any real-time way. No instant rescue across the Veil.

- **Information has cost.** Sending anything important across the gap costs money, time, favor, or all three. A fast House-grade courier between major systems runs into the hundreds of Credits.

- **Information has texture.** Every channel carries its own bias. A courier's news is days old. A resonance instrument gives feeling without fact. A relayed broadcast may be edited before it lands. The *same event* sounds different through different channels, and reconciling the accounts is half the work of figuring out what is really happening.

### HOW THE NETWORK IS BUILT

The replacement for the Q-Net is a **three-tier hierarchy**, each tier covering a different scale and running on different physics. A single message can pass through all three, and can be delayed, garbled, or lost at any layer.

- **Tier One, the Temples of Information.** Interstellar. Paired quantum crystals that speak in light.

- **Tier Two, orbital satellites and surface** **repeaters.** Intrasystem. Conventional radio, laser, tightbeam.

- **Tier Three, personal comm devices.** Local. Standard EM, line-of-sight to the nearest Tier Two relay.

A standard message typically travels: personal comm to orbital satellite to planetary repeater to ground station to Temple of Information, across the Veil to a partner Temple, then back down the far side. Each hop adds

latency and a point of failure. Three systems away takes hours under good conditions, days under bad, and may never arrive if a Temple is offline.

**Tier Two and Tier Three** are the long, slow, dependable web. Within a system, conventional signal relayed through satellites and repeaters is slow (light-speed delays apply) but reliable, bandwidth-rich, and cheap, so most data volume lives here. Personal and Long-Range comms never touch a crystal; they climb this web until they reach a Temple, and the Temple speaks for them. The reason the whole network has this strange shape, a vast slow web feeding a few precious instantaneous nodes, is not bureaucracy. It is physics.

### WHY IT WORKS THIS WAY: THE QUANTUM CRYSTAL

Everything above follows from how a quantum crystal behaves. The lore here is optional; the rules above are complete without it.

A **paired quantum crystal** is two stones cut from the same Veil-touched geological event, bound beneath ordinary physics. Whatever happens to one happens to the other in the same instant, at any distance. They are, to one another, the same crystal in two places. The way they express that bond is **light**: an active crystal glows, and its color is its state. Drive one to shine at a chosen hue and its partner, light-years away, instantly shines at the complementary hue on the color wheel, push one toward red and the far one answers green. Nobody fully understands the mechanism. The galaxy has a working medium, and that has been enough. The signal never crosses the gap. It simply *appears*, at once, in two rooms.

Two awkward facts about operating that miracle shape the entire network.

### CHEAP TO HEAR, COSTLY TO SPEAK

**Listening is cheap.** Reading a crystal means pointing a simple optical sensor at it and recording the color. The sensors are inexpensive and buildable from salvage. Anyone holding one end of a pair can read it for almost nothing.

**Speaking is expensive.** To change a crystal's state you must strike it with a tightly tuned, high-energy beam at exactly the target frequency. Only then does the distant partner answer. Painting one message means generating, aiming, and holding many distinct high-purity frequencies in rapid sequence, each a power-hungry act. Sending a paragraph can cost more power than a small settlement burns in a day.

This asymmetry is the hidden architecture of the network. You could hand everyone a *reader*. You could never hand everyone a *writer*. The cost of speech, in energy and precision machinery, is what concentrates interstellar communication into a few enormous installations and leaves everyone else to reach them the slow way.

### THE DISCIPLINE OF DARKNESS

A crystal can only be read in **absolute dark**. A glow is only legible against nothing. Let one stray photon fall on the stone, a reflection, a status light, a crack of glow under a door, and that light mixes with the crystal's emission and smears the color the reader records. The message arrives dirtied, a green read as yellow, a confirmation that cannot be trusted, and the far end never knows its words were soiled. So every working crystal lives sealed inside a **reading cell** engineered toward perfect, photonically silent darkness, tended by operators who work by touch. Much of a Temple's cost is, in the end, the cost of keeping a few rooms more completely dark than anywhere else in human space.

### TWO HUNDRED AND FIFTY-SIX COLORS

There is a large compensation. Old machine communication, like the conventional comms still carrying intrasystem traffic, is *binary*: on or off, two states, meaning built one bit at a time. A quantum crystal, read in true darkness by a calibrated sensor, resolves into **256 distinguishable chromatic states**, an alphabet of color where conventional tech has two letters. Operators call each state a **chroma**, and a single pulse carries a full byte of meaning, eight times what the old machines manage in one flash. This is why a Temple, slow to queue and costly to run, can still move dense, structured data across the galaxy in real time. The catch: painting all 256 chroma cleanly needs the full emitter bank and the full discipline of darkness. Strip those away, as you must aboard a ship, and the alphabet collapses back toward binary.

### THE TEMPLES OF INFORMATION

The Temples are where speech and darkness are gathered. Each is a substantial facility, often the size of a city block, built into a Core World's infrastructure or installed as a station at a system's edge. They are temples in the literal sense: cathedrals around the act of communication, staffed by orders of operators, IA-tenders, cipher-clerks, power engineers, darkness-wardens, and security, all devoted to keeping a few glowing stones fed, defended, and unlit. Inside sits the keystone of post-Silence civilization, a paired quantum crystal in its reading cell, served by a tuned emitter bank and watched by a filtering intelligence. One Temple speaks; its partner, anywhere in the galaxy, hears and answers.

**Range.** Any distance the galaxy presents. Distance does not degrade the signal. Veil disturbances do.

**Cost.** A power plant to feed the emitters, rooms held in flawless darkness, and a standing population of specialists. The crystals are *rare*: the right kind of Veil-touched geological event happens perhaps once every two decades, and a paired crystal *cannot be re-paired with anything else*. Destroy one Temple and both crystals

die forever. Temples are primary strategic assets, and their placement is political geography.

**Network.** Roughly **two hundred Temples** operate galaxy-wide, a sparse mesh. Each system's Temple is the **central node** that gathers all local traffic and distributes everything inbound. A message from the periphery to the Core hops Temple to Temple, often through three to six along the way. Each hop is instantaneous; the latency is the queuing, decoding, re-encoding, and prioritization at every node.

### THE KUROGANE MONOPOLY

The political fact every Keeper needs: **House Kurogane controls crystal alignment.** Not the raw stones, surveys are run by several Houses and the Explorers' Guild, but the *alignment* that turns two raw crystals into a working pair and the tuning that yields a clean 256-chroma read. The work is done in Kurogane-secret facilities, by Kurogane-trained technicians, under licenses that grant Kurogane a permanent share of every Temple's traffic. Every operational Temple pays Kurogane. Every crystal in service was aligned by them. The monopoly is complete, and it is the single largest source of both House Kurogane's revenue and its leverage.

This produces specific shapes:

- Houses out of favor find their Temple traffic *delayed*, never blocked, just mysteriously slow.

- Off-network communication means conventional alternatives (slow, system-bound) or *stealing* crystals, an act of war.

- A new Temple cannot be installed without Kurogane cooperation. Build one without alignment and you have built an empty dark room.

- The Spire of Verita and the Stellar Commerce Guild both quietly seek an alternative to the Kurogane process. Neither has succeeded.

For Keepers: the monopoly is a campaign-level antagonist that never has to fight the crew. It needs only to *delay their message by six hours* to ruin the job. Use it.

### IA FILTERING AND THE NOISE OF THE VEIL

Even with a perfect pair and a perfect dark cell, the read is not clean. Veil disturbances introduce phantom chroma, color-wheel echoes, and momentary inversions where a green flickers as red. Rendered raw, these produce gibberish, or worse, a plausible message that is quietly wrong. So every Temple runs a dedicated **filtering Synthetic Intelligence** that recognizes degradation and reconstructs clean signal from corrupted color. These IAs are narrow specialists and do nothing else; their failure is the main cause of real-time comms problems. When a filter drops, the Temple falls back to **binary mode**, abandoning the 256-chroma alphabet and passing only the crudest present/absent pulse, the same impoverished signaling a ship uses. Binary mode keeps terse emergency traffic moving. It cannot carry normal communication.

For Keepers: a Temple in binary mode is a useful condition. *"The cargo is compromised. Send extraction."* fits. Anything with nuance or proof waits for the filter to return.

### SHIPBOARD QUANTUM LINKS: SPEAKING IN THE OPEN

A ship can carry a crystal of its own, the **Quantum Comm** in the equipment table, with its partner held by an ally arranged in advance. It is the closest thing to the old Q-Net in a pocket. It is also crippled three ways, and every operator learns them fast.

- **It can only whisper in binary.** No ship carries a Temple's emitter bank or power plant. A shipboard unit cannot paint 256 clean chroma; it can only crudely flip its crystal on or off. Bandwidth collapses from a byte per pulse to a single bit, the difference between a conversation and tapping code on a pipe. A short confirmation is feasible. A document is not.

- **Its dark is never dark enough.** A starship hums, flexes, and leaks light from a hundred panels. A shipboard reading cell is a brave approximation of the Silent Dark, never the real thing, so even the binary read comes back noisy, and a noisy bit is sometimes a wrong bit.

- **It cannot speak quietly.** Driving a crystal, even crudely, takes a sharp energy spike, and a complex transmission stacks those spikes into a distinctive, easily recognized signature. A ship sending more than a flicker lights up to anyone running detection. The longer the message, the louder and more locatable the ship. Transmitting from a hull is a decision, not a convenience.

The table effect: shipboard quantum is for the terse, the rare, and the desperate. Treat any longer burst as an act that can be *heard*.

> **GEAR, THE SENDING HEARD** *(OPTIONAL TACTICAL RULE).* ADOPT THIS MODULE BEFORE PLAY. WHEN A CREW SENDS MORE THAN A BRIEF CONFIRMATION ON A SHIPBOARD QUANTUM LINK, ONE EQUIPPED HOSTILE LISTENER MAY SPEND ITS SENSORS ACTION AND MAKE A KNOWLEDGE ROLL: DC 15 FOR A CASUAL SWEEP OR DC 10 FOR A DEDICATED LISTENING POST OR EXTENDED TRANSMISSION. ON SUCCESS IT LEARNS THAT A SHIP TRANSMITTED AND ITS ROUGH BEARING; ON A CRITICAL SUCCESS IT ALSO FIXES THE SOURCE SHIP'S POSITION. ON FAILURE IT LEARNS NOTHING. THE DC IS FIXED BEFORE THE ROLL, AND NO DISCRETIONARY SUBSTITUTE PROCEDURE APPLIES.

**Out of coverage.** Ships in Veil transit, in disturbed regions, or in unsurveyed sectors are out of coverage entirely; at most they speak among themselves by tightbeam. A crew in deep space lives in enforced solitude, their last word from home days or weeks old, and news of wars and treaties reaches them as an accumulated packet the next time they dock at a Temple-linked port. *Veilfarers* leans into this: for the length of a voyage the crew is a small world unto itself, and rejoining the network can be its own culture shock.

### CRYSTAL REPLACEMENT AND LOSS

Crystals are finite, and they *fail*, occasionally, for reasons not fully understood. A Temple whose crystal fails is offline until a new pair is aligned and installed: months for a minor Temple, weeks for a major political center. When a Temple goes dark, the systems it served route around it, hops lengthen, latency climbs, capacity contracts, and the effects ripple across sectors. A campaign that wants to isolate a region for narrative reasons can do far worse than to quietly take its Temple offline. The silence is genuine, contained, and recoverable on a Keeper-determined timeline.

## WEALTH AND ACQUISITION

Veilfarers uses an abstract Wealth system rather than tracking individual transactions. Chapter 15 covers the full system; the summary:

| WEALTH TIER | MONTHLY FREE ACQUISITION |
| --- | --- |
| **Tier 0, Forgotten** | Improvised only |
| **Tier 1, Established** | 1× Tier 1 item (1 Credit) |
| **Tier 2, Prosperous** | 1× Tier 1-2 item (1-4 Credits) |
| **Tier 3, Affluent** | 1× up to Tier 3 (1-9 Credits) |
| **Tier 4, Powerful** | 1× up to Tier 4 (1-16 Credits) |
| **Tier 5, Transcendent** | 1× up to Tier 5 (1-25+ Credits) |

Items above your standard monthly allowance require a **Wealth Check** (Chapter 15): Knowledge or Presence vs. DC by item Tier (DC 10 for T1, 15 for T2, 20 for T3, 25 for T4, 30 for T5).

### COST VS. STORY

The Wealth-based system is intentionally abstract. The principle: every piece of equipment should be a *story*, where it came from, who they took it from, what it cost. Tracking individual credit amounts flattens this. The Wealth Tier system preserves the story.

## MAINTENANCE AND WEAR

Equipment in Veilfarers does **not** silently degrade over time. A pistol bought at Tier 1 is the same pistol six sessions later, unless something has happened to it, a Failure with Fear in a firefight, a story event, a Keeper decision to introduce a wear-and-tear arc.

This is deliberate. Tracking maintenance per-session is bookkeeping; tracking it narratively is character.

### REPAIR PROCEDURE

- **Field Repair.** Engineer (or any character with a tool kit): Knowledge Roll, DC 10. On success, functional for the rest of the scene. Critical Success: holds for the session.

- **Workshop Repair.** With proper workshop access, Engineer can perform full repair on Long Rest. Knowledge Roll, DC 10. On success, fully restored.

- **Replacement.** Some equipment cannot be repaired in the field. Specialized parts may be required.

### HEIRLOOM EQUIPMENT

Some equipment becomes *heirloom*, gear the character has carried so long, repaired so many times, and bonded with so deeply that it is an extension of them. Heirloom is descriptive in Core play and grants no bonus, extra absorbed hit, immunity to loss, or other mechanical benefit unless a complete optional module adopted before play defines one.

Define heirloom equipment in conversation with the Keeper. The Engineer's named wrench, the Pilot's repaired headset, the Soldier's father's dog-tag, all are candidates. The wrench is not stronger than another wrench; the wrench is *Vell's wrench*, and the table knows what that means.

## LOSS, THEFT, AND DAMAGE

Equipment is *lose-able*. This is part of the design.

A character can lose equipment through:

- **Failure with Fear on a relevant roll.** Weapon jams, armor seal breaks, kit dropped in a chase.

- **Combat damage.** A Severe or Overkill hit may damage equipment alongside the character.

- **Theft.** NPCs steal things. Pirates take weapons from defeated characters.

- **Story event.** The character makes a deliberate sacrifice.

**Lost equipment is not, by default, retrievable through standard advancement.** The character acquires replacements through normal Wealth-based purchasing, faction favors, or Keeper-mediated story events.

### RECOVERY ANCHOR AND EQUIPMENT LOSS

For **Sleeping characters**, the Recovery Anchor (Chapter 7) is often a piece of equipment. If lost or destroyed:

- The character cannot perform Recovery actions until the Anchor is replaced or recovered.

- Replacement is Keeper-mediated (not just "buy a new tea set at the next station").

- Until then, the character relies on standard non-Anchor Effort generation only.

This is intentional. The Anchor's losability is what makes it dramatic.

## A WORKED EXAMPLE: OUTFITTING VELL AT LEVELS 1, 5, AND 10

A walkthrough of how one character's equipment changes across a campaign.

### LEVEL 1: STARTING KIT

Vell Kurogane-Born begins as a Sleeping Engineer (Tech Specialist), Wealth Tier 1.

- **Class Items:** Tool Belt (with Logged Inventory), Personal Wrench (*Hela*).

- **Weapons:** Industrial Plasma Cutter (Tier 2 utility, used as improvised d4 melee in emergencies, she's not a fighter), Holdout Blaster (Tier 1, *Concealable*, 1 Credit).

- **Armor:** Mechanic's Coverall (counts as Mesh Armor, Common (TT1), Armor Slots 4, Thresholds 5/10, *Self-Repair*).

- **Personal Items:** Hela's notebook, three generations of repair logs, sealed jar of cultivated moss from home, faded photograph.

- **Tech:** Datapad, Hacking Kit (Tier 2, uses with Disadvantage until Tech Access 2).

- **Survival:** Environmental Suit (Tier 1).

- **Comms:** Personal Comm.

- **Burden total:** 7 carried against capacity **6** (6 + Strength modifier; Vell's Strength is +0). She is 1 above capacity, so movement is limited to one band per Spotlight and the listed Agility or Strength movement Rolls have Disadvantage until she drops at least 1 Burden.

### LEVEL 5: MID-CAMPAIGN

After multiclass into Sleeping Diplomat. Tech Access 2, Wealth Tier 2.

- **Class Items:** Same.

- **Weapons:** Gauss Pistol (Tier 2, *Silent*, 4 Credits). She has learned, since Tellurian Reach, that the corridor sometimes requires a sidearm.

- **Armor:** Composite Armor (Military (TT2), Armor Slots 4, Thresholds 8/16, *Resilient*, 4 Credits).

- **Mods:** Suppressor on the pistol; Reinforced Plating on the armor.

- **Augmentation (new):** Memory Chip (Tier 2 Neural, +1 Knowledge, 4 Credits, purchased after a salvage job; she values the perfect recall, accepts the data-overload risk).

- **Tech:** Encrypted Datapad, Hacking Kit (now Tech Access 2, used without Disadvantage), Universal Translator.

- **Hela's Wrench, repaired.** Broken in a salvage job session 14; rebuilt over three sessions. Heirloom, Keeper-noted +1 to repair rolls with this specific wrench.

### LEVEL 10: ENDGAME

Tech Access 3, Wealth Tier 3, full Mastery feature.

- **Class Items:** Same. The wrench is famous now.

- **Weapons:** Gauss Pistol (still); Vibro-Sword (Tier 2, *Vibration*, 4 Credits, backup for boarding actions).

- **Armor:** Powered Armor (Experimental (TT3), Armor Slots 6, Thresholds 13/28, *Powered*, 16 Credits). Acquired through a Tellurian shipyards job that paid in this piece.

- **Mods:** Servo-Assist, Veil Lining (Veil-Hardened), Sensor Integration, Tool Integration, Vacuum Seal Enhancement on the Powered Armor. Custom Grip and Smart Sight on the pistol.

- **Augmentations:** Memory Chip (still); Combat Chassis (Tier 3 Physical, +2 Strength, +1 maximum Armor Slot, 16 Credits, 1 Stress activation, acquired through a House Volkov contract).

- **Tech:** Encrypted Datapad, Hacking Kit, Universal Translator, Sensor Array, Quantum Crystal (acquired via Spire favor).

- **Survival:** Long-Duration Vacuum Suit (Tier 3).

- **Comms:** Encrypted Comm + Quantum Comm.

- **Heirloom items:** *Hela's Wrench* (famous in Free Fleet engineering circles); *the moss jar* (still kept; the smell of home).

### WHAT THE PROGRESSION SHOWS

Vell's equipment evolution is *narratively driven*. She did not "buy upgrades" at level-up; her equipment changed as the campaign demanded it. The Powered Armor came from a specific job. The Quantum Crystal came from a specific favor. The Combat Chassis came from a House contract. Even the new sidearm reflects a specific scene-driven change in her self-image.

This is what equipment looks like in a campaign that takes the equipment system seriously: not a shopping list, but a *story*.

## CLOSING: THE TOOLS ARE THE PERSON

A character's gear is part of the character: where it came from, what it cost, who else has touched it. The tables tell you what equipment does; what it *is* belongs to the table. Carry your gear well. It is carrying you.

# CHAPTER 14: DRONES AND REMOTE TOOLS


---

## Drones and Remote Tools

Drones are common across civilized space: maintenance beetles in station ducts, inspection motes crawling over hull seams, survey frames crawling through unstable ruins, and half-legal scout rigs carried by crews who would rather not risk a body every time a door opens onto darkness.

They are useful, fragile, and often expensive. A drone can extend a character’s reach, senses, or tools, but it cannot replace judgment, courage, improvisation, or the crew itself.

> **You can send a drone into the dark. That does not mean the dark has to send it back.**

*Dockside proverb, origin disputed*

---

## The Core Rule

**Drones are equipment, not characters.** They extend what a character can attempt, but they do not grant the crew extra Spotlights.

A drone is operated by a character. When a drone does something meaningful under pressure, the operator makes the roll, using the Trait and Experiences that best fit the action. The drone supplies the body, sensor, tool, or weapon. The operator supplies attention, timing, and nerve.


If a drone changes the scene in a meaningful way, someone is paying attention to it. In practice, that means the operator’s Action, a Reaction Roll, Stress, or a risk the Keeper can turn into a complication when Fear enters the scene.

A drone is never a second set of hands the crew gets for free.


| Drone Use | Typical Cost |
|---|---|
| Hold position, follow the crew, transmit a feed, shine a light | No significant cost, unless the scene is under pressure |
| Move precisely through danger, scout carefully, hold a signal through bad terrain | The operator’s Action |
| Repair, cut, hack, open, stabilize, manipulate something delicate | The operator’s Action |
| Attack, mark a target, intercept, suppress, or defend | The operator’s Action or a Reaction Roll, as fits the moment |
| Act while signal is lost | Only a simple loaded protocol |


---

## Using Drones Without Slowing Play

A drone takes a little time to configure, but it should not make every scene technical. Most of the work happens when the crew buys the drone, chooses its modules, and decides how it normally communicates. After that, play it like any other piece of gear.

In a normal scene, you usually only need three questions:

1. **Who is controlling the drone right now?**
2. **What module or sensor is the drone using?**
3. **Is the signal Stable, Unstable, or Lost?**

You do not need to recalculate the drone every time it appears. Once a crew knows what their drone does, whole sessions can pass with the technical details fading into the background. Bring the rules forward only when the drone is doing something risky, entering protected space, being attacked, losing signal, using an important module, or creating a meaningful choice.

None of this is meant to turn a drone into a minigame. It is meant to give the crew one more shared tool, the kind that quietly creates decisions instead of paperwork.
---

## Drones Are Light Vehicles

For rules purposes, treat a drone as a small, fragile vehicle (the vehicle and starship rules live in Chapter 17).

This single ruling does a lot of work:

- A Pilot’s class features and moves that apply to vehicles may apply to a drone when the fiction fits.
- A Void Power that targets a creature may target a personal-scale drone and uses its complete printed damage, duration, and effect unchanged. A Power that targets only a vehicle or ship affects a drone only when it explicitly includes personal-scale machines; no discretionary scaling applies.
- Counter-vehicle tools work on drones. Anything built to stop a vehicle, from a kinetic burst to an electromagnetic pulse, stops a drone faster, because a drone is the smallest, cheapest vehicle on the field.

A drone’s **Grade** is its chassis. Its **Modules** are its systems. Its operator supplies attention, timing, and nerve.

---

## Drone Access

Drone access follows the same access category as pistols.

If a character, crew, license, market, faction, or port would give access to **Common pistols**, it can usually provide access to **Common drones**. Access to **Military drones** follows the same assumptions as access to military-grade pistols. Access to **Experimental drones** is never ordinary market access: it requires a black-site contact, faction debt, rare salvage, prototype theft, or a Keeper-approved story reason.


| Drone Grade | Access Equivalent |
|---|---|
| **Common Drone** | Common pistols / commercial tools |
| **Military Drone** | Military pistols / restricted security gear |
| **Experimental Drone** | Experimental weapons / black-site or prototype gear |

Local law always matters. A drone that is legal on a frontier station may be contraband inside a House port. A drone that is tolerated on a salvage rig may trigger alarms in a corporate habitat.

---

## Drone Grades

A drone is built from a **Drone Grade** and installed **Modules**. The Grade defines its Tier, cost, HP, Evasion, thresholds, shields, and module slots. Modules define what the drone can actually do.


| Drone Grade | Tier | Cost | HP | Evasion | Thresholds | Armor Slots | Module Slots | Availability |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Common Drone** | Tier 2 | 4 Cr | 2 HP | 10 | Major 5 / Severe 11 | 0 | 2 | Civilian, commercial, frontier markets |
| **Military Drone** | Tier 3 | 8 Cr | 3 HP | 11 | Major 7 / Severe 14 | 1 | 3 | Restricted, licensed, House security |
| **Experimental Drone** | Tier 4 | 16 Cr | 5 HP | 12 | Major 9 / Severe 16 | 2 | 4 | Rare, unstable, black-site, prototype |

### Common Drones

Common drones are commercial tools. They scout, carry, record, repair lightly, relay signals, inspect dangerous spaces, and die quickly when shot.

Common drones are hard-locked against lethal weapon integration. They may carry legal utility tools, rescue equipment, sensors, signal modules, and non-lethal compliance systems where local law allows them. They cannot legally mount lethal weapons.

Tampering with a Common drone to carry lethal weaponry uses the complete **Weaponized Common Drones** procedure later in this chapter: tools, Downtime, Knowledge (Tech) DC 15, and its single d6 complication table. This paragraph creates no second installation procedure.

### Military Drones

Military drones are hardened field platforms. They may carry restricted weapon, armor, tactical, signal, and security modules. They often require licenses, faction authority, military contacts, or illegal markets.

A Military drone is harder to destroy than a commercial frame, but it is also easier to explain badly at a checkpoint.

### Experimental Drones

Experimental does not mean “better market gear.” It means rare, unstable, illegal, prototype, salvaged, or carrying a hidden cost.

If a crew is running Experimental drone technology, ask three questions:

- Who built it?
- Who wants it back?
- What does it cost to keep using?

Experimental drones may hold strange modules and survive conditions that would kill lesser machines, but they are never ordinary equipment. They should come with a story attached.

---

## Module Grade Compatibility

Drone modules are built in three Grades: **Common**, **Military**, and **Experimental**. A drone can always install modules of its own Grade or any lower Grade.


| Drone Grade | Modules It Can Install |
|---|---|
| **Common Drone** | Common modules only |
| **Military Drone** | Common or Military modules |
| **Experimental Drone** | Common, Military, or Experimental modules |

This is a matter of firmware, power architecture, safety limits, legal locks, and interface standards. A higher-grade frame can usually run simpler hardware. A lower-grade frame cannot safely run restricted or unstable systems without modification.

A **Military drone** can mount Common modules normally. A Military security frame may carry a commercial camera, relay node, manipulator arm, or repair kit without issue.

An **Experimental drone** can mount almost anything, but this does not make lower-grade modules stronger. A Common Low-Light Camera installed on an Experimental drone is still a Common Low-Light Camera. The frame may be stranger, tougher, or more expensive, but the module keeps its own limits unless another rule upgrades it.

### Installing Higher-Grade Modules

Installing a higher-grade module into a lower-grade drone is illegal modification and uses this complete procedure:

| Installation Attempt | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Military module into Common drone | Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 15; proper tools and Downtime |
| Experimental module into Military drone | Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 20; rare tools or specialist access and Downtime |
| Experimental module into Common drone | Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 20; rare tools and Downtime; the module consumes **one additional Slot** |

Critical Success or any Success installs the module. Failure leaves the module uninstalled and intact. On a Fear-dominant noncritical result, also roll once on the frame-complication table below; the complication applies whether or not installation succeeded. Matching dice never trigger this table.

| d6 | Frame Complication |
|---|---|
| 1 | The drone's serial is flagged as tampered when scanned. |
| 2 | While the module is installed, the drone loses 1 Evasion. |
| 3 | After the module is used, its signal becomes Unstable until the end of the next round. |
| 4 | The operator marks 1 Stress the first time the module is used each scene. |
| 5 | The first use sends a diagnostic ping to the established vendor, manufacturer, or local authority. |
| 6 | On the module's first Failure with Fear each scene, it goes offline until an Action and Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 10, restores it. |

---

## Link Modes

When deploying a drone, its operator chooses Local Mesh or Direct RF from the modes available in that location. Switching between them costs the operator's Action. Private Relay Chain applies only while a placed relay path exists. The Keeper states available infrastructure before the choice.

### Local Mesh

In inhabited planets, ports, cities, stations, and supervised habitats, drones can use local infrastructure: municipal repeaters, traffic beacons, port networks, public mesh towers, and House-controlled routing systems. This greatly extends practical range.

The cost is visibility. A drone using a Local Mesh is logged, routed, located, and subject to local rules. Its serial may be recorded. Its route may be audited. Security systems may geofence it, throttle it, force it to land, or cut the link when it enters restricted space.

### Direct RF Link

In wilderness, dead stations, ruins, frontier sites, or whenever the crew wants to avoid being logged, the drone relies on a direct radiofrequency link to its operator, ship, or carried controller. This is private, but fragile. Distance, dense structure, metal, water, terrain, radiation, electromagnetic emissions, jamming, and Veil interference matter much more.

### Private Relay Chain

A crew may place its own relays to extend a Direct RF Link without using public infrastructure. Each relay improves reach, but each one is also a physical object that can be detected, destroyed, spoofed, stolen, or traced back to the crew.

Public infrastructure buys reach, a private link buys discretion, and a chain of relays buys options, but none of the three has ever bought safety.

---

## Drone Range and Signal

Drones use the same range bands as the rest of the system: **Melee**, **Very Close**, **Close**, **Far**, **Very Far**, and any wider narrative distance your table already uses for vehicles, ships, or scenes.

Do not invent a separate measurement system for drones. The range band tells you **how far the drone is from its operator**. The environment tells you **how healthy the signal is**.

A drone at **Close** range behind thick military shielding may be unreachable. A drone at **Very Far** range across open ground through a relay may remain usable.

### Signal Quality

A drone’s signal has three practical states.


| Signal State | Meaning | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Stable** | The connection is clear enough for real-time command. | The drone works normally. |
| **Unstable** | The signal is delayed, noisy, partially blocked, or vulnerable. | Simple commands work normally. Every complex command makes its normal Roll with Disadvantage; the DC, Stress cost, and legal Actions do not otherwise change. |
| **Lost** | No useful command link remains. | The drone follows its one loaded protocol. If it has no protocol, it freezes and takes no Actions until signal improves. |

### Default Signal by Range

Use this table for Direct RF Link or other private links without strong infrastructure.


| Drone Range from Operator | Default Signal in Open Conditions |
|---|---|
| **Melee / Very Close** | Stable |
| **Close** | Stable |
| **Far** | Stable if line of signal is reasonable; Unstable if structure or interference is present |
| **Very Far** | Unstable; Stable only with Extended Link, a surviving Relay Node, ship support, or a declared clear open route |
| **Beyond Very Far** | Lost unless supported by a relay chain, ship systems, or special equipment |

A supervised Local Mesh treats Melee through Very Far as Stable unless a printed restriction applies, and logs the drone. Before deployment in a protected space, use the signal-obstruction table to declare its starting state; do not worsen it retroactively.

### What Hurts a Signal


| Condition | Usual Effect |
|---|---|
| Dense ship or station structure | Stable -> Unstable |
| Heavy doors, armored walls, shielded compartments | Unstable or Lost |
| Faraday cage, military vault, black-site architecture | Lost unless countered |
| Active jamming | Signal worsens by one step |
| High electromagnetic emissions | Signal becomes Unstable or rolls with Disadvantage |
| Veil interference | Unstable, often with feedback, echoes, or false images |
| Hostile network | Signal may stay active, but spoofing or hijack becomes possible |
| Stealth Shell or silent running | May reduce signature but limit strong transmission |
| Relay Node | May improve signal by one step while it survives |

An Extended Link module helps when distance or ordinary structure is the problem. It does not pierce military jamming, a sealed vault, a Faraday cage, or architecture built to kill signals.

In the end, a drone extends your reach exactly as far as your signal survives, and not one meter further.

---

## Losing the Signal

When a drone’s signal becomes **Lost**, check its loaded protocol. Most drones carry one simple fallback. Cheap or damaged drones may carry none.


| Protocol | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Freeze** | The drone stops and waits for connection to return. |
| **Return** | The drone tries to return to the last point where it had signal. |
| **Execute** | The drone completes one simple preloaded order. |
| **Dead Weight** | The drone goes inert until recovered. |

A drone cannot improvise while its signal is Lost unless a module explicitly allows it, and even then it follows instructions literally. It does not understand fear, mercy, a lie, or why the child hiding under the reactor console matters.

---

## Drone Movement

A drone does not fly by default.

Most drones move on small wheels, legs, tracks, articulated pads, or low-profile crawling rigs. They can cross ordinary terrain, move through corridors, climb shallow obstacles, and follow the crew as long as the fiction supports their frame.

A drone needs a module to fly, climb walls, maneuver in vacuum, or move through unusual environments.


| Movement Type | Required Module |
|---|---|
| Ordinary ground movement | None |
| Wall or ceiling movement | Wall-Crawler |
| Hovering or atmospheric flight | Flight Module |
| Tactical atmospheric flight | Military Flight Module |
| EVA or low-gravity maneuvering | Micro-Thrusters / EVA Kit |
| Underwater operation | Submersible Kit |

Flying drones are useful, but they are also louder, hotter, more visible to sensors, and easier to identify as active remote systems.

---

## Drone Evasion

A drone’s **Evasion** is the number an attacker must meet or beat with an attack roll to strike it. It represents size, movement profile, flight correction, signal responsiveness, and how hard the drone is to track under pressure.

A drone uses its own Evasion when attacked. If the operator spends an Action or Reaction Roll to actively maneuver, hide, evade, or reposition the drone, the operator rolls using the appropriate Trait and Experiences. On success, the drone avoids danger, gains better position, or forces the attacker to lose the clean shot, as fits the fiction.

If a drone’s signal is **Lost**, it cannot actively evade unless it has autonomy or a loaded defensive protocol. If a drone’s signal is Lost and it is under attack, reduce its Evasion by 2 unless its current protocol would reasonably keep it moving, hiding, or returning.

As a balance guideline, drones should not normally exceed the following Evasion values without rare Experimental modules or direct Keeper approval:


| Drone Grade | Suggested Evasion Cap |
|---|---|
| Common | 12 |
| Military | 14 |
| Experimental | 15 |

If a drone becomes too hard to strike, it stops feeling like fragile equipment and starts becoming a second character.

---

## Armor Slots

A drone may mark 1 Armor Slot to reduce the severity of a hit by one step, following the normal armor rules; characters, drones, and vehicles all use the same armor terminology. Once marked, that Armor Slot is unavailable until repaired, recharged, or restored during downtime.

Common drones usually have no Armor Slots by default. Taking one into open combat is often the fastest way to turn credits into scrap.

---

## Drone Control and Roles

Anyone can use a drone. The roll depends on the task and the fiction.

A Pilot may be best at moving one through hostile terrain, tight angles, pursuit, extraction, or failing signal. An Engineer may be best at repairing, modifying, or hacking one. A Scoundrel may be best at infiltration. A Soldier may use one for tactical support. A Medic may use one to reach the wounded. A Scholar may use one for survey, sample collection, or analysis.

The drone does not decide the roll. The fiction does.


| Role | Natural Drone Use |
|---|---|
| **Pilot** | Movement, routes, scouting, extraction, signal, angles |
| **Engineer** | Repair, modification, diagnosis, hacking |
| **Scoundrel** | Infiltration, surveillance, sabotage, bugs |
| **Soldier** | Marking, suppression, breaching, cover |
| **Medic** | Stabilization, biometrics, evacuation |
| **Scholar** | Analysis, sampling, scanning, archive work |
| **Diplomat** | Remote presence, safe negotiation, witness recording |

### Pilots and Drones

Many pilots use drones as a groundside extension of their craft instincts. A good pilot does not stop navigating when they leave the cockpit; they simply start navigating corridors, ducts, sightlines, signals, and exits.

Anyone can use a drone. Pilots make a drone move like it belongs to the scene; Engineers make sure it survives the scene.

---

## Neural Drone Link

A standard operator uses hands, voice, or a HUD. A neural drone link allows faster command and better sensory integration, but it does not create a second mind.

**Neural Drone Link:** You may issue one meaningful drone command while also acting. Before either resolves, choose one cost: mark 1 Stress, or make one of the two Rolls with Disadvantage. If either Roll is Fear-dominant and noncritical, worsen the drone's signal by one step until the end of the operator's next Spotlight. The command otherwise resolves by its normal result.

A neural link is multitasking under pressure, not free effect economy.


---

## Shared Drone Control

Most drones are paired to a single operator. This keeps the signal clean, the control profile simple, and liability obvious. Some crews prefer that. If the Pilot or Scoundrel enjoys running their own drone and the table enjoys watching, nothing else is required.

Other crews want the drone to be a shared tool. For them, the cheapest answer is a crew control interface.

### Neural Network Control

**Grade:** Common  
**Cost:** 1 Cr  
**Slots:** 0

A shared crew interface that allows multiple registered crew members to take control of the same drone during a scene. Despite the name, Neural Network Control does not require full neural implants. Most versions use HUD sync, haptic input, voice tags, eye tracking, biometric permissions, and low-grade predictive neural mapping.

While the drone’s signal is **Stable**, any registered crew member may take control of the drone on their Spotlight and use their own Action or Reaction Roll to command it.

The acting character rolls with their own Trait, Experiences, and applicable Domain Powers. The drone provides the body, sensor, tool, position, or signal. The character provides intent, skill, timing, and risk.

Only one character controls the drone at a time. Passing control is free while the signal is Stable and the spotlight naturally moves between characters.

If the signal is **Unstable**, passing control costs the receiving operator 1 Stress. If they cannot mark it, the handoff fails and the previous operator retains control. No additional Roll or discretionary complication is added.

If the signal is **Lost**, Neural Network Control does not function. The drone follows its loaded protocol.

### Crew Drone, Not Personal Drone

Neural Network Control exists to keep drone scenes shared.

A drone with this upgrade can become a crew tool rather than one character’s private toy. The Pilot may fly it through a collapsing duct, the Engineer may take over to open a port, the Scoundrel may use it to plant false evidence, the Medic may stabilize someone through its injector, and the Scholar may scan what it finds.

This never lets the crew act for free. Each character still spends their own Action or Reaction Roll when they take the drone in hand. What the upgrade moves is the spotlight, not the arithmetic of the turn.

### Domain Powers Through a Drone

A character may use a Domain Power through a drone only when the fiction supports it.

Good uses include powers that work through sensors, signal, voice, hacking, remote tools, a vehicle interface, line of sight from the drone, or a device the drone can touch, scan, mark, cut, or connect to.

Bad uses include powers that require the character’s own body, direct personal touch, a weapon the character is personally wielding, an aura centered on the character, emotional presence the drone cannot carry, or judgment the drone cannot understand.

The character pays all normal costs: Hope, Stress, uses, cooldowns, or other requirements. If the power requires a roll, the character rolls.

A drone is a catalyst, not a second soul.
---

## Common Modules

Common modules are commercial, civilian, salvage, or frontier-grade systems. They are cheaper, easier to find, and easier to repair, but they are limited by firmware locks, weak power buses, and legal safety restrictions.

A Common drone cannot install Military or Experimental modules without illegal modification.

### Common Signal and Control


| Module | Cost | Slots | Mechanical Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Extended Link** | 2 Cr | 1 | When distance or ordinary structure would worsen signal, treat it as one step better. Does not bypass hard Lost zones. |
| **Relay Node** | 2 Cr | 1 | Acts as a local repeater. One allied drone or short comm signal routed through it treats signal as one step better while the relay survives. |
| **Basic Autonomy Chip** | 4 Cr | 1 | When signal is Lost, execute one loaded protocol: Freeze, Return, Follow Beacon, Record, Deliver, or Trigger Module. Cannot improvise. |
| **Shielded Receiver** | 4 Cr | 1 | Gain Advantage on checks to resist spoofing, light jamming, or ordinary interference. Does not resist hard Lost zones. |
| **Neural Network Control** | 1 Cr | 0 | Allows registered crew members to take control of the drone by turns while signal is Stable. It moves spotlight, not action economy. |

### Common Movement


| Module | Cost | Slots | Mechanical Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Flight Module** | 2 Cr | 1 | The drone can hover, cross gaps, move vertically, and fly at low speed in normal atmosphere. Strong wind, storms, damage, or tight terrain may require a roll. While flying, the drone takes **-2 to Agility Rolls to avoid detection**. |
| **Wall-Crawler** | 1 Cr | 1 | Climb walls, ceilings, ducts, and uneven surfaces unless slick, electrified, shielded, or hostile. |
| **Cargo Grip** | 1 Cr | 1 | Carry small objects, drag light loads, or retrieve items. Cannot carry a conscious adult unless the frame is built for hauling. |

### Common Sensors


| Module | Cost | Slots | Mechanical Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Low-Light Camera** | 1 Cr | 1 | Ignore penalties from darkness short of total blackout, smoke, or sensor-obscuring interference. |
| **Thermal Camera** | 2 Cr | 1 | Detect heat signatures through darkness, smoke, or light cover. Insulation, decoys, cold-blooded species, and thermal masking can defeat it. |
| **Radiation/Chem Sensor** | 2 Cr | 1 | Detect radiation, toxins, corrosives, atmospheric hazards, or chemical traces. Grants Advantage on checks to identify environmental danger. |
| **Audio Suite** | 1 Cr | 1 | Directional listening and clean recording. Grants Advantage when eavesdropping through ordinary barriers. |
| **Medical Scanner** | 2 Cr | 1 | Reads vitals and triage data. Grants Advantage to assess injury or stabilize remotely, but does not replace a Medic. |

### Common Tools


| Module | Cost | Slots | Mechanical Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Manipulator Arm** | 1 Cr | 1 | Move small objects, plug cables, press controls, retrieve samples, or perform simple manual tasks. |
| **Tool Mount** | 2 Cr | 1 | Mount one small legal tool: welder, injector, scanner, lock probe, solder kit, sample drill. |
| **Cutter** | 2 Cr | 1 | Cut light doors, panels, cables, locks, and thin plating. Hardened targets require time or a successful roll. |
| **Repair Kit** | 2 Cr | 1 | With operator Action, grants Advantage on a repair roll or lets the drone perform minor repairs at range. |
| **Medgel Injector** | 2 Cr | 1 | Stabilize a wounded target at range with operator Action. Does not heal HP unless another rule allows it. |

### Common Stealth and Evasion


| Module | Cost | Slots | Mechanical Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Noise Dampener** | 1 Cr | 1 | The drone’s movement is silent to ordinary hearing. Does not hide heat, signal, light, airflow, or physical traces. |
| **Stealth Shell** | 4 Cr | 1 | Gain **+1 on Agility Rolls to avoid detection** while grounded or moving no more than one band and using no loud module. Attacking, cutting, boosting, a strong transmission, or moving more than one band ends the bonus until the drone spends a Spotlight meeting those requirements again. The flight penalty still applies. |
| **Agile Servos** | 4 Cr | 1 | +1 Evasion. |
| **Low-Profile Frame** | 4 Cr | 1 | +1 Evasion against ranged attacks while the drone is not carrying a heavy tool, weapon mount, cargo load, or armor plating. |
| **Decoy Flare Pod** | 4 Cr | 1 | One use per reload. Against ranged, missile, sensor-guided, or drone attacks, impose Disadvantage or gain +2 Evasion against that attack. |

### Common Non-Lethal Systems

Common commercial drones cannot legally carry lethal weapons.


| Module | Cost | Slots | Mechanical Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Smoke/Flash Pod** | 2 Cr | 1 | One use per reload. Create a brief escape, distraction, breach window, or Advantage on one repositioning or infiltration action. |
| **Compliance Taser** | 4 Cr | 2 | Operator Action. Close attack. On hit, mark 1 Stress and force the target to drop an object, lose footing, or suffer momentary stun if fiction allows. Non-lethal and obvious. |
| **Stun Dart** | 4 Cr | 2 | Operator Action. Close/Far attack. On hit, deal 1d6 non-lethal physical damage or mark 1 Stress. Limited ammo. Legal status varies by port. |
