## Restricted Military Modules in the Core

The following military modules are included here because they are common enough to define the basic boundary of drone use. Rust & Steel expands this list.


| Module | Cost | Slots | Mechanical Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Military Flight Module** | 6 Cr | 1 | The drone gains controlled tactical flight. While airborne, the operator gains **+1 on rolls to maneuver, evade, chase, reposition, or pilot the drone**. This bonus does not apply to attacks, hacking, repairs, scanning, or other non-movement tasks. While flying, the drone takes **-2 to Agility Rolls to avoid detection**. |
| **Military Stealth Shell** | 8 Cr | 1 | Gain **+2 on Agility Rolls to avoid detection** while grounded or moving no more than one band and using no loud module. Attacking, cutting, boosting, a strong transmission, or moving more than one band ends the bonus until the drone spends a Spotlight meeting those requirements again. The flight penalty still applies. |
| **Armor Plating** | 4 Cr | 1 | Gain +1 Armor Slot. The drone loses 1 Evasion while flying, sneaking, evading, or moving through tight terrain. |
| **Target Painter** | 4 Cr | 1 | Operator Action. Mark one visible personal-scale target until the start of the operator's next Spotlight. The next allied attack against it gains Advantage, then the mark ends. This is not a starship Sensor Lock. |
| **Micro-Laser** | 4 Cr | 2 | Operator Action. Far attack. Deal 1d6 energy. Precise, but easy to trace by heat or beam origin. Does not scale with Proficiency unless explicitly upgraded. |

---

## Flight and Stealth

Flying is never as quiet as staying grounded.

While a drone is flying, hovering, boosting, or using exposed lift systems, it takes **-2 to Agility Rolls to avoid detection**. Stealth modules do not remove this penalty; they add their own bonus as normal.

This means a drone with a **Flight Module** and **Stealth Shell** has both effects: **-2 from flying** and **+1 from Stealth Shell**, for a net **-1** while flying carefully.

A drone with **Military Flight Module** and **Military Stealth Shell** has **-2 from flying** and **+2 from Military Stealth Shell**, for a net **0** while flying carefully.

If that same drone stays grounded, it keeps the stealth bonus without the flight penalty.

Choosing whether to fly or stay grounded is always a tactical decision.

---

## Weaponized Common Drones

Common drones are sold with hard locks against lethal weapon integration. These locks are legal, technical, and practical: firmware refuses lethal mounts, power draw is capped, targeting software blocks lethal profiles, and commercial frames report illegal changes when scanned.

A character may attempt to bypass these locks with tools, downtime, and a **Knowledge (Tech) Roll at DC 15**.

On a success, the drone can accept one illegal lethal weapon integration. The module must still be acquired, installed, powered, and hidden.

On a failure, the lock remains and the materials are not consumed. No Slot damage, bricking, or extra repair requirement is added unless the result is Failure with Fear and the table below states it.

After resolving the normal success or failure, a Fear-dominant noncritical result also requires one d6 roll on the Illegal Modification Complication table. Do not choose the result; matching dice never trigger it.


| d6 | Illegal Modification Complication |
|---|---|
| 1 | The drone’s serial now flags as tampered if scanned. |
| 2 | The weapon works, but the drone loses 1 Evasion. |
| 3 | The weapon drains power; after use, the signal becomes Unstable. |
| 4 | The drone takes Disadvantage on its next attack Roll before the end of the scene. |
| 5 | Increase Heat by 1 with the local authority or manufacturer named before the installation. |
| 6 | The modification is unstable; on the first Fear-dominant noncritical result involving the drone in combat, roll a Drone Complication. |

If discovered by authorities, a weaponized Common drone is treated as illegal weaponized equipment. Consequences may include fines, confiscation, warrants, faction attention, port bans, or criminal charges.

---

## Drone Weapons and Proficiency

Drone weapon damage does not scale with character Proficiency unless a rule explicitly says it does.

A drone weapon is a pressure tool, not a replacement for a combatant. It can mark, distract, suppress, stun, intercept, breach, or open a window. It does not trade blows with a trained soldier and win.

Taking a drone into open combat is often the fastest way to turn credits into scrap.

---

## Repairing Drones

A drone can be damaged, disabled, recovered, repaired, or rebuilt.


| Condition | Repair |
|---|---|
| **Lost HP** | Requires downtime, parts, and a Knowledge (Tech) Roll if conditions are poor |
| **Marked Armor Slot** | Recharged or restored during downtime, at a drone bay, or with proper tools |
| **Module Malfunction** | Requires an Action in an emergency or downtime for clean repair |
| **Dead Weight** | Recoverable if the core is intact |
| **Destroyed** | Frame is lost unless protected by Redundant Core, Disposable Shell, Blackbox, or Keeper ruling |
| **Hijacked** | Requires winning control back, cutting the link, or physically recovering the drone |

A drone is only gone forever when its core is destroyed, unrecoverable, or not worth the credits to rebuild.

---

## Drone Burden

If your table tracks Burden or inventory pressure, use the following guideline:


| Drone | Burden |
|---|---|
| Common Drone | 1 Burden |
| Military Drone | 2 Burden |
| Experimental Drone | 2 to 3 Burden |
| Industrial or War-Frame | Vehicle cargo / ship storage only |
| Swarm Cells | 1 Burden per 3 cells |

Drones are portable until they are not. A crew can carry a scout mote in a pack. They cannot casually stroll through customs with a War-Frame under a coat.

---

## Drone Complications

At most once per drone per scene, after its operator resolves Failure with Fear on a Roll materially involving that drone, roll d12 on this table. Do not choose the result. Matching dice never trigger a Drone Complication.


| d12 | Complication |
|---|---|
| 1 | The signal worsens one step. |
| 2 | The drone's signal becomes Unstable until the end of the operator's next Spotlight, then returns to its prior state. |
| 3 | The drone becomes Restrained; clear it with the Core Strength Roll, DC 15, or an operator Action and Knowledge (Tech), DC 15. |
| 4 | The drone's signal becomes Lost until the operator spends an Action and succeeds on Knowledge (Tech), DC 15, to reroute it. |
| 5 | The drone loses Hidden and one established hostile observer in the scene learns its current zone. |
| 6 | The next Action performed through the drone before the end of the operator's next Spotlight has Disadvantage. |
| 7 | The drone loses 1 direct HP. |
| 8 | The operator chooses one installed module; it goes offline until an Action and Knowledge (Tech), DC 10, restores it. |
| 9 | The next Knowledge or Instinct Roll made through the drone before the end of the scene has Disadvantage. |
| 10 | The operator makes a Knowledge (Tech) Reaction Roll, DC 15; on failure the signal worsens one state, on success nothing changes. |
| 11 | The operator makes a Knowledge (Tech) Reaction Roll, DC 20; on failure the signal becomes Lost until an Action and Knowledge (Tech), DC 15, restores it. Control never transfers automatically. |
| 12 | The operator must spend an Action to confirm the current command before the drone can perform another complex task; simple return and stop commands still work. |

**Module Cost:** 2 Cr

**Use:** A cheap scouting drone that the whole crew can control by turns. Ideal for tables that want drone scenes to stay shared.

### Security Stun Drone

**Grade:** Military  
**Base Cost:** 8 Cr  
**Modules:** Stun Dart, Hardened Link  
**Module Cost:** 10 Cr  
**Total Cost:** 18 Cr  
**Use:** Restricted patrol, non-lethal control, crew security.

### Tactical Support Frame

**Grade:** Military  
**Base Cost:** 8 Cr  
**Modules:** Armor Plating, Target Painter, Smoke/Flash Pod  
**Module Cost:** 10 Cr  
**Total Cost:** 18 Cr  
**Use:** Breach support, marking, extraction.

### Ghost-Signal Infiltrator

**Grade:** Experimental  
**Base Cost:** 16 Cr  
**Modules:** Ghost-Signal Lattice, Reflex Kernel, Veil-Hardened Casing  
**Module Cost:** 40 Cr  
**Total Cost:** 56 Cr  
**Use:** Dangerous infiltration through bad signal and Veil interference. Leaves strange traces. Someone probably wants it back.

---

## Optional: Drones with Quirks

Most drones are not people, and most are not close. But old systems develop habits, especially after years of bad patches, nervous operators, station rot, damaged Pearls, or exposure to the Veil.

A quirk should color play, not stop it: a joke, a small complication, a ritual, or a memory. It should never become a constant punishment.

If a drone or tool truly seems to want something, it is no longer just equipment. It is a story hook, and that belongs in the Keeper’s Companion.

# CHAPTER 15: THE PEARL STANDARD

*"In the post-Silence galaxy, your wealth tier isn't just about the credits in your account. It's about whether the dock master gives you a priority berth or lets you rot in the queue. It's about whether the medic uses a sterile nano-suture or a rusty needle. It's about whether you'll live to spend it."*

*Free Fleet financial primer, Section One*

***At a glance.*** Veilfarers tracks money through six Wealth Tiers (0 to 5) rather than a credit ledger. Each Tier sets your lifestyle, what you acquire without rolling, and what you must Wealth Check to attempt. Tiers shift through narrative events; the black market, Crew Wealth, and a handful of alternative currencies layer on top. Read this to know what your character can afford, how to reach above it, and why almost everything in

*the Pearl Era ultimately runs through one House.*

Most science-fiction RPGs count credits to the unit. The bookkeeping is precise; the fictional return is small, and most groups quietly stop enforcing it by session five. Veilfarers skips the ledger. The credit subsystem exists if you want it, but the **Tier** is the system.

## THE PEARL STANDARD

One Imperial Credit is defined as **one milligram of Refined Chrono-Pearl Dust**. Pearls are mined under House Valerius license (Chapter 5); the Dust is refined under House Kurogane; the Credit itself is a small ceramic chip embedded with sealed pearl-derived matter, carrying a verification mark and a unique serial. It is, by design, **anti-digital**: it cannot be electronically duplicated, and counterfeiting requires actual Dust, which is scarce and tightly controlled. Most credit-scale transactions are physical chips changing hands or verified physical transfers through an Imperial Exchange.

Two things this makes true at the table:

- **Theft is meaningful.** A bag of credit chips is a *thing* you carry. Pickpocketing five Credits is a story event.

- **Large transactions are visible.** Five hundred Credits is a small but heavy parcel; major purchases attract attention, and the watching characters know what just happened.

The Pearl Standard is not universal. The Free Fleet runs on barter and favor-credit; Frontier Colonies use local **Scrip**; Ailuran communities trade in **secrets**, not chips. The Empire is the standard. Most of the galaxy is the exception.

## THE WEALTH TIER SYSTEM

Every character has one **Wealth Tier**, 0 to 5. It changes rarely. Each Tier defines four things: **the Feeling** (what life is like, how NPCs treat you), **Allowance** (what you acquire without a roll), **Savings & Purchasing Power** (what you can save toward via a Wealth Check), and **Assets** (one major acquisition per month of in-fiction time, no roll). Most starting characters are Tier 1; some Displaced or Sleeping concepts begin at Tier 0; the rare House cadet or wealthy heir begins at Tier 2.

The Tier describes your *position*, not your *float*: a Tier 3 character may have one Credit or several thousand on hand on any given day, depending on how the campaign has gone.

**Tier 0, Forgotten.** Nothing. You sleep between things, eat what others would not, are unregistered in Imperial systems. No allowance, no savings, no monthly asset. Your currency is **favors**, bought with blood and service. Hard to *begin* play at; appropriate for refugees, the lowest point of a redemption arc, or a dramatic late-campaign fall. Climbing out is two to four sessions of consistent earned work.

**Tier 1, Established.** You have a job and a bunk. You eat. The Imperial system knows your name. You acquire standard ammunition, rations, and routine gear maintenance without tracking; once per month you take one Tier 1 item (1 Credit) free. You may save toward one Tier 2 purchase per quarter (Wealth Check DC 15). This is the working-crew baseline.

**Tier 2, Prosperous.** Established and recognized in your field. Comfortable quarters, advanced ammunition without tracking, Military-tier maintenance. Once per month, one Tier 1 to 2 item (1 to 4 Credits) free; once per year, you may save toward a Tier 3 purchase (DC 20). Most working crews reach Tier 2 by mid-campaign, after ten to fifteen sessions including at least one major payday.

**Tier 3, Affluent.** Influential. You own a ship, a small business, or a property of significance; you employ or contract others on your own terms. Discreet services and

priority access at most stations. Monthly asset: one item up to Tier 3 (1 to 9 Credits). Tier 4 purchases possible by Check (DC 25) once per two years. Reached through campaign-defining success, twenty-plus sessions, formal faction promotion, or inheritance, never a small surprise.

**Tier 4, Powerful.** Operating at House scale without being a House member. Significant assets, a personal staff, standing relationships with major institutions, lines of credit. Monthly asset: one item up to Tier 4, 1 to 16 Credits. A Tier 5 purchase requires a Wealth Roll, DC 25, and access established before the Roll. Rare; the character is now outside the scrappy-crew premise, and the campaign should reflect that.

**Tier 5, Transcendent.** A House cadet's level, a faction Baron, a captain of multiple vessels. Effectively unlimited within reasonable scope; the limiting factors are political, relational, and ethical. The ceiling of the standard advancement curve; the base game does not assume any campaign will produce a Tier 5 PC.

### QUICK REFERENCE

| TIER | NAME | MONTHLY ACQUISITION | EQUIPMENT ACCESS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **0** | Forgotten | None (favors only) | Improvised only |
| **1** | Established | 1× Tier 1 (1 Credit) | Common, reliable |
| **2** | Prosperous | 1× Tier 1 to 2 (1 to 4) | Military, regular |
| **3** | Affluent | 1× up to Tier 3 (1 to 9) | Experimental, occasional |
| **4** | Powerful | 1× up to Tier 4 (1 to 16) | Experimental, routine |
| **5** | Transcendent | 1× up to Tier 5 (1 to 25+) | All tiers on demand |

## THE WEALTH CHECK

To acquire an item above your monthly allowance, roll a **Knowledge** (formal markets) or **Presence** (relationships) Duality Roll against the DC for the item's Tier. The Wealth ladder is the standard DC ladder (Chapter 9), one rung per Tier:

| ITEM TIER | DC |
| --- | --- |
| **Tier 1** | 10 |
| **Tier 2** | 15 |
| **Tier 3** | 20 |
| **Tier 4** | 25 |
| **Tier 5** | 30 |

You must be **at most one Tier below the item's Tier** to attempt the Check at all. On Success, the character acquires the item and the Keeper subtracts the appropriate reserves narratively; Critical Success acquires it clean and below cost; Failure does not acquire it and may produce a complication (a scammed contact, a flagged purchase); Failure with Fear makes the complication serious. Pacing is by Tier: Tier 1 Checks once per month, Tier 2 once per quarter, Tier 3 once per year, Tier 4+ once per two years. Wealth Checks are **story events**, not inventory management.

> **QUICK PROCEDURE - THE WEALTH CHECK**
>
> | STEP | WHAT HAPPENS |
> | --- | --- |
> | 1. Is it free? | If the item is at or below your **monthly allowance**, you simply have it. No roll. Stop here. |
> | 2. Are you allowed to try? | You must be **at most one Tier below** the item's Tier. Two or more below: no Check exists. (The black market lifts this by one, at a price.) |
> | 3. Has the clock reset? | Tier 1 once a month, Tier 2 once a quarter, Tier 3 once a year, Tier 4+ once every two years. |
> | 4. Roll | **Knowledge** (formal markets) or **Presence** (relationships) vs **10 / 15 / 20 / 25 / 30** by item Tier. |
> | 5. Read the outcome | *Critical:* acquired, clean and under cost. *Success:* acquired. *Failure:* not acquired, and possibly a complication. *Failure with Fear:* the complication is serious. |
>
> The Check answers *can you get it at all*, not *how much is left in the account*. There is no ledger to subtract from.

## WEALTH GAINS AND LOSSES

Tiers move through narrative events, usually one Tier at a time. Multi-Tier shifts are rare and dramatic.

**Gains:** a campaign-defining job's payoff; faction promotion within a House, Fleet, Guild, or Imperial Service; inheritance from a wealthy relative; sustained long-career success; a successful owned business; a valuable salvage. **Losses:** high-tier medical reconstruction (a character recovering from a Final-state injury may automatically drop one Tier); major theft or fraud; catastrophic loss of a primary asset; a debt called at a bad moment; loss of formal standing.

## THE BLACK MARKET

The Wealth Check covers legitimate markets. The black market handles three things the legitimate system cannot: **items above your Tier ceiling**, **restricted or contraband items** (military-grade weaponry, certain pharmaceuticals, prohibited Precursor equipment, forged credentials), and **anonymous acquisitions** the character can afford but cannot afford the *record* of.

### MECHANICS

A black-market Wealth Check uses the standard procedure with three changes:

- **Disadvantage** on the Check (the premium for negotiation, vetting, and price-gouging). The DC stays on its rung; the risk rides on the dice, as Chapter 9 prescribes for a task that is harder without being a whole step harder.

- **Tier limit lifted by one**: you can attempt **two** **Tiers above** your own (a Tier 1 character can attempt a Tier 3 purchase, at the same risk).

- **Black-Market Heat** is generated on Failure or on Success with Fear (see below).

The Check also requires a **contact** in the relevant segment, cultivated narratively over a session or more. No contact, no Check; finding the contact is often the first arc of a black-market campaign.

### BLACK-MARKET HEAT

**Black-Market Heat** is a personal track, 0 to 6, reflecting attention from parties who would prefer your business stay quiet. It is unrelated to a starship's **Heat** (the thermal-load track in Chapter 17); the two never interact, and a character can be Burned on one while the ship runs cold on the other.

| HEAT | STATE | EFFECT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **0 to 1** | Cold | Background. Unremarkable. |
| **2 to 3** | Warm | You are known enough that the black market's **Disadvantage no longer applies** to you; legitimate Reputation slightly harder to gain |
| **4 to 5** | Hot | Black-market Checks are made with **Advantage** - the wrong people trust you now; legitimate Imperial Checks attract scrutiny; law-adjacent Reputation locked at neutral or below |
| **6** | Burned | No black-market Checks at all; existing contacts cut ties; active investigation begins |

**Gain Heat** from: a failed black-market acquisition Roll (+1), Failure with Fear during a black-market acquisition (+2 instead), Success with Fear (+1), and a printed story trigger such as a captured contact or leaked record. **Clear Heat** by going dark for a session (-1 and one Tier's monthly allowance), completing a change-of-identity project (-3), or completing one clean quarter with no Heat-generating event (-1).

### COSTS BEYOND THE CHECK

Black-market acquisitions also carry the **Premium** (roughly 2 to 3× the legitimate-market reserves cost), the **Cut** (the contact's fee, sometimes paid in credits and sometimes in future favors that the contact's idea of fairness may interpret broadly), and the **Trace** (a serial, a

flag, or a slow-acting trigger; most never matter, some shape entire arcs).

### WHAT IT OFFERS, IN BRIEF

Tier 1 (forged basics, off-brand pharma, unregulated weapons), Tier 2 (unregistered mid-grade weapons, stolen vehicles, untracked Veil-route data), Tier 3 (military small arms, Precursor fragments, stolen House technology), Tier 4 (off-registry vessels, significant Precursor artifacts, off-the-books mercenaries), Tier 5 (capital-scale equipment outside Imperial registry, operational Precursor artifacts, weapons the Houses pretend they do not have). The higher the Tier, the smaller the market, the more dangerous the contacts.

## CREW WEALTH

A registered crew has its **own** Wealth Tier alongside its members'. The Crew Tier covers ship-scale and enterprise-scale economics (fuel, ship modifications, ship repairs, contracts at crew level, shared property); personal Tier covers character-scale (personal kit, lodging, individual acquisitions).

| CREW TIER | NAME | WHAT IT OWNS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **0** | Desperate | No registered vessel; session-to-session |
| **1** | Working | Tier 1 to 2 ship; shared operating account |
| **2** | Established | Tier 2 to 3 ship; small client base, modest reserves |
| **3** | Successful | Tier 3 to 4 ship; retained contacts, can weather a bad season |
| **4** | Prosperous | Tier 4 to 5 ship; possibly multiple vessels; non-PC employees |
| **5** | Magnate | Operates as a small commercial entity; rare |

A personal Tier 1 character on a Crew Tier 3 ship is not poor in practice (the ship's reserves cover crew business, the lifestyle aboard is comfortable, professional standing is the crew's), but personal acquisitions still operate at Tier 1. Where the boundary blurs, the table negotiates;

the Keeper should establish the crew's operating norm early. **Crew Wealth Checks** use the same DC table, rolled by whichever PC has financial authority (usually the Captain); the acquisition is a crew asset.

**Shared debts** follow the *enterprise*: a PC who leaves the crew does not shed crew-level obligations, unless a debt is **personally guaranteed** by one PC (in which case it may follow them out instead). Experienced captains avoid personal guarantees for exactly that reason.

## WEALTH TRANSITIONS

Tier movement needs three things together: **cumulative narrative weight** (sustained operation at the next-Tier level across several sessions), **a triggering event** (a contract signed, a promotion, an inheritance recognized, a property acquired) to make the move real in the fiction, and **no active blockers** (Black-Market Heat 4+ blocks climbing above Tier 2 in Imperial space; outstanding debts can stall the climb). Descent mirrors: a catastrophic event, or living above your means until the gap closes.

The rule of thumb is **two Tier movements** per character across a campaign, one up, sometimes one down and recovered. Tier stasis is also valid. **Avoid Tier inflation:** a Tier 1 crew reaching Tier 5 in twenty sessions has trivialized the system. Handle transitions with a brief table moment, the Keeper invites the move, the player names the triggering event in fiction, the table acknowledges it. The mechanical event carries social weight; let it earn its moment.

## PROPERTY AND SHIPS

At Tier 2 and above, you may own significant property; maintenance costs sit in the background as long as the property is within or one Tier above your reach. Property *above* your Tier is unsustainable: the character either climbs to support it or loses it within a session or two.

| TIER | PROPERTY | SHIP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | Bunk, apartment, cabin | (none personal) |
| **2** | Modest home, small business | Small courier or shuttle (the *Pelican* is here) |
| **3** | Significant business, ship of one's own | Cargo hauler, light freighter, armed merchant |
| **4** | Multiple smaller properties | Medium freighter, escort frigate, refit corvette |
| **5** | Estate, business empire | Heavy frigate, light cruiser, major mercantile vessel |

Ships above Tier 5 (heavy cruisers, capitals, dreadnoughts) are not normally PC-accessible. A Tier 3+ ship really wants more than one PC to run it cleanly; a solo character with one will operate it below spec.

## DEBT

Many Veilfarers characters owe somebody. Debt is not punishment; it is a piece of the setting.

- **Personal debts** to a named NPC, tracked narratively; the lender calls them at a dramatically appropriate moment.

- **House debts**: a signed contract, a stipend taken, a cadet status accepted. Until satisfied or terminated, the House has formal claims on time and Reputation (Chapter 16).

- **Free Fleet contracts**: the Fleet operates on contracts, not wages. Flexible but binding; a walked-out contractor finds Fleet doors closing.

- **Imperial Levies**: percentage taxes on declared income, paid annually or quarterly. Most active crews evade; getting caught is a story event.

A debt can also be *positive* leverage: a powerful NPC who owes the crew is a story engine in their own right.

## ALTERNATIVE CURRENCIES

Five worth naming, all in addition to (not instead of) the Pearl Standard where they overlap.

- **Ailuran secrets.** An Ailuran community trades in pieces of information of measured weight: a verified secret of suitable significance settles a debt the way a chip does in Imperial space. Outsiders are usually paid in chips, not in secrets.

- **Bloomstrider seed-trade.** Bloomstrider communities exchange living material, seeds, cuttings, propagules, on long-cycle ledgers measured in generations rather than seasons. Hard to evaluate; the Bloomstriders themselves do most of the math.

- **Free Fleet favor-credit.** A captain's word, written and signed in the Fleet's distinctive way, is legal tender across the Fleet's network. Outside the Fleet it is worth what the next Free Fleet ship decides to honor.

- **House Scrip.** Some Houses issue paper notes against their own reserves, valid within their territories and at recognized partner stations. Scrip is often worth slightly less than its face value off-territory.

- **Frontier barter.** Edge colonies often have no functional Imperial presence. Local goods (water, parts, time) are the currency, and a Pearl Standard chip is sometimes worth less than a working filter element.

## A CAMPAIGN IN BRIEF

To show the pacing, a sketched arc across a sixty-session campaign with a four-PC crew: they begin at personal Tier 1 on a Crew Tier 1 *Pelican*; by session 15 a major payday has lifted two PCs and the crew to Tier 2; sessions 16 to 30 climb through several smaller contracts; a campaign-defining mid-campaign job in sessions 31 to 45 takes the crew to Tier 3 and the Captain to Tier 3 with a Black-Market Heat reading of 3; late campaign, around session 46 to 60, sees a near-Burned recovery arc and the eventual quiet of a Captain at Tier 3, the crew at Tier 3, with several PCs at Tier 2. Movement is real, but bounded. The Tier mattered every time it changed.

## CLOSING: WEALTH IS WHAT YOU CANNOT TAKE WITH YOU

The Wealth Tiers exist so a change in fortune stays meaningful, and so the low Tiers gate the high-Tier gear that should feel hard-won; a Tier 1 character is not a lesser character, only one whose story has not yet turned on money. Spend deliberately, and remember the credits are temporary: the Tier is one of the few things that lasts a campaign, and even it is only one of the things you are.

# CHAPTER 16: YOUR NAME IN THE VOID

*"Credits come and go. A good ship can be rebuilt. But reputation? That's forever. In this galaxy, your word, your name, that might be the only currency that truly matters."*

*Elena Vasquez, Guildmaster of the Stellar Commerce Guild*

***At a glance.*** A character holds a Reputation Score with each major faction, tracked from -3 (Hated) through 0 (Unknown) to +6 (Legendary), advancing on Reputation Points (RP) awarded by the Keeper after sessions or arcs. Each level reshapes how the faction treats you and unlocks faction-specific Perks. Reputation is external (how the galaxy sees you publicly); it is separate from Affiliation Standing (Chapter 8), which is your position within an institution. The chapter also covers Crew Cohesion, the same kind of currency turned inward: how well the crew itself holds together.

After the Silence, trust became the rarest commodity in the galaxy. No central authority can enforce a contract; the only thing that crosses systems intact is the *weight of a name*. The Reputation system makes that weight mechanical.

## THE CORE CONCEPT

You do not have one Reputation; you have **one per faction**. The six Great Houses, the Stellar Commerce Guild, the Free Fleet, the Explorers' Guild, the Solara Compact, the Church of the Eternal Veil, and any other organization the Keeper marks as a Reputation-tracking entity each carry their own track. You may be Revered by

House Joric, Hated by House Volkov, and Trusted by the Commerce Guild at the same time, every relationship is its own arc.

Each track runs **-3 to +6**, starting at **0 (Unknown)** for every new character. Changes are *not automatic*; the Keeper awards RP at the end of a session or arc to reflect what the crew actually did.

Two numbers, not one. **Reputation Points (RP)** are the running total you accumulate; the **Reputation Level** (-3 to +6) is the rung that total has bought you. You gain and lose RP constantly; the Level moves only when a threshold is crossed. Do not confuse either with **Affiliation Standing**, a separate track that runs +5 to -5, starts at +1 (Good Standing), and measures your position *inside* the one institution you have sworn to - not the galaxy's opinion of you from outside. Standing is set during character creation (Chapter 8, Step 6) and is eroded by the forbidden conflicts each affiliation names (Chapter 5).

## THE REPUTATION LADDER


| LEVEL | TITLE | RP | WHAT IT MEANS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **+6** | Legendary | 35+ (and a world-changing deed) | Effectively unlimited access; you shape the faction's future |
| **+5** | Revered | 25 | Strategic counsel; significant resources at your call |
| **+4** | Honored | 17 | Senior officials take your calls directly; access to deep resources |
| **+3** | Trusted | 10 | Real perks: discounts, signature gear, sworn favors |
| **+2** | Respected | 5 | Doors crack open; small concessions without asking |
| **+1** | Recognized | 2 | They have heard of you; basic courtesy |
| **0** | Unknown | 0 | Starting position; professional indifference |
| **-1** | Distrusted | -2 | Watchlist; unhelpful officials, stops and searches |
| **-2** | Scorned | -5 | Open contempt; local bounties; ports denied |
| **-3** | Hated | -10 | Galaxy-wide bounty; kill-on-sight in their territory |

Crossing a threshold changes how the faction operates around the crew; the differences are concrete, not flavor.

## EARNING AND BURNING TRUST

**Gaining RP.** The Keeper awards points at the end of a session or arc, scaled to what the crew did.

- **Minor Success (+1 RP):** a standard mission delivered, a small piece of useful intelligence, cargo run clean.

- **Major Success (+2 to +3 RP):** a difficult mission completed, a significant asset saved, a meaningful blow to a faction's rival.

- **Legendary Deed (+4 to +5 RP):** a campaign-level achievement: a world saved, a battle won, a power-shifting secret uncovered.

**Losing RP.** The fall is usually faster than the climb.

- **Minor Transgression (-1 RP):** a simple failure, being seen with a known rival.

- **Major Betrayal (-3 to -4 RP):** active work against the faction, sabotage, aid to a sworn enemy at meaningful scale.

- **Act of War (-5 to -6 RP):** a faction leader killed, a major asset destroyed, a deepest secret exposed.

When totals cross a threshold, the Level shifts; the Keeper narrates the move so the table feels it.

> **QUICK PROCEDURE - MOVING A REPUTATION**
>
> | STEP | WHAT HAPPENS |
> | --- | --- |
> | 1. End of session or arc | The Keeper, not the dice, awards RP. Nothing here is automatic. |
> | 2. Score the deed | *Minor* +1 · *Major* +2 to +3 · *Legendary* +4 to +5. Against you: *Minor* -1 · *Major Betrayal* -3 to -4 · *Act of War* -5 to -6. |
> | 3. Pay the rival | Most gains cost RP with someone else. The Keeper names that cost **before** the crew commits, never after. |
> | 4. Add to the running RP total | Per faction. Separate track for each. |
> | 5. Did a threshold fall? | **+2** Recognized · **+5** Respected · **+10** Trusted · **+17** Honored · **+25** Revered · **+35 *and* a world-changing deed** Legendary. Downward: **-2** Distrusted · **-5** Scorned · **-10** Hated. |
> | 6. If the Level moved | New Perk unlocks - and the Obligation that comes with it. Narrate the shift at the table. |
>
> RP is the odometer; the Level is the gear you are in. A crew can bank RP for three sessions and see nothing change, then cross +10 and find every Joric door already open.

## WALKING THE TIGHTROPE

The galaxy is a web of rivalries. A lucrative contract for one faction is usually a problem for another. **The Keeper's job is to be transparent about the trade before the players accept**: "You can take this from Joric, but Volkov claims this territory; succeed and you make heroes of yourselves with Joric and enemies of yourselves with Volkov, are you sure?" A net +3 RP with one faction will often cost -2 with their rival; the crew should know this *before* committing.

Some standard rivalries (the Keeper may adjust):

- **Valerius vs Solari** (commerce vs imperial-traditional).

- **Joric vs Volkov** (defensive vs aggressive military doctrine).

- **Kurogane vs the Church of the Eternal Veil** (transhumanism vs mystic doctrine).

- **The Free Fleet vs Joric** (independence vs imperial governance).

- **The Solara Compact vs any House actively** **colonizing fringe systems**.

## MENDING FENCES

Burned bridges are rarely free to rebuild.

- **Distrusted (-1):** a sincere apology and a significant unrewarded favor may repair it.

- **Scorned (-2):** a sustained arc of unambiguous service across multiple sessions; a Major Success done *for* the faction at real cost.

- **Hated (-3):** a Legendary deed in the faction's interest, accepted formally by their leadership. Some Hated relationships never recover, and a character who tries should know that going in.

## AFFILIATION OBLIGATIONS AND REPUTATION PERKS

A character can stand in two different relationships to a faction, and they are not the same thing. **Affiliation** (Chapter 8) is sworn membership: you carry the faction's

mark, and with it a standing **Affiliation Obligation** that you owe whether the faction currently loves you or not. **Reputation** (this chapter) is external standing: the galaxy's running tally of your name. Each rung you climb hands you a concrete **Perk**, and with it an **Obligation**, because a faction that trusts you also expects more of you. Perks are benefits you can call on; Obligations are what the faction quietly expects in return, and a crew that takes the perks while shirking the obligations bleeds RP until the doors close again.

The tables below give, for each major faction, its Affiliation Obligation and what each tier grants and demands. The Keeper adapts specifics to the campaign. Two rules hold everywhere: **every called perk has a narrative consequence** (a borrowed squad commits you to its owner's interests; a called escort paints you in the eyes of that faction's enemies), and **nothing is free.**

### HOUSE AMARANTH (KEEPERS OF WISDOM)

**Affiliation Obligation.** Every significant thing you learn, a Vault decoded, a pre-Silence record recovered, a Veil phenomenon documented, belongs in the House archives. Knowledge withheld is theft; knowledge sold to a rival is heresy. You are also expected to keep the House's dangerous knowledge out of careless hands.


| REPUTATION LEVEL | PERK GAINED | OBLIGATION IT CARRIES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+1 Recognized** | A reading card to any public Amaranth library; junior archivists answer reasonable questions | Credit the House when its knowledge saves you; do not hand its texts to outsiders |
| **+2 Respected** | Scholarly discounts on data, tutoring, and translation; a named archivist contact | Bring at least one genuine discovery to the archives each arc |
| **+3 Trusted** | Access to the restricted stacks; one standing favor of expert consultation on any problem | Undertake a retrieval the House dare not risk its own people on, when asked |
| **+4 Honored** | Deep-archive access including catalogued Precursor fragments; a House cipher-key | Surrender Precursor artifacts you recover for study; you may petition to keep the findings |
| **+5 Revered** | The House shares strategic intelligence and lends a Loremaster to your crew for an arc | Act as the House's hand in a matter it cannot be seen to touch |
| **+6 Legendary** | A seat in the inner circle; you may steer a line of House research and read what almost no one reads | You now hold one of the House's deepest secrets, and the keeping of it may cost you everything |

*Distrusted or below: libraries close, archivists "lose" the records you need, and at Hated the House makes*

*sure your rivals learn exactly what you were searching for.*

### HOUSE JORIC (THE SENTINELS)

**Affiliation Obligation.** You answer the call to defend. When a Sentinel line is threatened and you are within reach, you hold it, and you do not start the wars you are sworn to end. The shield is not yours to use as a sword.


| REPUTATION LEVEL | PERK GAINED | OBLIGATION IT CARRIES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+1 Recognized** | Patrols treat you as friendly; safe passage through Joric-held lanes | Do not raise arms first in Joric space; report raiders you sight |
| **+2 Respected** | Standard-issue military gear at cost; field resupply at Sentinel posts | Lend a hand when a post you pass is shorthanded |
| **+3 Trusted** | A sworn squad will accompany you on one dangerous mission per arc; signature Joric arms | Spend that squad on defensive ends only, and bring them home |
| **+4 Honored** | Access to Precursor-tier defensive hardware; a Sentinel liaison officer | Hold a line the House names, even when it is not your fight |
| **+5 Revered** | Temporary command of Sentinel assets, a cutter and crew, for a sanctioned operation | Answer the House's muster in a genuine crisis, no matter your other plans |
| **+6 Legendary** | You stand among the architects of Joric doctrine; fleets move when you ask | Your name is now a Joric promise; breaking faith here is treason, not bad manners |

*Distrusted or below: posts deny resupply and "inspect" your hold; at Hated, Joric treats you as a hostile incursion.*

### HOUSE KUROGANE (THE GOD-MAKERS)

**Affiliation Obligation.** Progress is paid for in data. You feed the House what you learn from the tech you use and the bodies you augment, and you accept that to climb here is to be changed, willingly, by what the House builds.


| REPUTATION LEVEL | PERK GAINED | OBLIGATION IT CARRIES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+1 Recognized** | Entry to Kurogane workshops; basic repair and fabrication at cost | Log performance data on any House gear you field |
| **+2 Respected** | Prototype field-testing rights; discounts on cybernetics and implants | Return honest results, failures included, on what you test |
| **+3 Trusted** | Signature Kurogane gear and one bespoke modification per arc | Submit to one round of monitored augmentation or telemetry when asked |
| **+4 Honored** | Access to experimental and Precursor-derived tech; a House engineer on call | Carry a House device into a place it could never otherwise reach |
| **+5 Revered** | Authority over a slice of research budget; a prototype vessel system installed | Let the House study a result you would rather keep private |
| **+6 Legendary** | You help decide what humanity becomes next; the deepest labs open to you | You are now part of the experiment, and the House will not let its investment walk away freely |

*Distrusted or below: your augments flag in House systems; at Hated, Kurogane considers its property recoverable, including what it put inside you.*

### HOUSE SOLARI (THE FADING CROWN)

**Affiliation Obligation.** You uphold the forms. In Solari halls you observe rank, ceremony, and the fiction of the old Empire's continuity, and you never publicly suggest the Crown is fading, even when everyone in the room knows it.


| REPUTATION LEVEL | PERK GAINED | OBLIGATION IT CARRIES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+1 Recognized** | Admittance to minor court functions; the courtesy due a guest | Observe protocol; arrive presentable and unarmed where custom demands |
| **+2 Respected** | Imperial-tax reductions in Solari space; letters of introduction | Lend the Crown the dignity of your presence at one occasion per arc |
| **+3 Trusted** | Formal documents, writs, and pardons that open imperial doors | Perform a discreet service that lets a noble save face |
| **+4 Honored** | A court audience on request; a minor honorific attached to your name | Defend the legitimacy of the Crown in word and deed when it is questioned |
| **+5 Revered** | A granted title with real estate or revenue; decree authority in a small domain | Answer the Crown's summons and rule your grant as the Crown would wish |
| **+6 Legendary** | You become a pillar the Fading Crown leans on; your word carries imperial weight | You now share the burden of a dying order, and its enemies become yours |

*Distrusted or below: invitations dry up and old slights are remembered; at Hated, Solari brands you a traitor to the Empire that no longer quite exists.*

### HOUSE VALERIUS (THE PEARL MERCHANTS)

**Affiliation Obligation.** You honor your debts and your contracts to the letter, and you do not undercut the House's markets or carry its rivals' cargo. Profit secures peace, and a Valerius affiliate who breaks a deal breaks the only law that matters here.


| REPUTATION LEVEL | PERK GAINED | OBLIGATION IT CARRIES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+1 Recognized** | A trading account; 10% discount on goods at Valerius exchanges | Settle your accounts on time, every time |
| **+2 Respected** | Priority Exchange access; discount rising toward 20%; market tips | Route a fair share of your trade through House channels |
| **+3 Trusted** | Exclusive contracts and consignments; a line of credit | Give the House right of first refusal on Chrono-Pearl you find |
| **+4 Honored** | Access to the Pearl markets proper; a Factor who works on your behalf | Move a sensitive cargo no questions asked, when the House needs it |
| **+5 Revered** | Market-moving authority; the House backs your ventures with capital | Use that leverage in concert with House interests, never against them |
| **+6 Legendary** | You sit among those who set the price of the Pearl itself | Your fortune and the House's are now one ledger; its enemies will come for both |

*Distrusted or below: prices rise against you and credit dries up; at Hated, Valerius simply makes you*

*uninsurable, then unwelcome everywhere coin is counted.*

### HOUSE VOLKOV (THE WAR-MAKERS)

**Affiliation Obligation.** Strength is truth, and you prove yours. You answer challenges rather than dodge them, you do not show the weakness of broken word or abandoned ally, and when the warband marches you do not hide.


| REPUTATION LEVEL | PERK GAINED | OBLIGATION IT CARRIES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+1 Recognized** | Entry to the training pits; respect earned by showing up | Never refuse an honest challenge outright; back your words |
| **+2 Respected** | Discounts on weapons and armor; a sparring-mentor's ear | Stand your ground in a fight the warband shares |
| **+3 Trusted** | Signature plasma weapons and a war-token that opens hard doors | Take a dangerous mission the House respects, and finish it |
| **+4 Honored** | Command of a warband for an operation; access to heavy arms | Lead from the front; a Volkov leader who hangs back is no leader |
| **+5 Revered** | Temporary command of a warship and crew; a place at the war-table | March when the House calls its strength, even at cost to your own plans |
| **+6 Legendary** | You are reckoned among the great warlords; oaths are sworn to your name | Your strength is now the House's banner; to falter publicly is to fall completely |

*Distrusted or below: warriors test you on sight; at Hated, Volkov puts a price on you and treats your death as sport.*

### STELLAR COMMERCE GUILD

**Affiliation Obligation.** You keep goods and your word moving, and you stay neutral in the Houses' quarrels while under Guild colors. Dues are paid, contracts are honored, and Guild arbitration is respected as binding.


| REPUTATION LEVEL | PERK GAINED | OBLIGATION IT CARRIES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+1 Recognized** | Standard market access at Guild ports; fair posted rates | Pay your dues; do not run contraband under the Guild flag |
| **+2 Respected** | Bulk discounts and priority berths; a broker's contact | Take Guild arbitration over private feud when disputes arise |
| **+3 Trusted** | Guild legal protection and a standing letter of safe conduct | Carry a Guild cargo or message through dangerous space when asked |
| **+4 Honored** | Access to closed auctions and bonded warehouses; a factor's services | Stay scrupulously neutral in any House conflict the Guild is brokering |
| **+5 Revered** | A voice in setting routes and rates on a regional board | Put the flow of trade above your own short-term gain when the two collide |
| **+6 Legendary** | You help shape Guild policy across systems | The Guild's neutrality is now partly yours to guard, and partisans on all sides will test it |

*Distrusted or below: rates turn against you and berths fill up; at Hated, the Guild blacklists you from every port that flies its pennant.*

### THE FREE FLEET

**Affiliation Obligation.** A Fleet ship in need is your ship in need. You answer distress calls from your own, you never sell a fellow captain to a House, and you defend the one thing the Fleet holds sacred: that no one out here answers to a throne.


| REPUTATION LEVEL | PERK GAINED | OBLIGATION IT CARRIES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+1 Recognized** | Fleet hospitality: a safe berth, a meal, an honest repair | Answer a Fleet distress call you can reach |
| **+2 Respected** | Free harbor at Fleet anchorages; shared charts and warnings | Share what you know of hazards and House movements |
| **+3 Trusted** | Willing Fleet ships will sail with you on a shared cause | Spend that goodwill on the Fleet's freedom, not a House's errand |
| **+4 Honored** | A standing flotilla you can rally; deep discounts among Fleet traders | Shelter a hunted Fleet crew even at cost to yourself |
| **+5 Revered** | Command of a sanctioned Fleet action; a captain's vote that carries weight | Put the Fleet's independence above your own ambitions |
| **+6 Legendary** | A seat on the Council of Captains; the Fleet moves on your word | You now embody the Fleet's freedom; serve a crown even once and you lose it all |

*Distrusted or below: anchorages turn cold and charts stop reaching you; at Hated, the Fleet names you oathbreaker, and there is no harder word out here.*

### SMALLER POWERS

The same two-part design covers the rest. For each, the Affiliation Obligation is the price of belonging, and the tiers grant benefits the faction actually controls.

- **The Explorers' Guild.** *Obligation:* file your charts and findings, and answer a fellow explorer's rescue call. *Perks climb from* shared maps and outfitting discounts, to expedition funding and salvage rights, to first access to newly opened Vaults and a vote on where the Guild looks next. *The cost:* the Guild's maps are shared maps, and what you find is expected to be found for everyone.

- **The Solara Compact.** *Obligation:* protect colonists and oppose those who would strip a fringe world bare. *Perks climb from* safe harbor and resupply in Compact settlements, to militia support and colonial contracts, to a guiding hand in fringe policy. *The cost:* the Compact remembers who showed up when a colony was burning, and who did not.

- **The Church of the Eternal Veil.** *Obligation:* show reverence in sacred places and never desecrate a Veil-site or traffic in what the Church deems profane. *Perks climb from* sanctuary and healing, to Veil-lore and blessings, to access to relics and the counsel of the devout. *The cost:* the Church's favor binds you to its doctrine, and Kurogane's transhumanists are not the only ones who find that doctrine a cage.

For any other regional power, the Keeper designs along the same lines: name the Affiliation Obligation first, then let each tier grant one or two concrete benefits the faction truly owns, each paired with what it expects in return. A perk with no obligation is not a perk; it is a plot hole. House Joric's *+3 Trusted* entry above is the pattern in miniature: the sworn squad is genuinely yours to call, and the same line that grants it tells you to spend it on defensive ends only and bring those people home. Nothing is free.

## REPUTATION AS A STORY ENGINE

Watch for the patterns this system likes to produce. **The Triangulation** (Trusted with two rivals; a choice arises). **The Burn-and-Run** (deliberately tank one faction's RP for leverage with another, then live with the fallout). **The Slow Climb** (patient build with one faction

over a long arc, culminating in a Legendary deed). **The Redemption** (a character starts negative and works toward neutrality; the question is whether redemption is even possible). **The Faction War** (the crew rises to Honored or Revered during a conflict, and their actions tip the balance).

### A WORKED EXAMPLE: VELL'S ARC

Across the first three arcs of the Tellurian Reach campaign, Vell (Bloomstrider Engineer) and the *Vagrant Star* crew take work primarily from House Joric. The math at the table looks like this: **Session 6**, a kidnapped Sentinel-Lieutenant recovered from Volkov captivity (+3 Joric, -3 Volkov). **Session 12**, a Joric border post stabilized (+2 Joric -> Respected). **Session 18**, a senior officer's daughter rescued from a Veil-touched cult (+3 Joric, total +8). **Session 24**, a Volkov incursion stopped, a legendary deed (+4 Joric, -4 Volkov). After Session 24, Vell sits at **+12 Joric (Trusted)** and **-7 Volkov (Scorned)**: a Joric Sentinel squad is callable and signature Joric arms are available - but not yet the Sentinel liaison officer, which is an Honored perk and still five RP away, *and* Volkov ports deny docking, Volkov bounty hunters appear in two later sessions, and a Volkov sabotage drives a Session 28 plot beat. Both halves of that flowed from the same actions. The crew chose, accepted the cost, and the campaign now lives with the choice. That is the system working as intended.

> **Rule Take-Away:** Read the running RP total, then find its rung - they are not the same number. Vell's **+12** with Joric is not a Level; it is twelve points sitting above the **+10** threshold, which is what makes her *Trusted*. She will feel nothing new until she reaches **+17**. Meanwhile the **-7** with Volkov is likewise not a Level: it is past **-5**, so she is *Scorned*, and the ports close accordingly.

## CREW COHESION

***At a glance.*** Beyond external Reputation and personal Affiliation Standing, the crew itself has a Cohesion score (0 to 10) for how tightly the group operates as one. Cohesion grows through shared trials and erodes through betrayal or unresolved Friction. High Cohesion produces real mechanical benefits; low Cohesion costs the crew its edge.

A working Veilfarers crew is four to six people aboard a single vessel doing dangerous work across enormous distances. Whether they actually function as a unit is not abstract; it decides whether a heist holds when one member improvises, whether a fight survives a wound, whether a campaign holds together at all. **Connections** (Chapter 8) capture specific bonds between two people; **Cohesion** captures what those bonds *add up to* at the group level.

### THE COHESION SCORE

A single number from **0 (Broken)** to **10 (Forged)**. Starting crews usually sit at **3 (Working)**: they know each other well enough to function but have not been tested as a unit.


| RANGE | STATE | WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **0** | Broken | Each member operates alone; recent betrayals or institutional pressure have fractured the unit |
| **1 to 2** | Strained | The crew functions, but with friction; cooperation is conscious and effortful |
| **3 to 4** | Working | *Default.* Most jobs go smoothly; serious tests will reveal where the bonds are weak |
| **5 to 6** | Tested | Real trials passed; mutual trust extends beyond rationality |
| **7 to 8** | Forged | A single body with multiple limbs; coordination is instinctual rather than discussed |
| **9 to 10** | Legendary | Larger than its members; new members must earn their place against what the crew has done |

### GAINS

- **+1**, completing a major job together without interpersonal conflict during the work.

- **+1**, sustained successful operations across roughly 8 to 10 sessions of steady play (Keeper's call).

- **+1**, a mutual rescue, explicitly acknowledged.

- **+1**, a shared sacrifice the whole crew chose (a turned-down job, an accepted Reputation hit, a casualty for an outsider).

- **+2**, surviving a catastrophic event together, the kind of session that becomes legend.

### LOSSES

- **-1**, a significant lie between crew members, later discovered.

- **-1**, unresolved Friction (Chapter 8) sustained across many sessions.

- **-1**, one PC acting against the explicit wishes of the rest, when it affects the crew.

- **-2**, a betrayal of a specific Bond or Debt (Chapter 8), abandoning a Bond in danger, refusing a called Debt with no compensating service.

- **-2**, a public faction split between PCs aligning against each other.

- **-3**, a PC's death by another PC's hand, justified or not; the death stays in the room.

### HIGH-COHESION BENEFITS

- **Cohesion 5+ (Tested).** Once per session any crew member may **invoke crew unity** to grant another **+1** to a single roll, in-fiction motivated (they read each other's intent and move in coordination).

- **Cohesion 7+ (Forged).** The invocation bonus becomes **+2**, and two crew members may **pool Hope or** **Effort** for a single high-stakes roll, combining their resources for the moment.

- **Cohesion 9+ (Legendary).** The crew gains a shared **2-token reserve** of Hope/Effort per session, drawn from by any member, *unusable while any member is acting against another's interest*.

### LOW-COHESION PENALTIES

- **Cohesion 2 or below (Strained).** The crew unity invocation is unavailable. Once per session, after one crew member refuses or directly contradicts another crew member's declared help, the Keeper may invoke crew Friction before the next related Roll; that Roll takes **-1**. The trigger and target are announced before dice are rolled.

- **Cohesion 0 (Broken).** Each PC operates alone for mechanical purposes: no shared invocations, no pooled spends, no shared reserve. Bonds and Debt-call benefits remain available between individuals, but anything that touches *the crew as a unit* is paused until Cohesion is rebuilt above zero.

### RECOVERING FROM LOW COHESION

Cohesion is rebuilt the same way it was lost: through play, slowly. A **deliberate arc** spent repairing it (a session in port talking through the breach, a job taken specifically to prove the crew can still operate) returns **+1**. **Resolving a Bond, Debt, or Friction** explicitly between two members returns **+1**. **Surviving a catastrophic event together while Strained or worse** can return **+2** in the way it would gain at higher Cohesion, the crew rediscovering what it is. Recovery is rarely free; the price of the breach usually has to be paid before the trust returns.

### HOW COHESION RELATES TO CONNECTIONS AND REPUTATION

**Connections** (Chapter 8) are the *individual* trust links: A and B's First Bond, C's Open Debt to D, E's Friction with F. **Cohesion** is the *group-level* property those Connections compose. Active, healthy Connections push Cohesion up; broken or unaddressed Connections drag it down. **Reputation** lives outside the crew (the galaxy's view of you); Cohesion lives inside it (the crew's view of itself). The three together draw the social map a Pearl Era story lives in.

## CLOSING: THE WEB YOU WEAVE

Reputation is the political shape of your campaign: who helps you, who hunts you, which doors open as you cross the Pearl Era. Intentional play is rewarded either way, with allies or with bounty hunters. Build your name carefully; in the silence between the stars it is the only signal that travels farther than the Temples can carry.

# CHAPTER 17: THE VOID BETWEEN HULLS

*"There is a moment, just before the first salvo lands, when both ships are still flying, both crews still alive, both captains still sure they will be alive an hour from now. The moment lasts perhaps four seconds. It is the longest four seconds in this work. Spend it well. There are not many of them."*

*Captain Vren Skykaja, Free Fleet, on his fourth confirmed kill*

***At a glance.*** Starship combat uses the same Duality Dice as personal combat with four ship-scale layers: Hull (structural integrity), Armor Slots (active defense, four arcs; the ship's shield array provides them), Heat (thermal load), and Systems (functional components). Each round the Spotlight passes around the crew by Station (Captain, Pilot, Gunner, Engineer, specialists), so one ship's "turn" is several PC actions. Range is measured in kilometers across five bands. A defeated ship is often boarded or escapes rather than destroyed, and crew death is rare even when the ship is lost. Expect five to ten of these scenes in a campaign; each is a major event.

Personal combat (Chapter 10) covers firefights in corridors and on surfaces. Starship combat covers violence at the *scale of the vessel*, where distances are kilometers and damage is measured in hulls. It runs on the same bones as personal combat, the same Duality Dice, Hope and Effort, fiction-first resolution, with three differences: the scale is bigger, the Spotlight is shared across crew positions, and a beaten ship is more often taken or fled than killed.

## THE TWO SCALES


| ASPECT | PERSONAL | STARSHIP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Range bands** | Melee to Very Far | Adjacent to Extreme |
| **Damage unit** | HP | Hull Integrity |
| **Defense** | Evasion + Armor Slots | Ship Evasion + Armor Slots |
| **Resource** | Hope / Effort | Hope / Effort + Heat |
| **Spotlight scope** | One PC | Each PC spends their own Spotlight on a station; the crew's ship is a shared scene, not one puppet. The Keeper runs each enemy ship as a single entity. |
| **Death frequency** | Rare | Ship destruction possible; PC death rare |

The scales connect through **boarding** (which drops the boarders into personal combat) and a few Domain Powers; otherwise they run in parallel, and the same character's Hope pool feeds both.

## STATIONS

A ship in combat needs roles filled. One character per station per round; on a small ship (a Tier 2 light freighter such as the *Pelican*) one PC may hold several, and on a Tier 4 frigate each needs its own person.

- **Pilot (Instinct).** Holds the helm: maneuver rolls, range and facing, evasion, emergency FTL jumps. Pilots are the natural fit; anyone can fly at Disadvantage. Rotating pilots costs an action.

- **Gunner (Finesse or Knowledge).** Works the weapons console: attack rolls, targeting locks, point defense. A ship with several batteries can have multiple gunner stations, each one Spotlight per round. Finesse for precision weapons, Knowledge for missiles and sensor-coordinated fire.

- **Engineer (Knowledge).** Manages the energy budget: Heat dissipation, in-combat repairs, power rerouting, shield arcs, recovering downed subsystems.

- **Captain (Presence).** Commands rather than operating a station: coordinates the crew, issues orders, and grants buffs through class features (a Diplomat's *Standing Reputation*, a Soldier's *Rally*). A ship can run without one. A captained ship gains a concrete benefit each round: at the start of the round the Captain marks 1 Stress to grant the crew a pool of **Command Dice** equal to their Presence modifier (minimum 1); any crew member may add one Command Die (a d6) to a station roll this round before rolling, and unspent dice are lost at end of round. This is the Captain's whole turn unless they also spend their class action.

- **Specialists.** Sensor Officer (arrays, locks, threat ID, often shared with Gunner), Comms Officer (inter-ship signal, Veil-Frequency reception, jamming, often shared with Captain), and Medical Officer (First Aid on Stressed or wounded crew).

## THE STARSHIP SHEET

**Hull Integrity** is the ship's HP. At 0 the ship is *dying*. When a rule says a ship **loses Hull directly**, mark that amount on the Hull track without applying Armor Slots or converting through the Hull severity table.


| COMMON HULL | TIER | HULL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Courier / Shuttle** | 1 | 10 |
| **Cargo Hauler / Light Freighter** | 2 | 14 |
| **Armed Transport** | 2 | 22 |
| **Corvette** | 2 | 22 |
| **Frigate / Destroyer** | 3 | 30 |
| **Heavy Cruiser** | 4 | 40 |
| **Dreadnought** | 4 | 52 |
| **Legendary Set-Piece** | 5 | Variable; never a normal target |

**Armor Slots** absorb damage before Hull; a ship's shield array provides its Armor Slots, organized in four arcs (Fore, Aft, Port, Starboard), and a hit reduces the arc it comes from. Arc Slots **regenerate 2 per arc at end of round**, up to maximum (an Engineer can add to this).


| COMMON HULL | ARMOR SLOTS PER ARC |
| --- | --- |
| **Courier** | 3 |
| **Cargo Hauler / Light Freighter** | 4 |
| **Corvette** | 6 |
| **Frigate / Destroyer** | 9 |
| **Heavy Cruiser** | 12 |
| **Dreadnought** | 13 |

**Heat** is accumulated waste energy from weapons, hard maneuvers, shields, and some class features. Idle dissipation is 1 per round with no weapons fire. Reaching the **Heat Cap** causes no penalty by itself. Systems fail only when Heat rises **above** the Cap.


| COMMON HULL | HEAT CAP |
| --- | --- |
| **Courier** | 8 |
| **Cargo Hauler / Light Freighter** | 10 |
| **Corvette** | 12 |
| **Frigate / Destroyer** | 16 |
| **Heavy Cruiser** | 18 |
| **Dreadnought** | 22 |

**Systems** are named subsystems (Primary Drive, FTL Drive, Sensor Array, Comms Array, Life Support, Weapons per mount, Cargo). Each has its own **Integrity** track, typically **3**; at 0 the system is offline until repaired. Some carry side effects when damaged (Drive damage cuts maneuver speed; Sensor damage imposes Disadvantage on Gunner attacks).

***Emergency field patch.*** Reconstructive Nanites (Chapter 13) are built for Synthetic bodies, not hulls, but in a pinch a single dose can patch one small damaged ship or vehicle system temporarily, enough to coax a flickering Sensor Array or Comms relay back for a scene. They cannot restore Hull Integrity or repair a system properly; full repairs need a yard or an Engineer's in-combat repair, and patching anything larger costs more doses than it is ever worth.

**Ship Evasion** is the passive defense DC. Base Evasion is determined by the vessel's physical scale:

| SHIP SCALE | TIER | BASE EVASION | MOUNT RATING |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Small Craft** | 1 | **16** | **MR ×1** |
| **Standard Vessel** | 2-3 | **12** | **MR ×2** |
| **Capital Vessel** | 4-5 | **8** | **MR ×3** |

Smaller vessels are harder to hit because of their size and maneuverability. Larger vessels present much easier firing solutions, but their structure supports substantially more powerful weapon mounts.

The Pilot adds **+1 Evasion per +1 Instinct modifier**, up to any class maximum; maneuvers, Drive Modes, and explicit Features may modify it further.

### MOUNT RATING

**Mount Rating (MR)** represents the physical weapon-output scale a hull can support: reactor draw, capacitors, cooling, structural bracing, recoil management, and the space required by the mounting assembly.

Mount Rating is a **ship statistic**, not a character statistic:

- Tier 1 Small Craft: **MR ×1**
- Tier 2-3 Standard Vessels: **MR ×2**
- Tier 4-5 Capital Vessels: **MR ×3**

When a naval weapon deals damage, roll its complete printed damage expression, including its printed flat modifier, then multiply that result by the firing ship's MR.

**Mount Rating is completely separate from character Proficiency.** A Gunner's personal Proficiency never changes a ship's MR unless a specific feature explicitly uses that character's Proficiency for its own effect.

### MOUNT CAPACITY BY HULL SCALE

Weapon Hardpoints still determine how many weapons a ship may install. Hull Tier also limits the physical class of weapon that those Hardpoints can support:

- **Tier 1:** Light weapons only.
- **Tier 2:** Light and Medium weapons.
- **Tier 3:** Light, Medium, and Heavy weapons.
- **Tier 4:** Light, Medium, Heavy, and Spinal weapons.
- **Tier 5:** As defined by the set-piece stat block.

A Spinal weapon additionally consumes the number of Weapon Hardpoints printed in its entry and may be installed only on a Tier 4+ hull unless a specific unique hull explicitly states otherwise.

Weapon class determines installation size and weapon profile. **Mount Rating determines the power scale at which the firing hull can operate that weapon.**

## RANGE BANDS

Five bands, all in kilometers:

- **Adjacent (0 to 100 m).** Boarding range. A weapon may fire here only when its printed range or a complete tag explicitly permits Adjacent fire; otherwise use boarding rules.

- **Engagement (100 m to 5 km).** The standard weapons band. A weapon whose printed maximum is Engagement may fire at Adjacent only when its entry says so.

- **Standard (5 to 50 km).** Mid-range. There is no hidden penalty within the band; the weapon entry and adopted hazards state every modifier.

- **Long (50 to 500 km).** A weapon may fire only if its printed range is Long or Extreme, or it has [Long-Range]. Sensor Lock is Knowledge, DC 20, and follows the complete break procedure below.

- **Extreme (500 to 5,000 km).** A weapon may fire only if its printed range is Extreme or [Long-Range] permits it. The target must carry a pending Sensor Lock, and only Guided or explicitly sensor-guided weapons can exploit that Lock. [Long-Range] attacks at Extreme have Disadvantage. Beyond 5,000 km no combat attack is possible.

A successful ordinary Pilot maneuver moves one band. A hull Feature may grant different movement. Without such a Feature, an attempted two-band maneuver is DC 20. No hull has an unstated speed penalty or bonus.

## ROUND STRUCTURE

The crew's ship has no single turn. Instead, **each crew member spends their own Spotlight** on a station action during the round, exactly as they would in personal combat; the player ship is a shared scene, not one entity the table passes around. A loose order keeps it readable (the Captain may modify it): (1) Captain's orders and any class ability, no roll unless a feature is invoked; (2) Pilot's maneuver, which sets position and Evasion for the round; (3) each Gunner station's attack; (4) Engineer's action (Heat, repair, power, shields), one major action per round; (5) specialist and class actions. Any crew member may spend their Spotlight on their **class action** (see Class Actions in Ship Combat) in place of their station's ordinary action.

The Keeper then runs the **enemy ships** the opposite way: each hostile ship is a **single entity** with one block of actions (a maneuver, its weapons, one system action), not a crew of separate spotlights. This keeps the action economy tilted toward the players, who are many hands on one hull, against an enemy that is one hull with one will. **End of round:** Armor Slots regenerate (2 per arc), Heat dissipates 1 if no weapons fired, status effects progress, range and facing update.

## MANEUVERING

The Pilot declares intent, fixes the targeted movement-facing arc, and fixes a maneuver DC before rolling: **DC 10** for one-band movement or routine positioning, **DC 15** for Flanking, an Evasive Pattern under fire, or movement through an active hazard, and **DC 20** for a two-band or set-piece maneuver not granted by the hull. Roll Instinct with printed ship modifiers. Any success completes the intent; Critical Success also grants Advantage on the next Gunner attack from the ship. Failure with Hope leaves range and facing unchanged. Failure with Fear leaves range and facing unchanged, marks 1 Heat, and makes the declared arc **Exposed** until the start of the ship's next Pilot Spotlight. Attacks against an Exposed arc have Advantage; the state does not stack. Overdrive replaces that one consequence as stated below.

**Common maneuvers.** **Close Range** (DC 10: move one band inward); **Open Range** (DC 10: move one band outward); **Evasive Pattern** (DC 10, or DC 15 while under fire: hold range and gain +2 Evasion until the next Pilot Spotlight); **Aggressive Approach** (DC 10: close one band, gain +1 on Gunner attacks, and take -1 Evasion until the next Pilot Spotlight); **Broadside** (DC 10: hold range, choose Port or Starboard, and expose that arc until the next Pilot Spotlight; every ready mount installed in that arc may be used by its Gunner, subject to ordinary Spotlight and tag limits); **Flanking** (DC 15: name one target arc before rolling; on success the next Gunner attack from this ship before the next Pilot Spotlight has Advantage and must target that arc); **Disengage** (DC 10: open one band; if this reaches Long or Extreme, contact ends unless the opponent begins a Veil pursuit or closes range on its next Pilot Spotlight); **FTL Jump** (Pearl-Drive ships only, below).

**Drive Modes** are announced at the start of each round and last until its end. **Cruise** has no modifier or Heat cost. **Combat** grants +1 Evasion and +1 on Pilot maneuver Rolls, then marks 1 Heat when announced. **Overdrive** grants +2 Evasion and +2 on Pilot maneuver Rolls, then marks 3 Heat when announced. On a Pilot maneuver Failure with Fear in Overdrive, the Primary Drive loses 1 Integrity as that Roll's single consequence instead of exposing an arc; the maneuver still fails and Fear is generated normally.

## ATTACKS

The Gunner chooses a weapon (each has a damage expression, range band, and tags), rolls **Finesse or a Knowledge Duality Roll** plus any Aim, Sensor Lock, or Captain bonus, and compares to the target's Ship Evasion. Roll the weapon's complete printed damage expression, including its flat modifier, then multiply that total by the firing ship's **Mount Rating (MR)**. Mount Rating is determined by hull scale and is not character Proficiency. Never apply personal weapon Proficiency to a naval weapon unless a specific character Feature explicitly says otherwise. Damage then hits the **targeted arc's Armor Slots first, then Hull**.

When damage reaches Hull, the threshold system (Chapter 10) applies at ship scale:


| HULL DAMAGE | HULL LOSS |
| --- | --- |
| **1 to 5** | 1 |
| **6 to 12** | 2 |
| **13 to 20** | 3 |
| **21 to 30** | 4 |
| **31+ (Overkill)** | 5, +1 per 10 over |

A **Critical Hit** uses the same split as personal combat. When a **PC** fires the weapon, double the printed damage dice, add the printed flat modifier once, then apply the firing ship's **Mount Rating**. When a **Keeper-controlled vessel** fires, maximize the printed damage dice, add the flat modifier once, then apply the firing ship's **Mount Rating**. Before every attack Roll, name its targeted arc and at most one target System; the target crew confirms that System is reachable through that arc or names one reachable alternative before dice are rolled. If that Critical Success causes Hull loss, the declared System loses 1 Integrity once. If no System was declared before the Roll, no System Integrity is lost. A noncritical hit causes no System loss unless a printed property says so.

**Damage types and naval tags.** Naval damage uses the four universal types: Physical, Energy, Void, and Neural. Kinetic is a Physical delivery tag; Plasma is an Energy delivery tag. Void damage, a Precursor origin, and the Veil-Aligned tag never bypass Armor Slots by name alone; only [Shield-Bypass], [Shield-Piercing], [Penetrating N], or another complete printed rule changes protection. Apply the exact naval-tag procedures in the Ship Weapons section below and in the Rust & Steel registry.

## SENSOR LOCK

Sensor Lock is the ordinary Action of the Sensors station, taken by a Sensor Officer or by a Gunner doubling on sensors. It costs no Stress or path resource and requires a working Sensor Array. Spend your Spotlight and name one eligible target in sensor range. **Sensor Lock can target only a vehicle, starship, or other target using vehicle- or starship-scale statistics. Creatures, characters, and other personal-scale targets cannot carry a Sensor Lock.** Make an unmodified **Knowledge Duality Roll** against its current band: **Adjacent DC 5, Engagement DC 10, Standard DC 15, Long DC 20, Extreme DC 25**. Only Guided or explicitly sensor-guided weapons can exploit an Extreme Lock.

**Success.** The target carries a Sensor Lock. The next Gunner attack against it made from the locking ship gains Advantage; the Lock is then spent. This is the Sensor Lock bonus listed under Attacks and the ship-scale counterpart of personal Aim.

A target holds one Sensor Lock at a time. Establishing a lock needs a working Sensor Array: a ship whose Sensor Array is at 0 Integrity, or jammed (as by a Scoundrel's Cut the Cord), cannot lock. A lock stacks with a Scholar's **Read the Enemy**: that reading buffs the whole crew until the Scholar's next Spotlight, while the lock is a single Gunner shot, so the two run together rather than replacing each other.

Personal tracking data, personal Guided weapons, Target Painter effects, and awareness of a personal-scale target are **not Sensor Locks** and never grant Sensor Lock's Advantage.

**Breaking a lock.** The locked ship can shed a pending lock with an evasive Pilot maneuver (Evasive Pattern, Disengage, or opening a band): it breaks automatically at Long or Extreme; at Standard the Pilot rolls **Instinct + Duality against DC 15**; at Engagement or Adjacent it holds. A lock also drops if the locking ship's own Sensor Array goes offline before the shot lands.

## SHIELDS AND HEAT

The Engineer manages the trade-offs.

**Shield operations (one action).** *Reinforce a Shield Arc*: add 2 Heat, one arc gains +2 Armor Slots this round. *Reroute Shield Energy*: move 2 Armor Slot points between arcs. *Emergency Shield Boost*: spend all current Heat to fully restore every arc for one round; all systems take 1 Integrity from the strain.

**Heat operations (one action).** *Cool Systems*: dissipate 3 Heat. *Compensate*: name a system, its Heat generation drops 1 per round for the encounter. *Vent*: dump 5 Heat instantly, but the ship is Visible for one round (enemies +2 to attacks).

**Heat builds** from weapons fire (about 1 per shot, more for energy weapons), hard maneuvers (Combat +1, Overdrive +3), Emergency Shield Boost, and some class features.

**When Heat exceeds the Cap:** trigger one overflow event as soon as an increase takes the ship from Heat at or below the Cap to Heat above it. All systems lose 1 Integrity immediately; the Pilot makes an **Instinct Roll against DC 15** or the Primary Drive loses 1 additional Integrity; and the ship is Visible (enemies +2 to attacks) for one round. Further Heat gained while already above the Cap does not retrigger overflow. Heat must first fall to the Cap or lower. Reaching the Cap itself never makes the crew Overwhelmed.

## DYING SHIPS

**Hull 1 to 2, Critically Damaged.** Venting and leaking; all ship-station Rolls have Disadvantage, and repairs may restore Systems but not Hull during combat. **Hull 0, Dying.** Emergency reserves only. The crew chooses one final ship Action before the next enemy Spotlight: Fight On, Abandon Ship, or Survive Scarred as defined in Rust & Steel. If another hit would remove Hull, resolve that chosen option immediately. Abandon Ship starts a visible four-segment Escape clock; each crew Spotlight spent reaching pods, sealing a suit, or transferring to another vessel marks 1 segment, and the ship breaks apart when it fills. Characters still aboard then take 6d10 Energy damage and use normal personal Dying, Final, stabilization, and voluntary Death Move rules. No crew member dies by narration alone.

**System damage** comes from a ship-scale Critical Success, which costs 1 Integrity from one system established as exposed by that attack; Heat overflow, which costs every system 1 Integrity; or a specific weapon effect. A system at 0 is offline. The Engineer spends a full Action and makes a **Knowledge (Tech) Roll, DC 15**: Critical Success restores full Integrity; any other success restores 1; Failure with Hope leaves it offline; Failure with Fear leaves it offline and the Engineer marks 1 Stress.

## BOARDING

The signature ship-to-ship encounter; it drops the boarding party into personal-scale combat.

**Setup.** Both ships must be at **Adjacent** range (the attacker matches velocity; the defender cannot maneuver away without breaking the boarding). An entry is made, hard-dock, atmospheric breach, or boarding tube, each taking time during which the defender can counterattack. Once across, the party is committed.

**The two-scale round.** The ships and their remaining crews run a **starship-scale** Spotlight; the boarding party runs a **personal-scale** Spotlight inside the target; the Keeper alternates between the parallel scenes.

**Resolution** ends when the party clears the ship (taken as prize, salvaged, or destroyed), is repelled (ships disengage; combat may resume), or a side surrenders (ship and survivors pass to the victor).

## VEIL-DISTURBED COMBAT

**Veil Storms (Chapter 1).** At the start of each round in a storm, roll d6 once: **1 Calm Eye**, no effect; **2 Current Shear**, each Pilot makes Instinct Reaction Roll, DC 15, and on failure the ship moves one band in the direction that worsens its declared intent; **3 Sensor Failure**, Gunner attacks have Disadvantage; **4 Substrate Surge**, each Awakened crewmember gains 1 Hope and each Sleeping crewmember marks one Effort Track segment; **5 Drive Resonance**, every ship marks 1 Heat; **6 Veil Echo**, the first attack against each ship that round has Disadvantage. The effect ends with the round.

**Near Precursor Vaults.** Rare. Some Vaults emit resonance that activates dormant ship systems, good or bad, and may *notice* the combat. Once per round, after the first player makes a nonmatching Duality Roll in the region and before resolving it, that player may reroll the Hope die and must use the new face. The reroll may create matching dice and therefore a Critical Success; it can never create a negative critical result.

**FTL in combat.** A Pearl-Drive ship attempts an emergency jump in two Spotlights. First, **Pre-Jump Calculation:** roll Knowledge, DC 10, or DC 15 while under fire. Any success establishes the declared destination. Failure with Hope establishes no solution. Failure with Fear establishes no solution and marks 1 Heat as the Roll's single consequence.
